title: chore(deps): trust-tasks 0.17.3, and retire the consent-prompt debt entry
body:
**Yes — and VTI was further behind than just the one crate.** Four of the five were two releases back:

| crate | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.17.2 | **0.17.3** |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.17.1 | **0.17.3** |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm` | 0.17.1 | **0.17.3** |
| `trust-tasks-https` | 0.17.1 | **0.17.2** |
| `trust-tasks-proof` | 0.17.1 | **0.17.2** |

**No manifest change.** Every requirement is already `"0.17"`, which admits all of these — the drift was purely a stale lockfile, the kind nothing reports until something asks.

### The guard fired, as designed

0.17.3 carries `consent/approve-request/0.1`, published upstream in [dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#331](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/331). That makes the `PRODUCED_UNPUBLISHED` entry from #1181 stale, and its shrink-only guard said so on the first run after `cargo update`:

```
these have a published spec now and must be removed from PRODUCED_UNPUBLISHED:
  https://trusttasks.org/spec/consent/approve-request/0.1
```

Publishing a spec cannot silently leave debt recorded claiming otherwise. Entry removed; the full cycle — add entry, publish spec, guard fails, remove entry — has now run end to end.

### A new obligation, and a test for it

Publishing the schema creates something that did not exist while there was none: **what we send must match what we published.**

Nothing on this side would catch a divergence. The prompt is *produced*, never served, so it never reaches the dispatcher's `validate_payload` — the party that validates it is the approver's device. A mismatch would therefore surface as a refused prompt on someone's phone, not a failing build. That is precisely the shape of both shipped payload defects this workspace has had (#895, #919): found by a person, from a rejected request in production.

So the wake test now validates the document it builds against the published schema. I confirmed it has teeth by adding a member the schema forbids and watching it fail, rather than trusting that it would.

Closes the last VTI-side item on #1177. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets` → 0; full workspace suite passes.

title: feat(consent): specify consent/approve-request/0.1 with proof REQUIRED
body:
The prompt an agent's home service pushes to a designated approver, asking a human whether the agent may act on one conversation.

It was already being sent — by OpenVTC's VTA, over DIDComm to the approver's device — with no published schema on either side and no registry page a second implementation could work from. Found by a census in that repo ([OpenVTC#1177](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/issues/1177)).

### `proofRequirement: REQUIRED` is the substance

Not a formality. The document is **rendered to a person** and asks them to authorise an agent's access to a conversation. Without a proof the only thing vouching for it is the transport, so anything that can reach the approver's inbox can pose a question in the service's name — and the approver has no way to tell.

It is also the sole carrier of the `challenge` that the answering `consent/decision` must echo. An unauthenticated prompt therefore lets an attacker choose the value the approver will sign.

The consumer requirement is stated where it bites: **verify before rendering.** A prompt that fails verification is not a prompt, and rendering it anyway moves the authentication decision onto the one participant with no means to make it.

### Three payload decisions the prose argues rather than asserts

**`conversationRef` MUST be opaque.** A consent record naming raw platform addresses is a stored directory of who the subject talks to, readable by anyone who reaches the store. `displayHint` carries the recognisable name instead — bounded at 256 chars, and explicitly untrusted text a renderer must escape, since it's chosen by the requesting party.

**`kind` is not decoration.** Consenting to an agent reading a 1:1 exposes two parties; consenting on a group exposes everyone in it, most of whom are not being asked. An approver SHOULD be shown it.

**`firstMessageDigest` is a digest, not content.** The approver is deciding whether the agent may *read* the conversation; showing them the message in order to ask would disclose the very thing the decision gates.

### Shape

Fire-and-forget — no response document. The approver answers with a separate, separately-signed `consent/decision`, which is where the decision lives. `sideEffects: none` for the same reason: nothing is granted here.

`exposure.ingests: personal` while `discloses: metadata` — the asymmetry is deliberate and the rationale says why: the prompt puts a description of the subject's communications onto a device the requesting service does not control.

### Checks

`npm run build` clean — 350 specs validated, 66 shared schemas indexed, and it passes the freshness, free-text-bounds, error-code-casing and error-code-shadowing floors. Rust and TypeScript bindings regenerated in the same commit per CONTRIBUTING-SPECS; `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features` and workspace clippy both clean. DCO-signed.

title: feat(vtc-service)!: enforce Trust Task Context Binding on presented credentials
body:
Closes #1065.

`taskContext` had zero occurrences in `vtc-service`. DTG Credentials marks it
REQUIRED on the VWC and defines Trust Task Context Binding as the mechanism that
keeps a credential from escaping the exchange that produced it. Security
Considerations 5 names what its absence permits — **context collapse**: a
credential that is genuinely signed, correctly typed, unrevoked and in date,
presented as evidence that *this* ceremony reached its terminal state when it was
issued during some other exchange entirely.

The ceremony pipeline was exposed to precisely that. It evaluates credentials as
facts and decides on them, and nothing in a fact said which exchange a credential
came from.

## What this does

Follows the division of labour `credentials::witness` (#1161) established — the
host settles what needs storage or keys, the policy branches on a settled state.

**Captured.** `VerifiedPresentation` gains `task_context`, read at verify time
from the credential's top level. It had to be captured *there* for the same
reason `credential_status` is: the DI and bbs paths keep only
`credentialSubject` in `claims`, so a `taskContext` read downstream would have
been unconditionally absent on those paths — a verifier structurally unable to
see the binding it is required to enforce.

**Enforced on receipt.** A VWC with no `taskContext` is refused, at both ingress
points: `credentials::ingress::classify_dtg` for JSON-LD arrivals (where the
catalog's own `TryFrom<DTGCommon>` puts the identical check) and the
credential-exchange present path for SD-JWT-VC / DI / bbs arrivals. Refused
rather than defaulted to the current thread — defaulting would manufacture the
binding being checked, and would award the strongest possible verdict to the
credential least entitled to it.

**Asserted in the evidence.** `Context.thread_id` names the exchange the ceremony
*is*; `Credential.task_context` names where each credential came from, as a
resolved `TaskContextBinding` (`sameExchange` / `foreignExchange` / `absent` /
`unthreaded`). A policy asserting an outcome can now require `sameExchange`.
Without the pair, "a credential from another exchange" is not expressible at all.

The end-to-end tests are the argument: the *same* well-formed, signed, in-date
witness admits or is rejected under one policy depending only on the exchange its
`taskContext` names.

## Decisions a reviewer should check

1. **A mismatch is reported, not refused.** A VWC's `taskContext` names the
   exchange the *witnessing* happened in — never the join exchange it is later
   presented in — so rejecting on mismatch would refuse every honest witness. The
   specification draws the same line: a verifier "MUST NOT interpret a
   `taskContext`-bearing credential as proof that the associated trust task
   completed unless the matching trust task outcome evidence is also present and
   verified". So absence (a malformed VWC) is an error; a foreign exchange is a
   fact the policy weighs.
2. **No shipped policy was tightened.** For the reason above: the default join
   and personhood policies read a VWC as background evidence of personhood, not
   as terminal-state evidence, and requiring `sameExchange` there would deny every
   legitimate witness.
3. **Thread ids are compared verbatim.** DTG Credentials specifies no
   canonicalization for `taskContext`, so there is no sanctioned way to decide
   that `urn:uuid:x` and `x` are one thread. Guessing fails open (a foreign
   credential accepted as local); comparing verbatim fails the other way. Pinned
   by a test so a later normalization has to be a deliberate change.
4. **Facts keys stay `snake_case`.** `context.thread_id` and
   `task_context.thread_id` follow the Rego facts contract (`facts.rs` documents
   `snake_case` keys as load-bearing — compiled policies read the literals), and
   match `witness_binding.relationship_id` beside them. The camelCase in this
   feature is `taskContext`, read *off the credential*, where the DTG spec
   dictates it.
5. **`presentation_from_verified_set` became fallible**, and refuses the whole
   presentation rather than dropping the offending credential — silently
   discarding one turns a malformed submission into a decision taken on less
   evidence than the holder believes it supplied.

## Deliberately not included

**Issuance (the issue's part 1).** Nothing in this workspace mints a VWC —
`dtg_credentials::DTGCredential::new_vwc` has no caller anywhere in VTI — so there
is no issuance flow to carry `taskContext` through, and adding one would be
inventing a feature rather than closing this gap. The catalog constructor already
takes `task_context: String` as a required parameter, so the first issuance path
cannot omit it. `taskContext` is OPTIONAL on every other DTG type, so it was not
added to the VMC / VEC / VIC the VTC does mint — that would change the wire shape
of every credential this service issues for no requirement, and the spec's own
note warns against reading such a credential as proof a task completed.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --all`
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets` — 0 warnings
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --all-features` — pass
- `cargo test -p vta-service --all-features` — pass (rebased onto #1176)

Rebased on current `main` (`42cb978f`). The `semver report` check going red is
expected — no version was edited.

title: fix(inbound): validate the last two payloads still read by hand
body:
`parseTaskConsentRequest` was validated against its published schema in #128;
these are the two paths that were left.

**`parseRemovalNotice`** transcribed the `code` and `disposition` enums as
literals. That is correct only until the registry adds a value, at which point a
legitimate notice is dropped in silence and a member is not told they were
removed from a community. The schema is the copy that cannot fall behind
itself, and it enforces two things the hand version had no way to:
`additionalProperties: false`, and the bound on `reason` — the prose this
surface renders as the member's only account of why.

**The `decision/0.1#response` branch of `parseTaskConsentOutcome`** read
`status` as any string where the schema says `granted | pending | denied`, and
let a REQUIRED `payloadDigest` be silently absent. This is *not* the fail-open
the request path had — nothing branches on `status`, it is logged — so it is
validated for a narrower reason: "the executor said granted" should stay a claim
worth trusting when something eventually does branch on it.

**The `trust-task-error` branch is deliberately left unvalidated**, and says so.
It carries the executor refusing an approval a human already gave, and the one
thing that must not happen is failing to tell them. Rejecting a malformed error
document would drop that notification because the *refusal* was malformed —
strictly worse than reporting one whose members are read defensively, as they
are, member by member.

Validating found the same fixture drift a third time: `payloadDigest: "abc123"`
in five places, where the schema requires a `DigestMultibase`. The hand-read
accepted it every time. That is now three separate test files that had been
carrying non-conforming digests since the multibase cutover, each found by
turning a schema on rather than by anybody reading them.

Also documents the `tsc -b` trap that cost two wrong turns during the 0.5.0
release: `rm -rf packages/core/dist` leaves the `.tsbuildinfo`, so the next
build believes the output is current, prints nothing, exits 0 and emits no
files. Every dependent workspace then fails with "cannot find module", which
reads like a broken package. It is the nastier sibling of the stale-`dist` note
already in CLAUDE.md — there the build tells you something is wrong; here it
reports success.

title: test(vta): census the URIs this service produces, not just the ones it serves (#1181)
body:
test(vta): census the URIs this service produces, not just the ones it serves (#1181)

Three harnesses already police the task surface and a document can slip
between all three. `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` is per-URI and shrink-only
but tracks what the dispatcher **serves**. `producer_payload_conformance`
drives client methods, so it only sees payloads reached through a
`VtaClient` method. The VTC's manifest census scans source, but its prefix
is `https://trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/` — the VTC's private namespace — so
a public `spec/` URI never matches it wherever it runs.

`consent/approve-request/0.1` fell through all three, which is why it
shipped unsigned for as long as it did: **serving** an unspecced URI fails
the build, while **producing** one was invisible.

Every `spec/` literal under `vta-service/src` must now be published, served
(where the other harness owns the debt), or listed with a reason. Shrink-only
in both directions, matching the served-side list: a new entry fails rather
than being a line someone adds, and an entry whose spec has landed fails too.

It found two on the day it was written. `vta/attestation/{status,report}/1.0`
are REST-routed rather than dispatched, so the served-URI harness never saw
them — and `status` is unauthenticated and internet-reachable, the thing a
verifier checks before deciding to trust this VTA at all. Both recorded
against #1177.

Three literals are deliberately not counted, each stated rather than
silently skipped: `format!` templates carrying `{version}`, prefix constants
ending in `/`, and the `trust-task-error/*` family — which *is* in the
registry, but `schema_index` carries payload schemas for tasks, so
`schema_for` answers `None` and using that as the published-check would
report a published document as debt.

Negative fixtures are an explicit list, not a heuristic. Inferring "is this
inside a test module" from source text would be wrong occasionally and
silently, and this only works if a failure means something.

Both guards verified by mutation rather than assumed: renaming the produced
consent URI makes the census fail, and adding an already-published URI to
the tracked list makes the shrink guard fail.

Refs #1177.

title: fix(consent)!: sign the approve-request prompt sent to an approver's device (#1180)
body:
fix(consent)!: sign the approve-request prompt sent to an approver's device (#1180)

`consent/approve-request/0.1` was constructed as a bare `id` / `type` /
`issuedAt` / `payload` document and buffered to an approver's mediator for
delivery to their phone, where a human is asked to approve something. It
carried no proof, so nothing the device could check authenticated it.

This is the odd one out rather than a deliberate exception. The sibling
task-consent request in `consent_request.rs` already signs with this key and
cryptosuite, and the step-up prompt's mobile parser refuses to render
without a verified proof from an enrolled issuer
(`vta-mobile-core::task::parse_step_up_request` — "no valid proof from an
enrolled executor, no prompt"). Both end up in front of a person.

`issuer` and `recipient` come with the proof, not as decoration: SPEC §7.2
item 5b makes `recipient` REQUIRED and item 6 requires the in-band issuer to
match the transport identity. A proof over a document naming neither party
is replayable at a different approver, which is most of what the signature
was supposed to buy.

Fails closed. The wake path is best-effort and already warns on a failed
buffer, leaving the approver to mediator pickup; an unsignable prompt takes
the same route. "No prompt" is recoverable in a way "unverifiable prompt"
is not.

## Sequencing

This changes nothing about security on its own, because nothing verifies it
yet, and that is the reason to land it now rather than later: the fleet has
to be signing before devices can require a signature. Device-side
enforcement in `vta-mobile-core` follows, and must not ship first or it
breaks every VTA that has not deployed this.

Publishing the spec with `proof` REQUIRED is the third step, so the
requirement is normative rather than local convention. Tracked in #1177.

The test runs the real verifier over the document as sent rather than
asserting a `proof` member exists — a signature copied from another document
would satisfy the weaker check — and pins `issuer` and `recipient`.
Confirmed it has teeth by swapping the recipient DID and watching it fail.

Refs #1177.

title: feat(vtc): state artifact lifecycle precedence once, and apply it on read
body:
Closes #1079.

#1075 fixed an instance: an expired VRC became a permanent edge because
`routes/relationships.rs` read neither `validFrom` nor `validUntil`. It did not
fix the class. Nothing in the workspace established **precedence between a
cryptographically valid but stale artifact and a later lifecycle event**, and
the relationship graph had no vocabulary beyond "the row exists" and "the row
was deleted".

## The rule, stated once

`vtc-service/src/credentials/lifecycle.rs` is new and owns the vocabulary and
the precedence rule:

> A later recorded event takes precedence over the artifact's own earlier
> assertion, but only in the restrictive direction. An event can put an
> artifact out of force at any time; **no event can put an artifact into force
> that its own window excludes.**

Two clocks, kept separate:

- **validity time** — the window the issuer stated inside the artifact, fixed
  at issuance and covered by its signature (`ValidityWindow`).
- **transaction time** — what this service recorded about it afterwards
  (`LifecycleLog`, append-only and monotonic).

`resolve` combines them, and ignores events recorded *after* the instant being
asked about. That is what makes "was this in force last Tuesday" answerable at
all: without it, a suspension recorded today would retroactively make
yesterday's decision look wrong and the audit trail could not be reconciled
against the decisions it records.

**The asymmetry is the design.** Precedence exists so a community can end an
artifact's effect without waiting for its window and without a status list —
which is exactly why it matters here, since a VRC deliberately carries no
`credentialStatus` (D7). Running it the other way would let a recorded event
manufacture validity the issuer never signed for, a far worse failure than an
edge that lingers. So `Restored` returns an artifact to the governance of its
own window rather than extending it: restoring an edge that expired while
suspended succeeds and still reports `expired`.

**Restoration versus replacement is explicit.** `Restored` reverses a
suspension and nothing else. `Withdrawn` and `Superseded` are terminal — the
party relying on an artifact between a withdrawal and its reversal was entitled
to treat it as gone, and a log that can take a terminal state back cannot
answer the question it exists to answer. Effect is given back by issuing a
fresh artifact: a new signature, a new window, and a record that a *new*
assertion was made rather than an old one quietly resumed.

The module also states what a verifier elsewhere may conclude when current
state is deliberately undiscoverable (issue point 5): only that the artifact
was validly issued and is inside its window — never that it is in force, since
it cannot see whether a later event displaced it.

## Applied to relationships

- `Relationship` carries an append-only `lifecycle` log —
  `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = ...)]`, the same treatment `persona`
  got in #1067, so pre-existing rows decode and re-serialise unchanged.
- `Relationship::in_force_at` is the single resolution entry point. An
  unreadable window resolves to `Indeterminate` rather than defaulting to
  unbounded — rows written before #1075 entered the graph without their window
  ever being parsed, and treating an unreadable bound as "no bound stated" is
  the failure mode that makes the whole check ornamental.
- **`GET /v1/relationships/graph` now calls an edge `complete` only when an
  *in-force* VRC exists in both directions.** This is the direct fix for the
  symptom the issue names: a half-edge whose reciprocal had expired was
  indistinguishable from one that never arrived. Halves are still listed
  whatever their state — the credential was published, and hiding it would make
  a lapsed edge look like one that never existed.
- **`POST /v1/relationships/{id}/suspend` and `/restore`**, authorized by the
  same three routes revocation uses (issuer session DID, admin, or a `pop`
  proving control of a pairwise issuer), with distinct authorization `type`s so
  a suspend signature cannot be replayed to delete. That gate is now one
  function rather than a copy per verb — three copies of a three-branch
  authorization check is how the window check ended up implemented three ways
  and enforced on one path.
- **Supersession on republish.** Publishing a VRC to a counterparty the issuer
  already has an edge to records the displacement on the earlier row. An
  idempotent republish (same digest) returns early and displaces nothing.

`credentials::ingress` gains `validity_window`, sharing its reader with
`check_validity_window`, so admission and interpretation cannot disagree about
where a window's edges are. New audit variants `VrcSuspended` / `VrcRestored` /
`VrcSuperseded`; supersession is recorded under the *displaced* edge, not
folded into the publish entry for the credential that replaced it.

## Decisions a reviewer should check

**1. Automatic supersession on `(issuer, subject)`.** The judgement call in
this PR. DTG Credentials requires an R-DID to be unique per counterparty, so
the pair identifies the relationship and a second VRC for it is a new *version*
of one assertion rather than a second relationship. Before this both rows
accumulated and nothing said which one the issuer currently stood behind. If
the intended reading is that a member may hold several concurrent edges to one
counterparty (different endorsement types, say), this is wrong and supersession
should require the new credential to name the one it replaces — which DTG has
no field for today.

**2. `complete` changed meaning without the graph response saying why.**
`relationships/graph/0.2` pins the response with `additionalProperties: false`,
so a per-half `state` cannot be added here. An operator sees that a pair
stopped being complete but not which half lapsed and how. Fixing that needs a
`graph/0.3` upstream; the spec moves first.

**3. Same spec lag on the list route.** `Relationship` is both the stored row
and the item shape of `relationships/list/0.2`, whose schema predates
`lifecycle` — as it already predates `persona`. A listed edge with a lifecycle
event carries a member the published task does not describe. Recorded in the
field's doc comment rather than papered over by dropping it on the way out:
hiding the log from the one surface a member can read would leave them able to
be suspended and unable to see it.

**4. New routes carry no Trust-Task binding.** No canonical
`spec/vtc/relationships/{suspend,restore}` URI is published, and
`every_bound_canonical_task_exists_in_the_registry` requires a bound URI to
resolve in `schema_index`. Binding a URI that does not exist would trade a real
gate for a string, so these mount plain, the same exemption the `schemas`
routes carry, with a comment saying so.

## What this deliberately leaves

- **VPC, VMC and the recognition/VIC paths are untouched.** The types take a
  window and a log rather than a `Relationship`, so any of them can be brought
  under the same rule without a second precedence implementation appearing —
  but doing so is a change to each of those surfaces and belongs with them. The
  VIC and recognition paths in particular carry semantics the shared check does
  not (they *require* `validUntil`, and recognition clamps a minted session TTL
  to the earliest one), which is why #1075 left them alone and this does too.
- **`DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}` still deletes the row** rather than
  recording a `Withdrawn` tombstone. The vocabulary has the verb and the
  storage layer would take it; retaining a durable record that a pairwise edge
  once existed and was withdrawn is a privacy decision, not a refactor, and it
  is the same decision that removed `credentialStatus` from the VRC. Same
  reasoning for the VPC detach path the issue mentions.
- **Approval freshness after an authority change** (the last bullet of "what is
  missing") is not addressed. Re-evaluating an approval against a credential
  whose authority has since changed is `policy_gate`'s territory and needs the
  approval side to record what it relied on, which nothing does yet.

## Tests

`credentials::lifecycle` unit tests pin the rule directly: a later event beats
a still-valid artifact; no event puts one back inside a closed window; an event
does not apply before it was recorded; every terminal and transition boundary.
`routes::relationships` pins the graph read against expiry, suspension,
restoration, supersession and an unreadable window. `relationships::storage`
pins persistence, refusal-writes-nothing, and that supersession skips an
already-terminal row rather than failing an unrelated publish. Integration
tests exercise suspend/restore end to end through the HTTP surface, including
the 403/404/409 paths and the audit entries, plus supersession on the real
pairwise publish path.

title: Cross-artifact lifecycle precedence: suspension, supersession, restoration
body:
## Summary

#1075 fixed an instance: an expired VRC became a permanent edge because the
relationship route read neither `validFrom` nor `validUntil`. It did not fix the
class. Nothing in this workspace establishes **precedence between a
cryptographically valid but stale artifact and a later lifecycle event**, and
several credential types have no lifecycle vocabulary at all beyond "exists" and
"deleted".

Filing the general problem so the instance fix does not stand in for it.

## Why the instance was reachable

Two defensible decisions composed into an unreachable state:

1. The relationship graph is read **without re-checking dates**. Reasonable on
   its own — the edge was validated at ingress.
2. A VRC carries **no `credentialStatus`**, per planning-review D7. Also
   reasonable, and deliberately so: a status-list host learns which verifier
   checked which credential and when, which is the correlation the pairwise work
   exists to remove.

Neither is wrong. Together they leave `DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}` as the only
removal path, so a valid-forever artifact has no lifecycle at all.

**The deliberate absence of revocation is what makes precedence load-bearing.**
Where a credential type omits status for privacy reasons — which we think is
usually the right call — precedence and effective-time rules become the only
remaining lifecycle mechanism, not a refinement on top of revocation.

## What is missing

No shared vocabulary or precedence rule for:

- **suspension** — temporarily ineffective, not withdrawn
- **supersession** — a later artifact displacing an earlier one
- **restoration** — and its boundary against replacement or fresh grant
- **effective time and event precedence** across composed artifacts
- **transaction-time state discovery**, including what a verifier does when
  discovery is deliberately unavailable because the presentation must carry what
  it needs
- **approval freshness after an authority change** — we re-evaluate approver-set
  membership at execution (`policy_gate.rs`), but nothing re-evaluates an
  approval against a *credential* whose authority has since changed

## Where it already bites

- **VRC** — no status, no suspension; #1075 gated ingress only, and the VIC and
  recognition paths deliberately keep their own window semantics rather than
  sharing the gate. Three paths, three answers.
- **Relationship graph** — since #1073 an edge is complete or half-complete, but
  neither state has a notion of *suspended*. A half-edge whose reciprocal has
  expired is indistinguishable from one that never arrived.
- **VPC** (#1074) — a persona annotation has no lifecycle of its own. Detaching
  is the only reversal, and there is no record that a correlation once existed
  and was withdrawn.
- **VDC**, when it lands — this is where it gets expensive. A delegation that can
  be suspended and restored is the whole point of a bounded appointment, and the
  design note already commits us to freshness-by-re-issuance rather than live
  lookup, which puts the entire weight on precedence rules we have not written.

## Proposed shape

1. A common lifecycle vocabulary across credential types, rather than per-type
   ad-hoc handling.
2. Effective-time and precedence rules for composed artifacts — which state
   controls at decision time when two valid artifacts disagree.
3. One transaction-time evaluation gate that every ingress path calls, extending
   `credentials::ingress` where #1075 put the window check, with any deviation
   documented at the call site rather than implied.
4. Explicit restoration-versus-replacement semantics.
5. A statement of what a verifier may conclude when authoritative current state
   is deliberately undiscoverable.

## Provenance

The instance is ours (#1075, conformance-review finding F9). The generalisation
is external: it matches RAHP finding **F-003** in
`sankarshanmukhopadhyay/rahp-toolkit#66`, which arrived at the same residual from
a guardianship/fiduciary pressure test rather than from our code. Evidence from
our instance is posted there.

Note the numbering collision: RAHP's **F-003** and our conformance review's
**F3** are unrelated. This issue is the general form of our **F9**.

title: Trust Task Context Binding is not implemented
body:
## Summary

`taskContext` does not appear anywhere in `vtc-service` or `vta-sdk` — zero
occurrences. DTG Credentials marks it REQUIRED for the VWC and defines Trust
Task Context Binding as the mechanism preventing a credential from escaping the
exchange that produced it.

## Detail

From the specification:

- §Trust Task Context Binding: "For credential types where this specification
  marks `taskContext` as REQUIRED (currently only the VWC), issuers MUST
  include it."
- Security Considerations 5, **context collapse**: "A credential presented
  outside the trust task exchange in which it was issued may be misinterpreted
  as evidence of a completed ceremony. The requirements of Trust Task Context
  Binding exist to prevent this class of attack and must be enforced by
  verifiers."

This stack has a full ceremony engine (`ceremony/{facts,verify,evaluate}.rs`)
that evaluates credentials as facts and decides on them — and no binding
between a credential and the exchange it came from.

## Why it matters

The named attack is exactly the one the ceremony pipeline is exposed to: a
credential that is cryptographically valid, correctly typed, and issued during
some *other* exchange, presented as evidence that *this* ceremony reached its
terminal state.

## Suggested fix

1. Carry `taskContext.threadId` through issuance for the credential types the
   specification requires it on.
2. Require it on receipt where required, and reject its absence rather than
   defaulting.
3. Make ceremony evidence assert the thread it belongs to, so a credential from
   another exchange cannot satisfy a fact in this one.

Worth scoping against the planned DTG Core Trust Task Protocols specification —
some of the surface may be settled there first, and
trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#11 tracks the normative dependency on that
unpublished model.

Conformance audit finding **F3**.

title: feat(vtc-service)!: enforce Trust Task Context Binding on presented credentials (#1178)
body:
feat(vtc-service)!: enforce Trust Task Context Binding on presented credentials (#1178)

`taskContext` had zero occurrences in `vtc-service`. DTG Credentials marks it
REQUIRED on the VWC and defines Trust Task Context Binding as the mechanism
that keeps a credential from escaping the exchange that produced it; Security
Considerations 5 names what its absence permits — **context collapse**, where a
credential that is genuinely signed, correctly typed, unrevoked and in date is
presented as evidence that *this* ceremony reached its terminal state, when it
was issued during some other exchange entirely.

The ceremony pipeline was exposed to exactly that: it evaluates credentials as
facts and decides on them, and nothing in a fact said which exchange a
credential came from.

Three parts, following the division of labour `credentials::witness` (#1161)
established — the host settles what needs storage or keys, the policy branches
on a settled state:

- **Captured.** `VerifiedPresentation` gains `task_context`, read at verify
  time from the credential's top level. It had to be captured there for the
  same reason `credential_status` is: the DI and bbs paths keep only
  `credentialSubject` in `claims`, so a `taskContext` read downstream would
  have been unconditionally absent on those paths — a verifier structurally
  unable to see the binding it is required to enforce.

- **Enforced on receipt.** A VWC with no `taskContext` is refused, at both
  ingress points: `credentials::ingress::classify_dtg` for JSON-LD arrivals
  (where the catalog's own `TryFrom` puts the same check) and the
  credential-exchange present path for SD-JWT-VC / DI / bbs arrivals. Refused
  rather than defaulted to the current thread — defaulting would manufacture
  the binding being checked, and would award the strongest verdict to the
  credential least entitled to it.

- **Asserted in the evidence.** `Context.thread_id` names the exchange the
  ceremony *is*; `Credential.task_context` names where each credential came
  from, as a resolved `TaskContextBinding`. A policy asserting an outcome can
  now require `sameExchange`; without the pair, "a credential from another
  exchange" is not expressible.

A mismatch is reported, not refused. A VWC's `taskContext` names the exchange
the *witnessing* happened in, which is never the join exchange it is later
presented in, so rejecting on mismatch would refuse every honest witness. The
specification's own note draws that line: a verifier must not read a
`taskContext`-bearing credential as proof the associated task completed without
the matching outcome evidence. Thread ids are compared verbatim; there is no
specified canonicalization, and inventing one would fail open.

Not included: issuance. Nothing in this workspace mints a VWC — `new_vwc` has
no caller — so there is no issuance flow to carry `taskContext` through. The
catalog constructor already takes it as a required parameter, so the first
issuance path cannot omit it.

Refs #1065

title: fix(inbound): enforce the published schema on a consent payload
body:
A `sideEffects` value the schema forbids rendered to the human as the *safest*
thing the consent surface can draw.

`parseTaskConsentRequest` checked the payload with a hand-written block of
`typeof` tests. Those are not a cheap version of the schema — they ask weaker
questions, and in one place the difference reached a human.
`typeof payload.sideEffects !== "string"` admits any string; the schema admits
`none`, `mutating` or `destructive`. `confirm.tsx` renders severity by
comparing against those three:

    background: destructive ? danger : sideEffects === "mutating" ? warn : ok

so anything outside the enum — a typo, a re-cased value, a value from a peer
that disagrees about the contract — fell through to the `ok` branch and was
painted green, with the unrecognised string as its label. The most dangerous
outcome a schema violation can produce was presented as the most reassuring.

The same gap ran through the rest of the payload: `minApprovals` was checked as
a `number` where the schema says integer >= 1, so `0` passed and a surface would
have shown a threshold nothing has to meet; `effects` was `Array.isArray` with
no element shape; `exposure` was any object at all; `note` — bounded to 500 by
framework 0.5 §7.3 item 19 *precisely* so a consent surface is not handed
unbounded prose — was not checked; and `additionalProperties: false` went
unenforced, so a member the schema forbids arrived silently.

Validating the published schema also found a live drift it was not looking for:
the fixtures for this family still carried the *hex* form of the shared
cross-repo digest, long after the multibase cutover. `typeof === "string"` had
accepted it every time; the schema's `DigestMultibase` pattern did not.

**Why a real validator rather than a subset of one.** Surveying the 349 payload
schemas this package ships finds `$ref` 2583 times, `oneOf` 141,
`propertyNames` 669, `pattern` 1036, `format` 944, plus `not`, `uniqueItems`,
`dependentRequired` and `minProperties`. A partial implementation of that
under-enforces silently, which is worse than not validating — it reports success
it did not establish. `@cfworker/json-schema` is a complete 2020-12
implementation with no dependencies of its own, and this is the keyword set that
makes `unevaluatedProperties` enforceable at all: no generated *type*, in either
language, can express it (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#327 fixes the Rust
side of that, and has no TypeScript counterpart to fix because TS types are
structural and never rejected an unknown member at runtime).

`@openvtc/trust-tasks` deliberately ships no validator — zero runtime deps so it
loads anywhere — and defines the consumer seam instead. `trust-tasks/validate.ts`
fills it, compiles each schema once against a `WeakMap` keyed by the schema
object (the inbound path revalidates on every mediator redelivery after a worker
respawn), and reports every violation rather than the first. `validatePayload`
on `ParseTaskConsentOptions` lets a caller substitute a different validator;
there is deliberately no way to switch validation off, and an unusable schema
refuses rather than passes.

Cost: `offscreen` 167 -> 206 kB (45 -> 58 kB gzipped). `background.js` is
unchanged at 48 kB — the consent path is not in the service worker, so the MV3
single-bundle invariant is untouched.

---

**Stacked on #127** — it needs `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.16.0 for the embedded `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA`. Review this one's diff alone; merge #127 first and the base retargets to `main`.

title: chore(deps): trust-tasks-rs 0.17.2, and drop the permissive-type waiver
body:
0.17.2 carries the codegen fix from [dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#327](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/327): a schema that closes a *composed* object with `unevaluatedProperties: false` — the only way a composition can be closed — now generates `deny_unknown_fields`, where before only `additionalProperties: false` did.

That was the whole reason #1159 had to record `vta/credentials/issue/0.2` in `PERMISSIVE_GENERATED_TYPE` and skip the drifted-witness check for it. The schema was always strict, so **the wire was never affected**; what was missing was the type-level guard, and its absence made that witness pass vacuously.

With the fix in, the entry comes out and the check is unconditional again.

**No manifest change** — `trust-tasks-rs = "0.17"` already admits 0.17.2, so this is a lockfile move only.

I verified the strictness actually landed rather than assuming it: the generated `issue/v0_2.rs` in 0.17.2 carries `deny_unknown_fields`, and the conformance sweep passes with nothing waived. `cargo clippy -p vta-service --all-features --all-targets` → 0.

This is the last thing standing between #1119 and shipping with the check armed.

title: feat(core): adopt Trust Tasks 0.16.0, and close the specced-family gap
body:
Brings the repo onto `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.16.0 — which is the content the
Rust side calls 0.17.0; the two packages version their own APIs, not `SPEC.md`,
so there is no TypeScript 0.17 to wait for.

The bump itself needed no source change. What it surfaced did.

**SPEC §7.2 item 11 was not implemented.** `inbound/dedup.ts` recorded bare ids
and answered "seen / not seen", which cannot express the half of item 11 that
matters: a *different* document under a used `id` MUST be refused as
`idConflict`, not absorbed. It also keyed on the DIDComm message id — the
transport identifier §7.2 names explicitly as one that MUST NOT substitute for
the document `id`, and the one a mediator is free to change on redelivery.
`claimInboundDocument` now returns fresh/duplicate/conflict, keyed on the
document's own id plus a digest of its RFC 8785 canonicalization, so a
re-serializing intermediary cannot turn a §8.4 retry into a conflict. Durable
via KVStore, because MV3 tears the worker down mid-decision.

`idConflict` was also landing in `e.p.msg.bad_request` on the send path: it
postdates `coerceTrustTaskCode`'s switch, and is why the framework runtimes emit
`trust-task-error/0.5` — 0.3's enum cannot carry it. The standard/extended split
now comes from the runtime's `normalizeCode`/`isStandardCode` rather than a
local regex that also rewrote extended codes containing `_`.

**Coverage 130 -> 152 of 177.** Every family that is specced, published as a
binding, and named by `vta-sdk` is now implemented: `trust-task-discovery/0.1`,
`acl/update`, `vta/webvh/servers/retire-orphan`, `vtc/members/removal-notice`
(a parser — the wallet receives it), `vta/app-state/*` (6, new module),
`vta/services/*` (8), `vta/credentials/{issue,revoke}`, and
`auth/passkey/login/{start,finish}/0.2`. All 25 outstanding are unspecced, so
the number now moves when upstream lands a spec rather than when someone here
finds time.

**Versions.** `vtc/join-requests/submit` 0.1 -> 0.2 (a four-outcome `verdict`
replaces `status: "pending"`, so applicants who had been *admitted* were being
reported as pending); `vault/{list,get,upsert}` and `provision/integration` to
0.3 and `device/wipe` to 0.2 once VTI landed them; `vta/credentials/issue` to
0.2, which VTI shipped as a removal rather than a deprecation. No bare-hex wire
digest remains.

**Hand-copied wire types replaced by the generated ones** in `vta/protocol.ts`,
`vault/list.ts` and `provision/send.ts`. Each copy had drifted: `transports` was
typed required when the schema says optional (and used a DOM type in the
transport-free layer), the vault entry was written from `_shared/0.1` while the
module posted 0.2 and had lost the non-empty `targets` constraint, and
`keys/create` was missing `keyId` — the field `vta-sdk` 0.30.0 was cut for, and
not optional in practice for an `internal` key, which has no derivation path to
be named after.

**Compatibility folds removed.** Nothing is deployed — no Web Store release, no
consumers — so the trust-tasks #279 dual-accept and a legacy inbound-dedup
record were dead code that read like live constraints. VTI emits only the
current spelling; verified before deleting. Recorded as a rule in CLAUDE.md so
it is not reintroduced.

CI's admin-isolation check now names the two new `admin/` modules, and the
task-surface snapshot is refreshed to vta-sdk 0.30.0.

title: ci(rust): give codegen-drift its own workflow, so it can be required
body:
The Rust half of the follow-up #329 named. That PR dropped `ts.yml`'s `paths:`
filter so the TypeScript bindings guards could be made required — a
path-filtered job cannot be a required check, because on a PR touching none of
the listed paths it never runs, reports no status, and a required check then
blocks forever waiting for a result that will never arrive.

`codegen-drift` has the identical constraint and is the mirror guard: it is what
stops a spec edit merging with a stale `trust-tasks-rs/src`, the way
`build-ts-bindings drift` does for the TypeScript side. But the same fix was not
available, because `rust.yml` also runs clippy, the full workspace test suite,
`cargo package` and `cargo deny`. Dropping that filter would have bought one
guard's availability with several minutes of latency on every documentation
edit.

So the one cheap job moves to a workflow of its own with no filter. It runs
~33s and the Rust cache carries across PRs, which is a price worth paying on
every PR; the expensive jobs stay filtered exactly as they were.

The job body is unchanged and so is its `name:`, so the check context
`trust-tasks-codegen drift` is the same string a protection rule would name —
this can be added to the required set without renaming anything.

Both files parse; `rust.yml` keeps its other six jobs.

title: fix(inbound): validate the last two payloads still read by hand (#130)
body:
fix(inbound): validate the last two payloads still read by hand (#130)

`parseTaskConsentRequest` was validated against its published schema in #128;
these are the two paths that were left.

**`parseRemovalNotice`** transcribed the `code` and `disposition` enums as
literals. That is correct only until the registry adds a value, at which point a
legitimate notice is dropped in silence and a member is not told they were
removed from a community. The schema is the copy that cannot fall behind
itself, and it enforces two things the hand version had no way to:
`additionalProperties: false`, and the bound on `reason` — the prose this
surface renders as the member's only account of why.

**The `decision/0.1#response` branch of `parseTaskConsentOutcome`** read
`status` as any string where the schema says `granted | pending | denied`, and
let a REQUIRED `payloadDigest` be silently absent. This is *not* the fail-open
the request path had — nothing branches on `status`, it is logged — so it is
validated for a narrower reason: "the executor said granted" should stay a claim
worth trusting when something eventually does branch on it.

**The `trust-task-error` branch is deliberately left unvalidated**, and says so.
It carries the executor refusing an approval a human already gave, and the one
thing that must not happen is failing to tell them. Rejecting a malformed error
document would drop that notification because the *refusal* was malformed —
strictly worse than reporting one whose members are read defensively, as they
are, member by member.

Validating found the same fixture drift a third time: `payloadDigest: "abc123"`
in five places, where the schema requires a `DigestMultibase`. The hand-read
accepted it every time. That is now three separate test files that had been
carrying non-conforming digests since the multibase cutover, each found by
turning a schema on rather than by anybody reading them.

Also documents the `tsc -b` trap that cost two wrong turns during the 0.5.0
release: `rm -rf packages/core/dist` leaves the `.tsbuildinfo`, so the next
build believes the output is current, prints nothing, exits 0 and emits no
files. Every dependent workspace then fails with "cannot find module", which
reads like a broken package. It is the nastier sibling of the stale-`dist` note
already in CLAUDE.md — there the build tells you something is wrong; here it
reports success.

title: ci(ts): let the bindings guards report on every PR, so they can be required
body:
`provision/integration/0.3` shipped in `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.16.0 with a
schema that could never validate: `$defs/Response` required a `digest` its
`properties` no longer defined, the object being closed. A consumer that
validated a conforming response would have rejected it.

The guards caught it. On #324 both `build-ts-bindings drift` and
`bindings match specs` reported **fail**, correctly, before the merge — the
board is still there. It merged anyway, because `main` has no branch protection
and so no check is required. #326 then fixed the TypeScript half a release
later, and 0.16.0 stands as a published version where `trust-tasks-rs` and
`trust-tasks-ts` disagree about the wire contract.

Turning those two checks into required ones is the fix, and it is a repository
setting rather than anything a pull request can carry. **This is the half a PR
can do: make them eligible.** A path-filtered job cannot be a required check —
on a PR touching none of the listed paths it never runs, reports no status, and
a required check then blocks that PR forever waiting for a result that will
never arrive. The filter and the requirement are mutually exclusive.

So `ts.yml` drops its `paths:` filter. Its four jobs ran 16s, 9s and change on
their last green board; under a minute per PR is not a price worth paying a
correctness gap for. The `branches:` note above it records the same lesson from
the stacked-PR case, which is the same mistake in a different filter.

`rust.yml` keeps its filter deliberately. Its `codegen-drift` guard has the
identical constraint and would need the same treatment to be required, but it
carries a Rust toolchain and the workflow it lives in also runs clippy, the full
test suite, `cargo package` and `cargo deny` — several minutes on every
documentation edit. Extracting one job from beside the crates it checks is worth
doing deliberately, not as a side effect of this. Recorded here so the next
person meets the reasoning rather than the symptom.

Nothing else changes: same jobs, same steps, same check names.

title: consent/approve-request/0.1: an unsigned document rendered on a human's phone, invisible to every census
body:
## Summary

`vta-service` constructs a `consent/approve-request/0.1` Trust Task document and buffers it to an approver's mediator for delivery to their phone, where a human is asked to approve something. It carries **no `proof`**, and **no census in this repo can see it**.

## Verified facts

**No proof.** `vta-service/src/trust_tasks/consent.rs:411` builds the document inline:

```rust
let approve_request = serde_json::json!({
    "id": format!("urn:uuid:{}", Uuid::new_v4()),
    "type": CONSENT_APPROVE_REQUEST_TYPE,
    "issuedAt": chrono::Utc::now().to_rfc3339_opts(chrono::SecondsFormat::Secs, true),
    "payload": prompt_payload,
});
```

`id`, `type`, `issuedAt`, `payload`. That is the whole document.

**The comparable path does gate on a proof.** `vta-mobile-core/src/task.rs:93`, parsing `auth/step-up/approve-request`:

```rust
// The gate: no valid proof from an enrolled executor, no prompt.
let relying_party = crate::proof::verify_signed_request(&v, &trusted_issuers).await?;
```

The consent prompt has no equivalent parser and no proof. Both end up in front of a person being asked to authorise something.

**No spec.** `https://trusttasks.org/spec/consent/approve-request/0.1` is not in the registry. `consent/request/1.0` is the requester-side task, not the approver prompt, and `auth/step-up/approve-request/0.2` is a different ceremony — neither is a fold target.

## Why nothing catches it

Three harnesses exist and each misses it for a different reason:

1. **`UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`** (`vta-service/src/trust_tasks/mod.rs:237`) is shrink-only and fails the build on a new unspecced URI — but it tracks URIs this service **serves**. This one is only ever **produced**.
2. **`producer_payload_conformance.rs`** covers client methods in `vta-sdk` that build payloads by hand. This document is constructed inline in `vta-service`, through no client method.
3. **`trust_task_manifest.rs`**'s census (`BINDING_SITES`) does not scan `vta-service/src` — but note that adding it **would not help**, and an earlier read of this suggested it would. That census's `PREFIX` is `https://trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/` (`trust_task_manifest.rs:25`), the VTC's private namespace. This URI is in the public `spec/` namespace, so the scan would not match it wherever it ran.

So the gap is structural: **there is no census over outbound producer URIs in the public namespace.** Serving one is caught; producing one is not.

## Why it matters

The named risk is not schema drift. It is that the one thing standing between an attacker and a human tapping "approve" is whatever the mediator and transport authenticate — with nothing in the document itself for the device to verify against an enrolled issuer, which is precisely the check the step-up path performs.

## Suggested fix

1. Give the document a `proof`, signed with the VTA's issuer key — the same key task-consent requests and step-up approve-requests are signed with (`operations::credentials::load_vta_issuer_secret`).
2. Verify it device-side before rendering a prompt, mirroring `parse_step_up_request`.
3. Publish `consent/approve-request/0.1` with `proof` REQUIRED, so the requirement is normative rather than local.
4. Close the structural hole: extend the tracked-debt harness to cover **produced** URIs, not just served ones, so the next inline-constructed document is visible the day it lands.

## Not a release blocker

This ships today and is not a regression introduced by the pending release. Filing it so it is tracked rather than rediscovered from a rejected request in production — which is how the two shipped payload defects (#895, #919) were found.

title: release(core): @openvtc/pnm-core 0.5.0
body:
npm has served 0.4.0 since 2026-08-17, which predates everything from #123
onward. Diffing the published tarball's runtime exports against this build: 35
added, one removed (`markInboundHandled`). `matchesTrustTaskCode` does not
appear as removed because it never shipped — it landed in #126, after 0.4.0 was
cut — so deleting it broke nothing for a consumer.

Breaking under 0.x rules, hence the leading component: the inbound de-dup call
changed shape, the vault and passkey wire types became the generated ones (a
non-empty `targets`, an optional `transports`, an attachment digest that is
`digestMultibase` rather than hex), and `@cfworker/json-schema` is a new runtime
dependency. The changelog leads with a Migration section for exactly those.

Also refreshes the two runtime dependencies this package actually ships —
`@noble/curves` ^2.4.0, `cbor-x` ^1.6.6, both in-range, no advisories. The
toolchain and UI dependencies of the private workspaces are left alone; `vite`
in particular touches the MV3 bundle and should be attributable to its own
commit.

Corrects one stale claim in the changelog while here: the `admin` entry said the
agent implements `internal` on `keys/create` and `origin: "internal"` with the
published schema having neither. The schema has both now, and the local
widenings were removed in #127.

`packages/extension` and `packages/pwa` move to `^0.5.0`; their old `^0.4.0`
would not have resolved to it.

title: fix(inbound): enforce the published schema on a consent payload (#128)
body:
fix(inbound): enforce the published schema on a consent payload (#128)

* fix(inbound): enforce the published schema on a consent payload

A `sideEffects` value the schema forbids rendered to the human as the *safest*
thing the consent surface can draw.

`parseTaskConsentRequest` checked the payload with a hand-written block of
`typeof` tests. Those are not a cheap version of the schema — they ask weaker
questions, and in one place the difference reached a human.
`typeof payload.sideEffects !== "string"` admits any string; the schema admits
`none`, `mutating` or `destructive`. `confirm.tsx` renders severity by
comparing against those three:

    background: destructive ? danger : sideEffects === "mutating" ? warn : ok

so anything outside the enum — a typo, a re-cased value, a value from a peer
that disagrees about the contract — fell through to the `ok` branch and was
painted green, with the unrecognised string as its label. The most dangerous
outcome a schema violation can produce was presented as the most reassuring.

The same gap ran through the rest of the payload: `minApprovals` was checked as
a `number` where the schema says integer >= 1, so `0` passed and a surface would
have shown a threshold nothing has to meet; `effects` was `Array.isArray` with
no element shape; `exposure` was any object at all; `note` — bounded to 500 by
framework 0.5 §7.3 item 19 *precisely* so a consent surface is not handed
unbounded prose — was not checked; and `additionalProperties: false` went
unenforced, so a member the schema forbids arrived silently.

Validating the published schema also found a live drift it was not looking for:
the fixtures for this family still carried the *hex* form of the shared
cross-repo digest, long after the multibase cutover. `typeof === "string"` had
accepted it every time; the schema's `DigestMultibase` pattern did not.

**Why a real validator rather than a subset of one.** Surveying the 349 payload
schemas this package ships finds `$ref` 2583 times, `oneOf` 141,
`propertyNames` 669, `pattern` 1036, `format` 944, plus `not`, `uniqueItems`,
`dependentRequired` and `minProperties`. A partial implementation of that
under-enforces silently, which is worse than not validating — it reports success
it did not establish. `@cfworker/json-schema` is a complete 2020-12
implementation with no dependencies of its own, and this is the keyword set that
makes `unevaluatedProperties` enforceable at all: no generated *type*, in either
language, can express it (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#327 fixes the Rust
side of that, and has no TypeScript counterpart to fix because TS types are
structural and never rejected an unknown member at runtime).

`@openvtc/trust-tasks` deliberately ships no validator — zero runtime deps so it
loads anywhere — and defines the consumer seam instead. `trust-tasks/validate.ts`
fills it, compiles each schema once against a `WeakMap` keyed by the schema
object (the inbound path revalidates on every mediator redelivery after a worker
respawn), and reports every violation rather than the first. `validatePayload`
on `ParseTaskConsentOptions` lets a caller substitute a different validator;
there is deliberately no way to switch validation off, and an unusable schema
refuses rather than passes.

Cost: `offscreen` 167 -> 206 kB (45 -> 58 kB gzipped). `background.js` is
unchanged at 48 kB — the consent path is not in the service worker, so the MV3
single-bundle invariant is untouched.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(deps): take trust-tasks 0.16.2, which makes provision/integration/0.3 satisfiable

0.16.0 shipped that spec's `$defs/Response` requiring `digest` while its
`properties` carried only `digestMultibase` — the member the 0.2 -> 0.3 rename
replaced. The object is closed, so the schema admits nothing: a consumer that
validated a conforming response would have rejected it.

Upstream #324 corrected the schema and regenerated the Rust bindings but not the
TypeScript ones, so the two libraries disagreed about the wire contract until
#326 ran `build-ts-bindings` as well. That is the failure `check-bindings`
exists to catch, and did.

It mattered here only because this branch starts executing the schemas this
package ships rather than merely carrying them. So it comes with a guard: a
sweep asserting no shipped schema has a `required` naming a member its
`properties` does not define, where the object is closed — the cheap, decidable
half of satisfiability, and the half that would have caught this. All 349
schemas pass on 0.16.2.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(core): adopt Trust Tasks 0.16.0, and close the specced-family gap (#127)
body:
feat(core): adopt Trust Tasks 0.16.0, and close the specced-family gap (#127)

Brings the repo onto `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.16.0 — which is the content the
Rust side calls 0.17.0; the two packages version their own APIs, not `SPEC.md`,
so there is no TypeScript 0.17 to wait for.

The bump itself needed no source change. What it surfaced did.

**SPEC §7.2 item 11 was not implemented.** `inbound/dedup.ts` recorded bare ids
and answered "seen / not seen", which cannot express the half of item 11 that
matters: a *different* document under a used `id` MUST be refused as
`idConflict`, not absorbed. It also keyed on the DIDComm message id — the
transport identifier §7.2 names explicitly as one that MUST NOT substitute for
the document `id`, and the one a mediator is free to change on redelivery.
`claimInboundDocument` now returns fresh/duplicate/conflict, keyed on the
document's own id plus a digest of its RFC 8785 canonicalization, so a
re-serializing intermediary cannot turn a §8.4 retry into a conflict. Durable
via KVStore, because MV3 tears the worker down mid-decision.

`idConflict` was also landing in `e.p.msg.bad_request` on the send path: it
postdates `coerceTrustTaskCode`'s switch, and is why the framework runtimes emit
`trust-task-error/0.5` — 0.3's enum cannot carry it. The standard/extended split
now comes from the runtime's `normalizeCode`/`isStandardCode` rather than a
local regex that also rewrote extended codes containing `_`.

**Coverage 130 -> 152 of 177.** Every family that is specced, published as a
binding, and named by `vta-sdk` is now implemented: `trust-task-discovery/0.1`,
`acl/update`, `vta/webvh/servers/retire-orphan`, `vtc/members/removal-notice`
(a parser — the wallet receives it), `vta/app-state/*` (6, new module),
`vta/services/*` (8), `vta/credentials/{issue,revoke}`, and
`auth/passkey/login/{start,finish}/0.2`. All 25 outstanding are unspecced, so
the number now moves when upstream lands a spec rather than when someone here
finds time.

**Versions.** `vtc/join-requests/submit` 0.1 -> 0.2 (a four-outcome `verdict`
replaces `status: "pending"`, so applicants who had been *admitted* were being
reported as pending); `vault/{list,get,upsert}` and `provision/integration` to
0.3 and `device/wipe` to 0.2 once VTI landed them; `vta/credentials/issue` to
0.2, which VTI shipped as a removal rather than a deprecation. No bare-hex wire
digest remains.

**Hand-copied wire types replaced by the generated ones** in `vta/protocol.ts`,
`vault/list.ts` and `provision/send.ts`. Each copy had drifted: `transports` was
typed required when the schema says optional (and used a DOM type in the
transport-free layer), the vault entry was written from `_shared/0.1` while the
module posted 0.2 and had lost the non-empty `targets` constraint, and
`keys/create` was missing `keyId` — the field `vta-sdk` 0.30.0 was cut for, and
not optional in practice for an `internal` key, which has no derivation path to
be named after.

**Compatibility folds removed.** Nothing is deployed — no Web Store release, no
consumers — so the trust-tasks #279 dual-accept and a legacy inbound-dedup
record were dead code that read like live constraints. VTI emits only the
current spelling; verified before deleting. Recorded as a rule in CLAUDE.md so
it is not reintroduced.

CI's admin-isolation check now names the two new `admin/` modules, and the
task-surface snapshot is refreshed to vta-sdk 0.30.0.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.17.2
body:
### Fixed

- **codegen**: Carry unevaluatedProperties strictness into the generated type ([#327](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/327))

* fix(codegen): carry unevaluatedProperties strictness into the generated type

  A specification that reuses a shared definition and adds members of its own
  has exactly one way to close the result: `unevaluatedProperties` at the
  outer level. `additionalProperties` cannot do it — both keywords are
  evaluated against the whole instance from within the subschema that declares
  them, so one inside either the shared definition or the composing schema
  rejects the other's members. That is why `credentials/_shared/0.2`'s
  `IssuedCredentialBase` is deliberately left open and
  `vta/credentials/issue/0.2` closes over it.

  typify does not model `unevaluatedProperties`. It flattens the `allOf` into
  a single struct carrying every member — the right shape — but emits no
  `deny_unknown_fields`, because it maps only `additionalProperties: false`.
  The generated type is then more permissive than the schema it came from: a
  validator rejects an unknown member, the Rust type silently accepts it.

  `issue/0.1` closes with `additionalProperties` and generates
  `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`. `issue/0.2` says the same thing the only
  way a composition can, and generated nothing. That is a silent weakening
  across a version bump whose whole purpose was to stop the two definitions
  drifting.

  This flattens the composition before typify sees it, so the strictness
  survives. The struct is unchanged; only the attribute is added.

  Two things it deliberately does not do:

  - It runs after `raw` is captured, so `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA` still carries the
    published `allOf` + `unevaluatedProperties` text. Runtime validation is
    against the real schema, not this rewrite.
  - It declines any composition whose members are not plain object schemas —
    a nested combinator, an `if`/`then`, a member that closes itself, an
    unresolvable `$ref`. The merge would not be sound there, and a wrong
    `deny_unknown_fields` rejects valid documents, which is worse than the
    permissiveness it would fix.

  Only `vta/credentials/issue/0.2` uses the pattern today, so the regenerated
  output is one file. It is the composition style the registry is moving
  toward, which is why it is worth fixing at the generator.

title: chore(deps): azure_identity 1.0, with the Key Vault bump it requires
body:
Replaces Dependabot's #1169, which bumped `azure_identity` alone and failed with:

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `DeveloperToolsCredential:
             azure_core::credentials::TokenCredential` is not satisfied
note: there are multiple different versions of crate `azure_core` in the dependency graph
```

That second line is the whole story, and it's easy to read past. **Nothing about `DeveloperToolsCredential` changed.**

| crate | azure_core |
|---|---|
| `azure_identity` 1.0 | 1.1 |
| `azure_security_keyvault_secrets` 0.14 | 0.35 |

The credential implements 1.1's `TokenCredential`; `SecretClient::new` wants 0.35's. Same trait by name, a different trait to the compiler.

This is the **same shape as #1166** (k8s-openapi / kube): Dependabot bumped one half of a coupled pair, and the resulting error names a type rather than the version skew that produced it. So `azure_security_keyvault_secrets` goes 0.14 → 1.0 alongside, and the lockfile is back to exactly one `azure_core`.

**No source changes.** `SecretClient::new(vault_url, credential, None)` and the `DeveloperToolsCredential::new` call are identical across both majors.

- `cargo check --workspace --all-features` clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets` → 0
- `cargo test -p vti-secrets --features azure-secrets` passes

Closes #1169.

title: chore(deps): k8s-openapi 0.28, with the kube bump it requires
body:
Replaces Dependabot's #1166, which bumped `k8s-openapi` alone and failed with:

```
None of the v1_* features are enabled on the k8s-openapi crate.
```

…pointing at **`k8s-openapi v0.27.1`** — a version the PR had just moved away from. The message names the copy that has no version feature rather than the mismatch that produced it, which is what makes it read as a feature-declaration problem when it's a resolution one.

`kube` depends on a specific `k8s-openapi` major:

| kube | k8s-openapi |
|---|---|
| 3.1 | 0.27 |
| 4.2 | 0.28 |

Bumping only `k8s-openapi` puts **two copies** in the tree, and the workspace's `features = ["latest"]` applies to just one. The other has none, and its build script panics. k8s-openapi's own error text says exactly this — *"check your Cargo.lock or run `cargo tree -i k8s-openapi` to ensure that this version is the only one being used"* — but it's easy to read past when the error names a version you thought you'd removed.

So the two move together. `kube` 3.1 → 4.2 leaves exactly one `k8s-openapi` in the lockfile, and the comment above the declaration now records why they're coupled, so the next bump doesn't rediscover it.

**No source changes.** The core/v1 `Secret` shape this backend uses is long-stable and `Client::try_default()` is unchanged across the major.

- `cargo check --workspace --all-features` clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets` → 0
- `cargo test -p vti-secrets --features k8s-secrets` passes

Closes #1166.

title: fix(codegen): carry unevaluatedProperties strictness into the generated type
body:
### The problem

A spec that reuses a shared definition *and* adds members of its own has exactly one way to close the result: `unevaluatedProperties` at the outer level. `additionalProperties` cannot do it — both keywords are evaluated against the whole instance from within the subschema that declares them, so one inside either the shared definition or the composing schema rejects the other's members. That's why `credentials/_shared/0.2`'s `IssuedCredentialBase` is deliberately left open and `vta/credentials/issue/0.2` closes over it. The definition says so itself.

typify doesn't model `unevaluatedProperties`. It flattens the `allOf` into a single struct carrying every member — the right shape — but emits no `deny_unknown_fields`, because it maps only `additionalProperties: false`.

| | closes with | generated |
|---|---|---|
| `issue/0.1` | `additionalProperties: false` | `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` |
| `issue/0.2` | `unevaluatedProperties: false` | *(nothing)* |

So the generated type is **more permissive than the schema it came from**: a validator rejects an unknown member, the Rust type silently accepts it. That's a silent weakening across a version bump whose whole purpose was to stop two definitions drifting.

Found by the VTI conformance sweep, whose drifted-witness check asserts the generated type rejects an unknown member. It failed on 0.2 and passed on 0.1.

### The fix

Flatten the composition before typify sees it, so the strictness survives the round-trip. The struct typify produces is unchanged; only the attribute is added.

Two things it deliberately does **not** do:

- **It runs after `raw` is captured**, so `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA` still carries the published `allOf` + `unevaluatedProperties` text. Runtime validation is against the real published schema, not this rewrite. Verified on the regenerated output.
- **It declines** any composition whose members aren't plain object schemas — a nested combinator, an `if`/`then`, a member that closes itself, an unresolvable `$ref`. The merge wouldn't be sound there, and a wrong `deny_unknown_fields` rejects valid documents, which is worse than the permissiveness it fixes. Each decline path has a test.

### Regenerated output

One file: `trust-tasks-rs/src/specs/vta/credentials/issue/v0_2.rs`, gaining `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` on `Response`. Only `issue/0.2` uses the pattern today, but it's the composition style the registry is moving toward, which is why it's worth fixing at the generator rather than per-spec.

`cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features` and `cargo test -p trust-tasks-codegen` green; workspace clippy 0.

title: chore(deps)!: aes-gcm 0.11, and stop the nonce conversions panicking
body:
Replaces Dependabot's #1167, which was red on **ten** checks. 0.11 removes two things this workspace was reaching through the cipher rather than depending on directly.

### `aead::OsRng` is gone

Nine sites across five crates generated nonces and salts through `aes_gcm::aead::OsRng` — a re-export, borrowing whatever CSPRNG the cipher happened to vendor. They now use `rand::rng()`, which is what the rest of the workspace already uses for exactly this. `vta-backup` gains a direct `rand` dependency it always needed and was getting by accident.

### `aead::generic_array` became `hybrid_array`

The `GenericArray::from_slice` calls in `vta-tee`'s KMS bootstrap move to the public `Key` / `Nonce` aliases — infallible `.into()` where the source is a fixed-size array, `try_from` where it's a runtime slice out of a CMS envelope.

### The part worth reading

Not required by the bump. `Nonce::from_slice` is deprecated in favour of `TryFrom`, and CI runs clippy with `-D warnings`, so all nineteen call sites had to move. **They were not equivalent.**

`from_slice` **panics** on a wrong length, and every one of those sites parses a stored or transmitted blob. `vta-backup` already knew:

```rust
// Hard length check before `Nonce::from_slice` — the `aes-gcm` impl of that
// constructor panics on the wrong length, which a crafted backup envelope
// would otherwise weaponise into a process-killing DoS on `/backup/import`.
```

…with regression tests for it. That hand-written guard was the only thing between the parser and the panic, and it had to be remembered at every new call site.

With `TryFrom` the panic is gone **by construction**. The length checks stay, because they produce the better error — `invalid nonce length: 11 (expected 12)` rather than a bare conversion failure — but they're no longer load-bearing for safety, and the comments now say so. The DoS regression tests stay too: they assert the *rejection*, which is still the contract.

One site was genuinely reachable rather than defence-in-depth: `vta-keys::wrapping` unwrapping a wire-supplied nonce, where the length is attacker-controlled and nothing checked it first.

### Verification

- clippy **0** across the workspace, all features, all targets
- the crypto crates' **146 tests** pass — including the CMS envelope round-trip and the wrong-length-nonce DoS regressions
- `vtc-service` 866 pass; full `cargo test --workspace --all-features` clean

Closes #1167.

title: fix(ci): stop Dependabot emitting chore(deps)(deps) titles, and let a fixed title clear the check
body:
Every cargo PR Dependabot opened in its first hour is red on `commit lint`:

```
#1170 chore(deps)(deps): bump tower-http from 0.6.11 to 0.7.0
#1169 chore(deps)(deps): bump azure_identity from 0.35.0 to 1.0.0
...
```

`include: scope` appends the scope itself, so a `prefix` that already carries one doubles it. The commit-lint job checks the **PR title** against the conventional-commit regex, which rejects `chore(deps)(deps):` — a check failing for a reason unrelated to the bump, on every PR, which is the fastest way to teach people to ignore it.

My bug, from #1160 an hour ago. The `github-actions` and `docker` entries were already correct — they set a scoped prefix and *don't* set `include`, which is the other consistent way to spell it. I'll retitle the six open ones by hand, since the check reads the title rather than the branch's commit messages.

title: Specify both VMC directions so membership requires member consent
body:
The spec asserted in five places that two VMCs form a complete membership edge, but the normative schema required `issuer` to be the VTC/VTN C-DID and the subject to be the member, making the reverse credential unconstructible. Issue #8 correctly flagged this as a structural contradiction rather than an editorial one.

The pair is deliberate: the member-issued VMC is the member's consent artifact. A community can always issue a credential naming someone as a member, but it cannot produce the acknowledgement without that party's signature, so requiring both directions makes an unconsented membership claim unprovable. That rationale appeared nowhere in the text, which is why the contradiction was reachable in the first place.

So the prose was right and the schema was the defect. The two directions are now distinguished by issuer and subject rules rather than by a new credential type, matching how the VIC's two variants are handled.

- `spec/body.md`: VMC schema gains direction-qualified issuer/subject rules and a `digest` binding the acknowledgement to the grant, reusing the existing VWC digest algorithm verbatim; a second worked example; a new "Membership Edge Completion" subsection carrying the completeness, ordering and verifier rules plus the consent rationale; and a lifecycle editor's note deferring revocation to the planned Trust Task Protocols spec.
- `spec/body.md`: the per-direction witnessing rule generalised from VRCs to both edge-credential subtypes, so a witnessed membership edge has a defined `credentialSubject.id` binding.
- `spec/body.md`: new Security Consideration for unconsented membership assertion; "Digest integrity" extended to cover the VMC acknowledgement digest.
- `spec/terms-definitions/`: seven files corrected, including the "always ... C-DID" clause in `verifiable_membership_credential.md` that was the term-level source of the contradiction, and the CTA being "automatically" made a member without acknowledging.
- `CONTEXT.md`: VMC entry rewritten to describe both directions.

The verifier rule is deliberately direction-sensitive, which is the part worth reviewing closely: a member presenting their own community-issued VMC is accepted alone, since the act of presenting is itself the consent. A blanket "both always" would have broken the Community-Anchored ZKP and PHC constructions, which rely on the member holding only the community-issued half.

Resolves #8

title: Resolve the contradiction in VMC bidirectionality
body:
## Summary

The specification describes membership as a bidirectional graph edge formed by two Verifiable Membership Credentials, one in each direction. However, the normative VMC schema appears to permit only a community or network C-DID to issue a VMC to a member.

Under the current issuer and subject rules, it is not clear how the reverse-direction credential could be created.

## Detail

The specification indicates that:

* two VMCs, one in each direction, form a complete membership edge;
* the VMC issuer is the VTC or VTN C-DID; and
* the VMC subject is the member’s M-DID, or a VTC C-DID in the network-membership case.

A credential issued by the member to the community would therefore appear to violate the normative issuer rule.

This creates a structural inconsistency in the membership model rather than only an editorial ambiguity. Implementers cannot determine whether membership is:

* a unilateral community-issued assertion;
* a mutually issued credential pair;
* a community assertion plus member acceptance;
* or another form of bidirectional protocol state.

## Requested clarification

Please clarify what constitutes the reverse direction of the membership edge and specify the applicable issuer, subject and validation rules.

One possible resolution would be to model a VMC as a unilateral, community-issued membership assertion that creates a directed graph edge, while representing member acceptance or possession separately at the protocol or presentation layer.

Alternatively, if two credentials are required, the second credential and its semantics should be defined explicitly.
