title: feat(compliance)!: enforce SPEC §7.2's flag-driven checks, and sign what we send
body:
The VTA enforced **none** of the four checks a *Trust Task specification* declares for itself. It now enforces all of them, and the SDK produces documents that satisfy them.

| SPEC §7.2 | check | dispatched specs declaring it |
|---|---|---|
| item 5b | `recipient` REQUIRED | **109 / 109** |
| item 7a | `proof` REQUIRED | **72 / 109** |
| item 8 | audience binding | non-bearer specs |
| §7.3 item 17 | `issuedAt` REQUIRED | **70 / 109** |

## Why it was unreachable

`TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy` reads those constants off `P`. The dispatch spine holds a `TrustTask<Value>` and routes on a URI string, so it had no `P` to read them from.

`spec_policy_for` — added upstream in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#321, authored for this — keys the same constants by Type URI. The alternative was a **109-entry URI→type table** in this repo, duplicating what the codegen already emits, and going stale the first time a spec was added.

The spine's own comment claimed *"each slice's typed handler runs it after `parse_payload`"*. No handler did: that comment was the **only** occurrence of `enforce_audience_binding` in the repository.

## This is an auth-model change, not a wire-format one

A bearer token authenticates the *connection*. §7.2 item 7 admits no transport substitute, so every producer must now sign every document.

`vta-sdk` gains `ClientIdentity` (client DID, its key, the VTA's DID) and signs in `dispatch_trust_task`. `SessionStore::connect` supplies it from the stored session — re-read **after** `ensure_authenticated`, because a session that needed rotation now holds a different DID and key, and signing with the pre-rotation pair produces a document whose `issuer` no longer matches the identity its token authenticates (item 6).

`issuer` and `recipient` are set in `build_task_document` rather than at ~200 call sites, for the same reason `issuedAt` already was: a member the framework requires of *every* document belongs to the one function that builds every document.

Signing is unconditional rather than keyed on the flag — a proof on a task that merely RECOMMENDs one is legal and strictly more attributable. What it must never do is attach a proof with **no** in-band recipient (item 8 refuses that on a non-bearer spec), and both come from the same `ClientIdentity`, so they cannot come apart.

## Test identities are derived from seeds now

`did:key:zTestAdmin` was not a `did:key`. Nothing resolves it, and no document issued by it can carry a verifiable proof. Fine while proofless documents were accepted; fatal once 72 specs demand one.

`did_for_seed(u8)` / `sign_as(u8, doc)` give a DID and the key behind it from one place — which is what item 6 needs, since a test that mints a token for one DID and signs with another is refused for *that* rather than for whatever it meant to check.

## A real bug in the fixtures

`delegated_consent_e2e`'s `sign_as` did not clear an existing proof before signing. `prepare_sign_input` hashes the document as given, so signing over one that already carries a proof yields a signature covering bytes no verifier reconstructs — it fails as `proofInvalid`, which reads like a key problem and is not one.

## Also here

- pins `trust-tasks-rs` 0.17.1 (carries `spec_policy_for` and the `provision/integration/0.3` schema fix from #324)

## Verification

- `vta-service --all-features`: **0 failed**, zero response-conformance violations — including the 12 `mock_vta` tests that drive a fully-enforcing VTA through the real `VtaClient` over HTTP
- `vta-sdk`, `vti-common`, `vta-mobile-core`, `vta-vault`, `vta-webvh`: 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets` and the CI combination: exit 0
- `cargo fmt --all --check`: exit 0
- `TRUST-TASK RESPONSE COVERAGE 88/109 (81%)` — unchanged

## Downstream

Any client dispatching Trust Tasks must now carry a `ClientIdentity`. `SessionStore::connect` does it automatically; a caller constructing `VtaClient::new(url)` directly needs `.with_identity(…)`. That includes **pnm, the browser plugin, and mobile-core's REST paths**.

title: Use did:webvh in examples and state what each VID role needs of a DID method
body:
## Summary

Two related changes to how this specification treats DID methods.

**The examples showed `did:web` for durable issuers.** The VTC (`chess-club.example`), the witness service, and the IDVC issuer were all `did:web`. That method resolves to a document with no verifiable history: a verifier can establish which key is authoritative *now*, but not which key was authoritative *when the credential was signed*, and there is no recovery path on key compromise. Since DTG credentials may be presented long after issuance, and [Security Considerations](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#security-considerations) requires verifiers to validate the verification method, `did:web` understates what the specification assumes of a C-DID.

These examples now use [`did:webvh`](https://identity.foundation/didwebvh/), whose DID log publishes an append-only history of document versions, commits to successor keys via `nextKeyHashes`, and may be witnessed. Pairwise subjects are unchanged and stay on `did:key` / `did:peer`.

**The specification was silent on what it needs from a DID method.** It mandates none — correctly, and this PR does not change that — but it also never said what it relies on a method to provide, leaving implementers no basis for choosing one. The new informative `DID Method Considerations` subsection separates the two property sets, which pull against each other:

| | Durable (C-DID, M-DID) | Pairwise (R-DID, P-DID) |
|---|---|---|
| Key history | Verifiable, so signing-time key state is recoverable | Not required |
| Rotation | Without changing the identifier | Not required |
| Successor keys | Pre-rotation or equivalent commitment | Not required |
| Creation cost | Amortised over the identifier's life | Cheap, no registration step |
| Resolution origin | Independent of a single operator | **Not shared across identifiers** |
| Service endpoints | Discoverable (VTA, `credentialStatus`, trust registry) | Not required |

The conclusion is that implementations should expect to use more than one method rather than seeking one that serves every role. Nothing here requires an `issuer` and a `credentialSubject.id` to share a method, and the examples now reflect that.

## Privacy consideration 7

Correlation does not require the credentials themselves. Where several of a party's R-DIDs or P-DIDs resolve through common infrastructure — a shared web origin, a shared registry, or a shared set of witnesses observing their updates — that infrastructure can associate identifiers the credential structure was designed to keep apart, and can observe when each is used.

The existing considerations (1–3) cover correlation through credential *content*; none covered correlation through the *resolution layer*. This makes DID method choice for pairwise roles a privacy decision, not only a key management one — and it is the reason the table above marks "no shared resolution origin" as the property that distinguishes the two sets.

## Notes for reviewers

- **Entirely informative.** No normative requirement is added, changed, or removed. No schema changes.
- **No method is mandated.** `did:webvh` appears in examples and as an illustration of a method satisfying the durable-role properties; the text is written in terms of properties so that other methods can be assessed against it. This is deliberate — it is what makes a later conformance statement for, say, a KERI-based method cheap to write.
- **SCIDs in the examples are illustrative placeholders**, truncated in the house style used elsewhere for `did:key` and `did:peer` values. They are not real, resolvable SCIDs.
- Independent of #19; the two touch different parts of the document.

Use did:webvh in examples and state what each VID role needs of a DID method (#20)

* Use did:webvh in examples and state what each VID role needs of a DID method

The examples showed `did:web` for the VTC, witness service, and IDVC
issuers. Plain `did:web` resolves to a document with no verifiable
history, so a verifier can establish the current key but not the key
that was authoritative when a credential was signed, and there is no
recovery path on key compromise. For a C-DID expected to outlive any
particular key or hosting arrangement, that understates what the
specification assumes of a durable issuer.

Switch those examples to `did:webvh`, whose DID log publishes an
append-only history of document versions, commits to successor keys
via `nextKeyHashes`, and may be witnessed. Pairwise subjects stay on
`did:key` and `did:peer`.

Add an informative `DID Method Considerations` subsection. The
specification mandates no DID method and should not start doing so,
but it was silent on what it relies on a method to provide, which
left implementers no basis for choosing one. The subsection separates
the two sets of properties that pull against each other:

- Durable identifiers (C-DIDs, M-DIDs) need verifiable key history,
  rotation without changing the identifier, pre-rotation, independence
  from a single operator, and discoverable service endpoints.
- Pairwise identifiers (R-DIDs, P-DIDs) need cheap creation, no shared
  resolution origin, and no dependency on infrastructure that observes
  their use.

Because those pull in opposite directions, implementations should
expect to use more than one method rather than seeking one that serves
every role.

Add privacy consideration 7. Correlation does not require the
credentials themselves: where several of a party's R-DIDs or P-DIDs
resolve through common infrastructure — a shared origin, registry, or
witness set — that infrastructure can associate identifiers the
credential structure was designed to keep apart, and observe when each
is used. The existing considerations cover correlation via credential
content but not via the resolution layer.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Qualify DID log witnesses and widen the durable-identifier framing

Review feedback on #20.

The specification already uses "witness" for the VWC-issuing role, and
the previous commit introduced did:webvh's log-witness sense into the
same document without distinguishing them. Name the new sense "DID log
witness" at each of its three uses, and state once that it countersigns
DID document versions rather than attesting to an edge.

Widen the durable-identifier framing. It was scoped to C-DIDs and
M-DIDs, but the witness service in the VWC example is neither: §VWC
permits the issuer to be "the DID of a VTA acting according to VTC
policy", which none of the four VID types name. Rather than extend the
taxonomy, state that what determines the requirement is how long the
identifier must remain verifiable, and note in the introduction that
not every DID in a deployment is one of the four.

(The identity verification issuer of the PHC example is not affected: a
PHC is a VMC issued by a VTC, so that DID is a C-DID.)

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Correct the portability and did:web claims, and drop RFC 2119 keywords

Three corrections from review, all within the informative DID Method
Considerations subsection.

Portability was overclaimed. The paragraph said methods publishing an
append-only history "satisfy these properties", which included
independence from a hosting location. did:webvh resolves its log at a
web origin and relocates only where `portable` was set in the first log
entry; it defaults to off and a later entry cannot enable it, so a
did:webvh identifier created without it is as domain-bound as did:web
and cannot be retrofitted. The claim is now scoped to the first three
properties, with the creation-time trap stated outright and generalised
into guidance that applies to any method, since it is exactly what an
informative section of this kind exists to catch. did:scid is noted as
an example of the other shape, where the identifier carries no location
and the choice does not arise.

did:web was undercounted. It was described as satisfying "the last
property only", which sat oddly beside the rotation bullet above it:
did:web does rotate without changing the identifier, by republishing the
document. What it lacks is verifiable rotation and any commitment to
successor keys, which is the point the sentence was reaching for. Saying
it precisely also makes the argument against did:web stronger, since a
republished document leaves a legitimate rotation and an attacker's key
substitution indistinguishable to a verifier.

The subsection is marked informative but used three uppercase SHOULDs,
which spec/intro.md binds document-wide via RFC 2119, making them
normative regardless of the label. No other informative section in the
document contains an RFC 2119 keyword — Privacy Considerations uses
lowercase "should" throughout — so these are lowercased to match and to
make the claim that this subsection adds no normative requirement true.

No normative requirement is added, changed, or removed. No schema
changes. Renders clean with no broken references.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(ts): regenerate the provision/integration/0.3 binding
body:
#324 corrected the schema — `required` named a `digest` the 0.2→0.3 rename had already removed from `properties` — and regenerated the **Rust** bindings. It did not regenerate the **TypeScript** ones.

So `trust-tasks-ts` still shipped `"digest"` in `required` for both the request and response schemas while `trust-tasks-rs` no longer did. That is what is failing on #325:

> `provision/integration/0.3`: the request schema shipped by trust-tasks-ts and the one shipped by trust-tasks-rs are not the same document. The two $ref inliners have diverged, so the two libraries would disagree about which payloads conform.

`npm run build-ts-bindings` — **two lines removed, nothing else moved**:

```diff
       "required": [
         "bundle",
-        "digest",
         "summary"
       ],
```

(once in `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA`, once in `RESPONSE_PAYLOAD_SCHEMA`.)

## Verification

- `npm run check-bindings`: **349 specifications checked against 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust modules — all agree**
- `npm test` in `trust-tasks-ts`: 79 pass, 0 fail
- `tsc --noEmit`: clean

## For next time

A spec edit needs *both* generators run — `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` and `npm run build-ts-bindings`. Running only one leaves the two libraries disagreeing about the wire contract, which is precisely what `check-bindings` exists to catch, and did. My oversight in #324.

title: feat(tasks): catch up to the registry on vault 0.3, device/wipe 0.2 and credentials/issue 0.2
body:
Five of the six families `vta-sdk` lagged the registry on. Hard cutover — no deprecation window, per the brief.

**The sixth is not here.** `provision/integration/0.3`'s response schema **could never validate**: `required` named a `digest` that the 0.2→0.3 rename had already removed from `properties`, against `additionalProperties: false`. Fixed upstream in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#324 (merged); VTI adopts it once that publishes.

## vault/{list,get,upsert} 0.3

`AttachmentRef.sha256` — hex, with SHA-256 pinned by an `^[0-9a-f]{64}$` pattern — becomes `digestMultibase`, a multibase multihash that names its own algorithm.

Worth stating plainly: **nothing in this service has ever constructed an `AttachmentRef`.** Every construction site is `vec![]`, and `vault/upsert` only carries forward whatever an entry already had. The member has never reached the wire, so this is a type-level rename *today*. What changes is the contract — moving off SHA-256 later becomes a value change rather than another schema revision.

## device/wipe 0.2

`cache-and-keys` → `cacheAndKeys`, the same recasing the rest of the device slice took.

Its constant carried **"No 0.2 spec exists upstream; this stays on 0.1"** while `specs/device/wipe/0.2` had been published for some time. The replacement comment records why that mattered: *a comment asserting an absence is a claim about the registry that nothing re-checks*, and it is why nobody looked again.

## vta/credentials/issue 0.2

Request payload unchanged. The response stops restating the shared `IssuedCredential` inline and composes it through `allOf` + `unevaluatedProperties` — same members, same required set, **identical wire form**. So the two versions share a dispatch arm rather than needing a transform.

## The edge-transform table is now n:1

`WireSpecV02.uri_0_2` becomes `uris_wire: &[…]`. `vault/*` 0.3 differs from 0.2 only in `AttachmentRef`, which is not an enum value and not at any path the transform touches — so it down-converts to the same canonical handler by the same casing rules. Giving it its own row would have duplicated every enum path and left two copies to keep in step by hand.

`upconvert_response` now answers as the version the caller **sent**. With several wire URIs per spec, retyping a response to a fixed one would be refused by a client validating against the version it asked for.

## Two guards needed widening, and both were right to fail first

- **`superseded_tasks_are_dispatched`** did not count an edge-transformed URI as served. Its premise is that a row whose counter can never move reads the same as "safe to retire" — but the counter *does* move for these: `dispatch_trust_task_core` reads the superseded row from the URI **as it arrived**, before the down-convert, and says so in a comment. The successor half of the same pair already accepted them.
- **the wire/deprecation parity test** checked only the 0.1 hop. A spec accepting 0.1, 0.2 *and* 0.3 needs a row per superseded version, or the middle one is retired on no evidence at all. Now checked per hop.

`ALL_URIS` and `retry_safety` carry the four new URIs — the census caught their absence, which is what it is for.

## For the browser-plugin side

`task-surface.json` should now name `vault/{list,get,upsert}/0.3`, `device/wipe/0.2` and `vta/credentials/issue/0.2`, none of them deprecated. `provision/integration` stays at 0.2 until #324 publishes.

## Verification

- `vta-service --all-features`: **0 failed**, zero response-conformance violations
- `vta-sdk`, `vti-common`, `vta-mobile-core`: 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets` and the CI combination: exit 0
- `cargo fmt --all --check`: exit 0
- `TRUST-TASK RESPONSE COVERAGE 88/109 (81%)` — unchanged

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.17.1
body:
### Added

- **rs**: Index the consumer policy by Type URI, not just the schema ([#321](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/321))

`schema_index` exists, in its own words, "for consumers that dispatch on the
  URI". Such a consumer holds a `TrustTask<serde_json::Value>` and has no `P`, so
  it cannot reach `TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy` — the one API that applies the
  flag-driven §7.2 checks. The index handed it the schema and stopped there, so
  the only way to enforce recipient-REQUIRED, proof-REQUIRED, audience binding or
  §7.3 item 17's issuedAt-REQUIRED was to hand-maintain a URI → payload-type
  table. That is a second source of truth for data this file already generates,
  and it goes stale the first time a spec is added.

  `spec_policy_for(type_uri) -> Option<SpecPolicy>` closes that, emitted from the
  same loop as `schema_for` so the two cannot drift.

  `SpecPolicy` is a value, not four public constants, because the point is to
  share the *checks* rather than re-apply them. `TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy`
  and `enforce_audience_binding` now delegate to `SpecPolicy::enforce`, so the
  typed path and the URI-keyed path are one implementation. A new flag-driven
  rule added to `enforce` reaches both; there is no second copy to forget.



### Fixed

- **specs**: Provision/integration/0.3's response could never validate ([#324](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/324))

The 0.2 → 0.3 change renamed the bundle digest from a bare-hex `digest` to a
  multibase `digestMultibase`. It moved the member in `properties` and left
  `digest` behind in `required`.

  The object also declares `additionalProperties: false`, so the two rules
  contradict: a document MUST carry `digest`, and `digest` is not a member it may
  carry. No response can satisfy the schema, which makes the whole 0.3 response
  side unusable — and 0.3 is the version a consumer moves to for the multibase
  digest in the first place.

  The codegen then compounded it. A `required` entry with no property schema has
  no type to read, so `trust-tasks-rs` emitted

      pub digest: ::serde_json::Value,

  a required, untyped field. The generated Rust type demanded a member the schema
  forbade, so the two halves of the same release disagreed about the wire form.
  Both are correct now: `digest` is gone from `required`, and the regenerated type
  carries `digestMultibase` as the optional member the spec describes.

  Nothing caught it because every existing shape check reads one keyword at a
  time — `required` is checked for presence, `properties` for casing and bounds,
  `additionalProperties` for being declared at all. The contradiction only exists
  between them.

  So the guard is added at that level: for any object closed by
  `additionalProperties: false`, every name in `required` must appear in
  `properties`. It runs over the whole registry — 349 specs — and this was the
  only instance. Restricted to `additionalProperties: false` deliberately: under
  `unevaluatedProperties` an `allOf` branch may legitimately supply the member,
  and failing those would punish exactly the composition the registry is moving
  towards.

trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#324; VTI adopts it once that publishes.

**vault/{list,get,upsert} 0.3.** `AttachmentRef.sha256` — hex, with SHA-256
pinned by an `^[0-9a-f]{64}$` pattern — becomes `digestMultibase`, a multibase
multihash that names its own algorithm. Worth stating plainly: nothing in this
service has ever constructed an `AttachmentRef`. Every site is `vec![]` and
`vault/upsert` only carries forward whatever an entry already had, so the
member has never reached the wire and this is a type-level rename today. The
wire contract is what changes, and it changes so that moving off SHA-256 later
is a value change rather than another schema revision.

**device/wipe 0.2.** `cache-and-keys` → `cacheAndKeys`, the same recasing the
rest of the device slice took. Its constant carried "No 0.2 spec exists
upstream; this stays on 0.1" while `specs/device/wipe/0.2` had been published
for some time. The replacement comment says so: a comment asserting an absence
is a claim about the registry that nothing re-checks, and it is why nobody
looked again.

**vta/credentials/issue 0.2.** The request payload is unchanged. The response
stops restating the shared `IssuedCredential` inline and composes it through
`allOf` + `unevaluatedProperties` — same members, same required set, identical
wire form. So the two versions share a dispatch arm rather than a transform.

The edge-transform table goes from one wire URI per spec to a list.
`vault/*` 0.3 differs from 0.2 only in `AttachmentRef`, which is not an enum
value and not at any path the transform touches — so it down-converts to the
same canonical handler by the same casing rules. Giving it its own row would
have duplicated every path and left the two to be kept in step by hand.

`upconvert_response` now answers as the version the caller *sent*. With several
wire URIs per spec, retyping a response to a fixed one would be refused by a
client validating against the version it asked for.

Two guards needed widening, and both were right to fail first:

* `superseded_tasks_are_dispatched` did not count an edge-transformed URI as
  served. Its premise is that a row whose counter can never move reads the same
  as "safe to retire" — but the counter *does* move for these, because
  `dispatch_trust_task_core` reads the superseded row from the URI as it
  arrived, before the down-convert. The successor half of the pair already
  accepted them.
* the wire/deprecation parity test checked only the 0.1 hop. A spec accepting
  0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 needs a row per superseded version, or the middle one is
  retired on no evidence at all.

`ALL_URIS` and `retry_safety` carry the four new URIs; the census caught their
absence, which is what it is for.

title: fix(specs): provision/integration/0.3's response could never validate
body:
The 0.2 → 0.3 change renamed the bundle digest from a bare-hex `digest` to a multibase `digestMultibase`. It moved the member in `properties` and left `digest` behind in `required`.

```json
"additionalProperties": false,
"required": ["bundle", "digest", "summary"],
"properties": { "bundle": …, "digestMultibase": …, "summary": …, "ext": … }
```

The two rules contradict: a document MUST carry `digest`, and `digest` is not a member it may carry. **No response can satisfy the schema** — which makes the whole 0.3 response side unusable, and 0.3 is the version a consumer moves to *for* the multibase digest.

## The codegen compounded it

A `required` entry with no property schema has no type to read, so `trust-tasks-rs` emitted:

```rust
pub digest: ::serde_json::Value,
```

A required, untyped field. The generated Rust type demanded a member the schema forbade — the two halves of the same release disagreeing about the wire form. Both are correct after the fix: the regenerated type carries `digestMultibase` as the optional member the spec describes, and the phantom `digest` is gone.

## Why nothing caught it

Every existing shape check reads one keyword at a time — `required` for presence, `properties` for casing and bounds, `additionalProperties` for being declared at all. The contradiction only exists *between* them.

The guard is added at that level: for any object closed by `additionalProperties: false`, every name in `required` must appear in `properties`. Verified by reintroducing the bug:

```
provision/integration/0.3/payload.schema.json: $defs.Response: required names `digest`,
which is not in `properties`, and additionalProperties is false — no document can
satisfy this schema
```

Restricted to `additionalProperties: false` deliberately: under `unevaluatedProperties` an `allOf` branch may legitimately supply the member, and failing those would punish exactly the composition the registry is moving towards (`vta/credentials/issue/0.2` is the recent example).

## Verification

- `npm run validate`: 349 specs, **this was the only instance**
- `cargo test --workspace --all-features`: 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets`: exit 0

## Found

Moving a URI-dispatching VTA onto the 0.3 families. It cannot adopt `provision/integration/0.3` at all until this lands.

title: Trust Task Context Binding on published mechanisms, taskContext re-anchoring, and W3C proof/digest alignment
body:
Consolidated Working Draft 01 batch from the task force's working fork, superseding #15 by carrying it: the first commits are @bmiller59's #15 restructuring (authorship preserved), with three further changes built on top of it and the #15 first-pass review addressed. Closes #11. Resolves #17.

## What's inside, in order

**1. The #15 restructuring** (@bmiller59) — Trust Task Context Binding depends only on mechanisms already defined in the Trust Tasks core specification; the "qualifying specification" profile; outcome evidence travels with the presentation.

**2. `taskContext` re-anchoring and framework-0.4 alignment** — the outcome of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#173: `taskContext` carries the **`id` of the originating exchange's initiating document** (globally unique per the core specification's §4.3; the innermost exchange that attests the event, per §4.9.1), retiring the issuer-side uniqueness workaround. The qualifying profile is reworded against framework 0.4 (per-variant proof; the error variant honestly excluded — a task specification cannot strengthen `trust-task-error`'s own declaration; the no-`#response` escape hatch dropped). Outcome Interpretability cites the core specification's reply-disposition classification (§8.6) rather than hand-rolling the terminal/non-terminal split, and states the verifier's pairing checklist for retained evidence. A `trust-task-error` is failure evidence only, attributable to third parties when it carries `inResponseTo` (§8.2).

**3. W3C proof and digest alignment** (#17, all three items) — the VWC digest becomes `digestMultibase` (multibase multihash over the JCS canonical form the definition already named); multibase headers restricted to `z`/`u` per CID 1.0 §2.4 with alphabets enforced; proofs move from `Ed25519Signature2020` to the `DataIntegrityProof` envelope with `eddsa-jcs-2022` as the RECOMMENDED default suite (offline-verifiable; one canonicalization shared with `digestMultibase`) and `bbs-2023` named as the selective-disclosure path.

**4. The #15 first-pass review, addressed** — normative citations are commit-pinned permalinks (framework 0.4, `fbe196a`) so "pinned" is literally true; the stray subsection marking is removed; the per-issuer-uniqueness comment is mooted by the re-anchoring; and the term **"Trust Tasks core specification"** is now defined (`spec/terms-definitions/`), stating the core-vs-individual-specification architecture, explaining the upstream document's own "framework 0.4" version labels, and explicitly disclaiming the ToIP governance-framework sense.

## Evidence

The pairing checklist and the anchoring rule are executable: [`tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange) runs the witnessed exchange end-to-end — the VWC's `taskContext` lands on the ceremony's initiating document `id` structurally, and the retained `submit#response` passes exactly the checks the text states. The digest change is encoding-only for implementations already canonicalizing with JCS (verified against the Keyring witness implementation's own digest function).

Spec-Up-T render verified locally: every `[[ref:]]` resolves, no unresolved terms. Review history: Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#2, Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#3, Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#4.

body:
## The bug release-plz sized the pending release ([#312](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/312)) as: | crate | proposed | correct | |---|---|---| | `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.14.0 → **0.15.0** | ✅ breaking, right | | `trust-tasks-https` | 0.16.0 → 0.16.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks` | 0.2.0 → 0.2.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks-proof` | 0.13.0 → 0.13.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks-didcomm` | 0.15.0 → 0.15.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` | 0.14.0 → 0.14.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks-tsp` | 0.14.0 → 0.14.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.14.0 → 0.14.1 | ❌ patch | Every dependent exposes `trust-tasks-rs` types in its **own public API** — `trust-tasks` re-exports the whole crate with `pub use trust_tasks_rs::*`, and the bindings take and return `TrustTask

` / `TrustTaskCode`. So the core's breaking change is *their* breaking change, and they were about to ship it as a patch. ## Reproduced, not theorised A probe consumer holding the caret ranges it had before this release: ``` error[E0308]: expected `TrustTask`, found a different `TrustTask` note: there are multiple different versions of crate `trust_tasks_rs` in the dependency graph ``` `^0.14` admits `0.14.1`, so that break arrives on a routine `cargo update` with **no version signal at all**. VTI is exactly such a consumer. crates.io versions are immutable — publishing it would have been permanent. ## Why `semver_check` didn't catch it It can't. `cargo-semver-checks` compares each crate's rustdoc against *that crate's own* published baseline and does not track type identity across dependency versions — so it cheerfully reports "✓ API compatible changes" for a crate whose public API just changed underneath it. A green semver check says nothing about breaks arriving through a public dependency. ## The fix A `version_group` makes the relationship the code already had explicit: the eight crates share one version, so a break anywhere in the unit is a break everywhere. `version_group` alone was **not** enough, and I verified that before settling on this. Applied to today's versions it lands the whole group on `0.16.1` — still a patch for `trust-tasks-https`, still broken. It needs a shared floor, which is why this lands as a breaking change. Verified end to end with a local `release-plz update`: ``` trust-tasks-rs 0.14.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks 0.2.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-https 0.16.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-proof 0.13.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-didcomm 0.15.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-didcomm-v1 0.14.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-tsp 0.14.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-capability-client 0.14.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-ceremony 0.2.0 (unchanged) trust-tasks-codegen 0.1.0 (unchanged) ``` `0.17.0` is a correct breaking signal from every one of the eight. From then on release-plz's highest-next-version rule keeps it right by itself: once they share a floor, a break in the core dominates the group. ## Not in the group - **`trust-tasks-ceremony`** — has no `trust-tasks-rs` dependency at all, so it versions independently. (`version_group` across the whole workspace would have swept it to 0.16.1 for no reason.) - **`trust-tasks-codegen`** — `publish = false`. ## Also here Each crate gains a `# Versioning` doc section explaining the public-dependency relationship, and `release-plz.toml` carries the reasoning. This trap is invisible in the diff of any single crate, so it needs to be written down where the next person will hit it. ## Consequence for #312 Do **not** merge #312 as it stands. Once this is on `main`, re-run the workflow and it regenerates with 0.17.0 across the unit.

## 🤖 New release * `trust-tasks-rs`: 0.14.0 -> 0.15.0 (✓ API compatible changes) * `trust-tasks-didcomm`: 0.15.0 -> 0.15.1 (✓ API compatible changes) * `trust-tasks-https`: 0.16.0 -> 0.16.1 (✓ API compatible changes) * `trust-tasks`: 0.2.0 -> 0.2.1 (✓ API compatible changes) * `trust-tasks-capability-client`: 0.14.0 -> 0.14.1 * `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1`: 0.14.0 -> 0.14.1 * `trust-tasks-proof`: 0.13.0 -> 0.13.1 * `trust-tasks-tsp`: 0.14.0 -> 0.14.1
Changelog

## `trust-tasks-rs`

## [0.15.0](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/compare/trust-tasks-rs-v0.14.0...trust-tasks-rs-v0.15.0) — 2026-08-26 ### Added - **specs**: Require issuedAt on every live consequential spec, and make the §7.3 item 17 floor fatal ([#302](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/302)) * spec: make the §7.3 item 17 freshness floor a hard failure - **rs**: Make SPEC §7.3 item 17's issuedAt MUST expressible ([#300](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/300)) Framework 0.5.0's §7.3 item 17 says a Trust Task specification defining a consequential Trust Task MUST require the `issuedAt` member, raising §4.2's SHOULD to a MUST for documents conforming to it. There was no way to declare that: the meta-schema had `proofRequirement` for the `proof` envelope member and nothing equivalent for `issuedAt`, so the MUST was unexpressible and none of the 209 consequential specs in the registry could comply. Adds `issuedAtRequirement` to the front-matter meta-schema, modelled on `proofRequirement` — same two forms (a single `requirement`, or a per-variant `request`/`response` pair), same enum, same `rationale`. It governs an envelope member, admits a per-variant reading because request and response are relied on differently, and reading one declaration now teaches the other. Declared rather than derived, with the derived floor checked and reported: * `sideEffects` and `exposure` are DESCRIPTIVE (§7.3 items 13/14). Deriving `issuedAt`-REQUIRED from them would mean that correcting `sideEffects.level` from `none` to `mutating` for accuracy silently changed which documents every consumer of that spec must reject. * §2 makes the *handler* authoritative for consequentiality, not the front matter — so a value computed from the front matter would enforce something the front matter does not authoritatively state. * A non-consequential spec may legitimately require `issuedAt` anyway; a derived-only mechanism cannot express that. * Deriving would flip 209 specs' wire behaviour in one commit, invisibly. So the build derives the floor instead of substituting for the declaration. `npm run validate` prints a `Freshness floor (§7.3 item 17)` line counting the consequential specs that have not declared it (currently 0/209), *fails* on a spec that declares something weaker than REQUIRED, and escalates the undeclared case to a hard error under `TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT=1` — the ratchet that becomes the default once the registry has caught up. Enforcement reaches consumers the same way `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` does: * `Payload::IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED` (Rust) and `SpecPolicy.isIssuedAtRequired` (TypeScript), emitted per variant by both generators from the front matter. * `TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy` / `enforceSpecPolicy` reject a document with no `issuedAt` as `malformedRequest`. Not `expired`: §8.3 defines no dedicated code, `expired` names a document that was once acceptable, and §7.2 item 13 already uses `malformedRequest` for the other freshness rejections. * The trait constant has a default of `false`, so hand-written impls — the crate's own `trust-task-error`, hand-modelled in `error.rs` because it is in the codegen's SKIP_SLUGS, and every downstream impl — keep compiling. * `check-bindings` compares the new key across front matter, Rust and TypeScript, so the two languages cannot drift on it. Distinct from `FreshnessPolicy::require_issued_at`, which is a *consumer's* own posture applied to every document it sees. This is the *specification's* requirement, published in the registry and not the consumer's to relax. No specification declares `issuedAtRequirement` yet — that is a follow-up, spec by spec. The generated Rust tree is therefore byte-identical (the const is emitted only on override) and the generated TypeScript gains one `isIssuedAtRequired: false` line per policy object. Nothing that was accepted before is rejected now. Also documents the declaration in CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md, and teaches `npm run new-spec` to emit it on a scaffold whose declared classes make the task consequential. ### Fixed - **rs**: Enforce both halves of the SPEC §6.1 slug reservation ([#293](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/293)) * fix(rs): enforce both halves of the SPEC 6.1 slug reservation TypeUri rejected a published framework specification and accepted a reserved one, in the same function pair: REJECTED trust-task-control published since 0.1; its Type URI would not parse PARSES trust-ceremony-evil reserved by 6.1, accepted from any party is_reserved_namespace checked only the trust-task half of ^trust-(task|ceremony)($|-|/), so the ceremony half of the reservation — which exists precisely so the ceremony layer has a namespace no other party can claim first — protected nothing. And is_allowed_framework_slug listed five slugs where specs/spec.meta.schema.json lists seven, so two published specs sat inside the reservation with no permission to be there. The allowlist is one of two hand-maintained copies. The new test reads the meta-schema's copy and fails naming the missing slug if they drift again; verified by removing trust-task-control and watching it fail. Found while retiring trust-task-ok ([#292](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/292)), which swept for references to the slug and noticed the two lists disagreed. ### Specifications - Bound the remaining free-text payload members and state who reads them ([#301](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/301)) SPEC.md §7.3 (framework 0.5.0) item 19 has three parts. ## [0.15.0](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/compare/trust-tasks-rs-v0.14.0...trust-tasks-rs-v0.15.0) — 2026-08-26 ### Added - **rs**: Make SPEC §7.3 item 17's issuedAt MUST expressible ([#300](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/300)) Framework 0.5.0's §7.3 item 17 says a Trust Task specification defining a consequential Trust Task MUST require the `issuedAt` member, raising §4.2's SHOULD to a MUST for documents conforming to it. There was no way to declare that: the meta-schema had `proofRequirement` for the `proof` envelope member and nothing equivalent for `issuedAt`, so the MUST was unexpressible and none of the 209 consequential specs in the registry could comply. Adds `issuedAtRequirement` to the front-matter meta-schema, modelled on `proofRequirement` — same two forms (a single `requirement`, or a per-variant `request`/`response` pair), same enum, same `rationale`. It governs an envelope member, admits a per-variant reading because request and response are relied on differently, and reading one declaration now teaches the other. Declared rather than derived, with the derived floor checked and reported: * `sideEffects` and `exposure` are DESCRIPTIVE (§7.3 items 13/14). Deriving `issuedAt`-REQUIRED from them would mean that correcting `sideEffects.level` from `none` to `mutating` for accuracy silently changed which documents every consumer of that spec must reject. * §2 makes the *handler* authoritative for consequentiality, not the front matter — so a value computed from the front matter would enforce something the front matter does not authoritatively state. * A non-consequential spec may legitimately require `issuedAt` anyway; a derived-only mechanism cannot express that. * Deriving would flip 209 specs' wire behaviour in one commit, invisibly. So the build derives the floor instead of substituting for the declaration. `npm run validate` prints a `Freshness floor (§7.3 item 17)` line counting the consequential specs that have not declared it (currently 0/209), *fails* on a spec that declares something weaker than REQUIRED, and escalates the undeclared case to a hard error under `TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT=1` — the ratchet that becomes the default once the registry has caught up. Enforcement reaches consumers the same way `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` does: * `Payload::IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED` (Rust) and `SpecPolicy.isIssuedAtRequired` (TypeScript), emitted per variant by both generators from the front matter. * `TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy` / `enforceSpecPolicy` reject a document with no `issuedAt` as `malformedRequest`. Not `expired`: §8.3 defines no dedicated code, `expired` names a document that was once acceptable, and §7.2 item 13 already uses `malformedRequest` for the other freshness rejections. * The trait constant has a default of `false`, so hand-written impls — the crate's own `trust-task-error`, hand-modelled in `error.rs` because it is in the codegen's SKIP_SLUGS, and every downstream impl — keep compiling. * `check-bindings` compares the new key across front matter, Rust and TypeScript, so the two languages cannot drift on it. Distinct from `FreshnessPolicy::require_issued_at`, which is a *consumer's* own posture applied to every document it sees. This is the *specification's* requirement, published in the registry and not the consumer's to relax. No specification declares `issuedAtRequirement` yet — that is a follow-up, spec by spec. The generated Rust tree is therefore byte-identical (the const is emitted only on override) and the generated TypeScript gains one `isIssuedAtRequired: false` line per policy object. Nothing that was accepted before is rejected now. And is_allowed_framework_slug listed five slugs where specs/spec.meta.schema.json lists seven, so two published specs sat inside the reservation with no permission to be there. The allowlist is one of two hand-maintained copies. The new test reads the meta-schema's copy and fails naming the missing slug if they drift again; verified by removing trust-task-control and watching it fail. Found while retiring trust-task-ok ([#292](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/292)), which swept for references to the slug and noticed the two lists disagreed. ### Specifications - Bound the remaining free-text payload members and state who reads them ([#301](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/301)) SPEC.md §7.3 (framework 0.5.0) item 19 has three parts. PR #296 closed most of part 1 for eight member names (`reason`, `note`, `detail`, `description`, `message`, `text`, `label`, `comment`), 92 members in all. Sweeping the whole corpus rather than a name list finds **48 more** unbounded free-text members across 27 draft specifications and 10 shared schemas, under names the earlier sweep did not look for: `purpose`, `deviceLabel`, `displayName`, `explanation`, `summary`, `title`, `name`, `blurb`, `filename`, `trace`, `error`, `lastError`, `deniedReason`, `displayHint`, `consequences`, `rpName`, `userName`, `userDisplayName`. The one the earlier review named specifically is here: `task-consent`'s `Effect.summary` — the member its own schema calls "the ONLY member a consent surface is guaranteed to be able to render" — was unbounded on the surface a human reads to approve an action. It is now 500, the same figure as the `note` beside it. Bounds are drawn from the vocabulary the corpus already uses and sized per member, not applied uniformly: 64 WebAuthn entity names (`rp.name`, `user.name`, `user.displayName`, `rpName`, `userName`, `userDisplayName`) — the length WebAuthn tells authenticators to truncate to, so a longer value would be silently cut on the device rather than carried. 128 `purpose` where it names a decision slot or a declared intent. This is consistency repair, not a new judgement: policy/activate/0.1 and policy/active/0.1 already declared `maxLength: 128` on the request member while the response that echoes it declared none. 256 display labels and names — `deviceLabel`, `displayName`, `displayHint`, `label`, `title`, `name`, `blurb`, `filename`; matches #296's reasoning that a display name is not prose. 500 consent-surface prose a human reads while deciding — `Effect.summary`, `consequences[]`, credential-exchange `purpose`, `deniedReason`; matches task-consent/request/0.1 `note`. 1024 operator or service diagnostic prose — `explanation`, `trace[]`, `error`, `lastError`, and vta/credentials/issue `purpose`. **Part 3 of the MUST is the half nobody had done.** Item 19 also requires each specification to state who reads a free-text value, whether the recipient is expected to retain it, and whether it is trusted. These are the only two shared schemas in this change's blast radius that a retired spec reaches; the ten this PR edits are draft-only. * Members item 19's own last paragraph excludes: identifiers, opaque handles, digests and references; and values carried verbatim from an external vocabulary — DNS domains, did:webvh agent-name local parts, DID logs, Rego source, RFC 6901 pointers, HTTP header and cookie names, APNs topics, IANA media types, BCP 47 language tags, and maintainer- or community-defined role and kind vocabularies. Two members were bounded where the schema's own description calls the value an undeclared closed set (`nature`, `wired` in vtc/ceremonies/list) — deliberately left alone, because the right fix there is the closed enumeration item 19 prefers, not a length. All 48 members sit in `status: draft` specifications and are amended in place per SPEC §5.2. `npm run validate` re-checks all 533 fenced example documents against the amended schemas; none is rejected by a new bound. **Still open, and deliberately not in this PR:** item 19's "SHOULD be OPTIONAL" half. 18 of the 48 members bounded here are REQUIRED — `CredentialCreationOptions` `rp.name`/`user.name`/`user.displayName`, credential-exchange `purpose` (both copies), `Effect.summary`, `ContextRecord.name` and vta/contexts/create `name`, the three `enroll-challenge` WebAuthn names, `CommunityProfile.name`, `CommunityProfileView.name`, `CommunityProfileSnapshot.name`, and the four decision-slot `purpose` members. Added to the 13 #296 found, that is 31. Making any of them optional is a wire-compatibility change and belongs in its own PR; several (purpose binding, `Effect.summary`) are required by design and the specification should say so rather than change. This is **breaking**, on the same terms #296 judged itself so: typify emits a bounded member as a validating newtype, so `Option` becomes `Option`, `Option`, `Option` and so on, and the newtype rejects in `Deserialize` a document the library previously accepted. `@openvtc/trust-tasks` generates unchanged *types* — TypeScript has no length refinement — but its embedded schemas now reject over-long values at runtime. ## [0.2.1](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/compare/trust-tasks-v0.2.0...trust-tasks-v0.2.1) — 2026-08-26 ### Specifications - Bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength (§7.3) ([#296](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/296)) * spec: bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength SPEC.md §7.3 (framework 0.5.0) requires that any member holding free text declare a `maxLength`. 92 free-text string members across 83 draft schemas carried none, leaving the wire contract unbounded and every consumer to invent its own ceiling — or none, which is what §10.3 (schema-validation DoS) exists to prevent. title: spec(registry): gate SPEC §7.3 item 19 instead of counting it
body:
Auditing the five remaining backlog items. **Four were already closed**, and two of the counts I had been carrying were wrong in both directions.

| Item | quoted | actual |
|---|---|---|
| Unbounded free-text members | ~68 | **0 live** (17 in retired specs) |
| Redundant `permissionDenied` | 90 | **0 live** (4 in retired specs) |
| Security & Privacy sections | open | **37/37** sensitive specs have one |
| `max_age` follow-up | open | **done** — all three bindings default to `FreshnessPolicy::consequential` |
| Five proof-required responses unsigned | open | **genuinely open** — VTI-side, see below |

## Why there was nothing to fix

Every remaining instance of the first two sits in a `retired` spec. SPEC §5.3 freezes a retired specification's schema *at the moment of retirement*; adding `maxLength` narrows which documents validate, which §5.2 would require a MAJOR increment for — on a spec that is terminal and can take none.

Their live successors already bound them: `confirm/request/0.1` → `task-consent/request/0.1`, which bounds `note` at 500 and `reason` at 1024. **Exempt, not debt.**

## …and that is the problem

#296 and #301 bounded 112 members and left the corpus at zero. Nothing stopped the next spec from reintroducing one. The error-code shadowing rule has a gate; the `issuedAt` floor has a gate; item 19 had a number quoted in a backlog. **A count is not a check.**

This adds the missing lint on the same shape as its two neighbours — a `check*` function, a frozen/offending/conforming counter, an explicit §5.3 exemption, and a failure message stating the rule, the fix, and the pattern to copy.

## Detection is by name, deliberately

Only strings with no closed shape (no `enum`/`const`/`format`/`pattern`/`$ref`/`contentEncoding`) whose member name is in the free-text vocabulary. `did`, `contextId` and `cursor` are unbounded strings too — but bounding an identifier is §10.2's job at the transport, and a lint demanding `maxLength` on all **863** of them would be ignored. That is how the last backlog got its size.

## Verified it fires

A gate that never fires is worthless — this repo has already paid once for a guard that only proved a valid state *existed*.

```
$ # remove maxLength from 'note' in the DRAFT task-consent/request/0.1
Free-text bounds (§7.3 item 19): 336 spec(s) clean; 17 frozen in 12 retired spec(s); 1 unbounded
Build failed with the following problems:
  - task-consent/request/0.1/payload.schema.json: free-text member(s) 'note' declare no 'maxLength'. …

$ # restored
Free-text bounds (§7.3 item 19): 337 spec(s) clean; 17 frozen in 12 retired spec(s); 0 unbounded
Done.
```

The frozen count stays 17 throughout, so the §5.3 exemption holds while the live rule bites.

## Still open, and not in this PR

**The five proof-required responses that return unsigned** — `audit/list`, `auth/whoami`, `credential-exchange/present`, `trust-task-discovery`, `vta/memory/list`. All five specs do require proof on the response; the gap is in VTI, where e.g. `audit/list` returns `Json(AuditListResponse{…})` — a bare payload with no envelope and no proof.

Not attempted here: it needs the VTI 0.12 → 0.17 upgrade first, it spans `vtc-service` and `vta-sdk`, it needs a decision about which key the service signs responses with — and VTI's working tree is currently on another branch with uncommitted changes.

title: fix(ci): exempt workspace path dependencies from the wildcard ban
body:
**`cargo deny` is red on `main`** ([run 33031926033](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/actions/runs/33031926033)), and has been since #316 merged. Found while raising #317, whose CI it blocks. Two commits.

## 1. The wildcard ban and the release fix are in direct conflict

#316 deliberately dropped the `version` field from `trust-tasks-https`'s dev-dependency on `trust-tasks-proof`. That fix is correct: `cargo publish` resolves any dev-dependency carrying a `version` from the registry, which constrains publication order — while release-plz does **not** count dev-dependency edges when ordering the publish. That mismatch is what half-published 0.17.0.

But a path dependency with no version is precisely what cargo-deny reports as a wildcard:

```
error[wildcard]: found 1 wildcard dependency for crate 'trust-tasks-https'
```

**Fix:** `allow-wildcard-paths = true`, narrowing the ban to registry crates — where an unpinned requirement is an actual supply-chain risk. A path dependency resolves in-tree and cannot float to something the author did not intend, so the check was never buying anything there. The comment records *why* the `version` field is absent, so a future reader doesn't helpfully add it back and re-break the release.

## 2. `deny.toml` was not in the Rust workflow's `paths` filter

Found because the first commit's own PR ran no Rust CI: `deny.toml` was absent from the filter, so **the file that decides what the supply-chain check bans was the one file that change could not be tested by.** This is the same gap the filter's existing comment records for `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1`, `-capability-client` and `-ceremony`.

Adding it makes the fix self-validating, which is how the `cargo deny | pass` on this PR was produced rather than asserted.

## Verified

Locally with cargo-deny 0.19.8 — `advisories ok, bans ok, licenses ok, sources ok` — and now in CI: all twelve checks pass, including `cargo deny`, `cargo test (stable, full workspace)`, `trust-tasks-codegen drift` and `publication order is satisfiable`.

Independent of #317, which is docs-only and needs this merged (or its check re-run) to go green.

title: docs(spec): say what identifierScope is, and that it is not a scope taxonomy
body:
Companion to [`dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#6`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec/pull/6), which carries the same clarification into the framework specification proper. Addresses [`dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#5`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec/issues/5).

Two files, +8/−1. **No binding, crate, or package is affected.**

## What and why

`identifierScope` and the DTG credentials specification's proposed declared correlation scope ([`dtgwg-cred-spec#22`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22)) read as two vocabularies competing for one axis, with `community` and `linked` having no target here. Working through it, they are not competing — but neither document said so, and the member's name invites the misreading.

`identifierScope` is a machine-readable restatement of §10.5 item 1, which is **binary**: relationship-scoped, or reused across relationships and justified. Not a taxonomy of correlation width. Two consequences now stated in the text:

- It is declared by a **specification about a party role**, before any identifier exists — not by a holder about an identifier it controls. The two are assertions about different subjects; neither overrides the other. This is what lets #22 land in any form without this member moving.
- **A bounded-recognisability identifier is cross-relationship for item 1's purposes** — the joins item 1 forecloses are available to any two of that set who compare what they hold — so it is declared `public` and carries the justification obligation in full. That answers the reported gap without growing the enum.

## Changes here

1. `SPEC.md` — the same three paragraphs as the framework PR, adapted to this copy's `*VID*` emphasis and `[§10.5]` link conventions.
2. `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` — **`description` string only.** It previously called the member "the identifier correlation scope this party's VID is expected to have", which is exactly the reading the framework PR corrects.

## Why this touches no code

The enum is unchanged at three values, so all 56 existing declarations (37 `pairwise`, 19 `public`) stay valid, and `spec.meta.schema.json` is excluded from both generators **by name**:

- `scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs` — `NOT_PAYLOAD_SCHEMAS = new Set(["spec.meta.schema.json", "trust-task.schema.json"])`
- `trust-tasks-codegen/src/main.rs` — walks `payload.schema.json` only

No `IdentifierScope` or `identifier_scope` symbol exists in any `.rs` or `.ts` in the workspace. The one Rust site that opens the meta schema is a `#[test]` reading the *slug* allowlist, which early-returns on the published crate. So: no `codegen-drift`/`bindings-drift` exposure, no lockstep version bump, and none of the struct-literal breakage an additive *payload* member would cause.

## Validation

- `npm run validate` — 349 specs, 66 shared schemas, **no errors** (warnings are pre-existing `additionalProperties` ones).
- `node scripts/build-registry.mjs` — clean, `SPEC.md → website/SPEC.md` synced. The website copy is gitignored, so the diff stays at the two source files.
- The `checkIdentifierScopeJustification` lint is unaffected: it keys on `identifierScope === 'public'`, and this PR adds no value and moves no declaration.

title: ci: patch the npm Release PR over REST instead of `gh pr edit`
body:
The `release-ts-pr` job failed in [run 32991642096](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/actions/runs/32991642096):

```
GraphQL: Your token has not been granted the required scopes to execute this query.
The 'login' field requires one of the following scopes: ['read:org'], but your token
has only been granted the: ['repo'] scopes.
... 'name' ... 'slug' ...
```

## Why

`gh pr edit` resolves *editable metadata* before it writes — assignees, reviewers, milestones and organization **teams** — so it queries GraphQL for `login`, `name` and `slug`. Those need `read:org`. The release token has `repo`, which is the scope it ought to have: it pushes a branch and moves a PR, it does not read the org.

## Why this one mattered more than a red check

The branch had **already been force-pushed** when the edit failed:

```
+ 882be144...aeaa866f release-ts -> release-ts (forced update)
```

So the job died leaving **#303 titled `release @openvtc/trust-tasks 0.15.1` over a branch that releases 0.16.0** — a release PR whose description contradicts its own diff. That is the one state a release PR must never be in, because the title is what a reviewer reads before merging a publish.

## Fix

Patch title and body over REST. It resolves no metadata and is satisfied by `repo`; `{owner}/{repo}` is expanded by gh from the checkout, so no new env var:

```sh
gh api --silent -X PATCH "repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/$existing" \
  -f title="$title" -f body="$(cat "$body_file")"
```

`gh pr create` on the other branch of the `if` already has a `--label`-less fallback, so it is unaffected.

title: feat(rs): index the consumer policy by Type URI, not just the schema
body:
`schema_index` exists, in its own words, *"for consumers that dispatch on the URI"*. Such a consumer holds a `TrustTask` and has no `P` — so it cannot reach `TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy`, the one API that applies the flag-driven §7.2 checks. The index handed it the schema and stopped there. The only way to enforce recipient-REQUIRED (item 5b), proof-REQUIRED (item 7 clause A), audience binding (item 8) or §7.3 item 17's issuedAt-REQUIRED was to hand-maintain a URI → payload-type table — a second source of truth for data this file already generates, which goes stale the first time a spec is added. ## What's added ```rust pub fn spec_policy_for(type_uri: &str) -> Option ``` Emitted from the same loop as `schema_for`, so the two cannot drift. ## `SpecPolicy` is a value, not four public constants The point is to share the **checks**, not to hand a caller the flags and hope they re-apply them the same way. So: - `SpecPolicy::of::

()` reads the constants off a generated payload type - `SpecPolicy::enforce(&self, doc)` applies them - **`TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy` and `enforce_audience_binding` now delegate to it** The typed path and the URI-keyed path are one implementation. A new flag-driven rule added to `enforce` reaches both, and there is no second copy to forget — which is what the existing doc comment on `enforce_spec_policy` already promises ("so the two cannot diverge on the check set as new flag-driven rules are added") and could not previously deliver for a URI-dispatching consumer. ## Why `enforce` is generic over the payload and never reads it Every rule is about `recipient`, `proof` and `issuedAt`. Keeping it that way lets a URI-dispatching consumer run the full check set against a `TrustTask` **without first deserializing into the generated type** — which it may not want to do (its own body types are often not the generated ones), and must not be *required* to do: a payload that fails to parse would otherwise skip proof-REQUIRED entirely, which is the wrong way round. ## Request side only The rules are about a document a consumer *received*. A `#response` carries no audience-binding or proof requirement of its own, so there are no `#response` entries and `None` is the answer for one — asserted in `a_response_uri_has_a_schema_but_no_policy`. ## The coverage invariant is checked in the generator The crate exposes no list of every Type URI to iterate, so a runtime test could only sample. Both matches come from one loop, so a generator edited on one side and not the other is a bug *in that function* — and is now caught there: ``` anyhow::ensure!(request_arms == policy_arm_count, …) ``` 344 arms today; the build fails if the counts part. ## Tests - `a_dispatching_consumer_can_find_a_policy_by_type_uri` - `a_response_uri_has_a_schema_but_no_policy` - `the_uri_keyed_policy_matches_the_typed_one` — `spec_policy_for(uri) == SpecPolicy::of::

()` - `enforcing_by_uri_refuses_what_enforcing_by_type_refuses` — same verdict from both paths on a `TrustTask` That last one is worth reading: the fixture sets `recipient` deliberately, because `authenticate` is recipient-REQUIRED *and* proof-REQUIRED and the recipient rule fires first — leaving it off refuses for the wrong reason and proves nothing about proofs. ## Verification - `cargo test --workspace --all-features`: **0 failed** - `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets`: exit 0 - `cargo fmt --all --check`: exit 0 - codegen re-run: 344 payload modules, generated `schema_index.rs` compiles ## Motivation Found while making a URI-dispatching VTA conform to 0.17. It enforces none of these four checks today, and the alternative to this change was a 109-entry hand-maintained table in the consumer.

title: chore(deps)!: move VTI to trust-tasks-rs 0.17
body:
Every `trust-tasks-*` pin to **0.17**, plus the TDK crates that had to publish first — `affinidi-tdk` 0.10, `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.21, `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` 0.4 (affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#744). Two `trust-tasks-rs` versions in one graph fail to compile, so the messaging stack had to move before this could.

## What 0.17 changes

The generated payload, response, component structs **and enums** are `#[non_exhaustive]`. Struct literals become builders; matches gain a wildcard. That is what lets the registry add an optional member or an enum variant without breaking every consumer that spelled out the old list.

The cost is worth stating: **"is every required member set?" moves from compile time to the builder's conversion** — the builder starts each required member as `Err("no value supplied for …")`. Every call site here sets its required members explicitly and lets only optional ones default.

## The wildcard arms are decisions, and they went different ways

| site | unknown variant | why |
|---|---|---|
| `step_up` `evidence` | **refuse** | It chooses *which cryptographic gate to verify*. Falling through to the did-signed arm would check a gate the approver never presented, and report the step-up satisfied on evidence this VTA did not understand. |
| `services/{enable,update,disable,rollback,get}` | **refuse** | Every arm mutates the DID document; picking one writes the wrong service. `get` additionally exists to tell "never configured" from "configured and disabled" — answering about another transport destroys exactly that. |
| `device/register` kind / form factor / service kind | **refuse** | Writes an ACL entry, and the kind is what policy keys off. `wire_kind_to_internal` became fallible to say so. |
| `push/wake` reply status | **log and continue** | The only one. Wake is best-effort with a mediator-queue fallback, so an unknown status deserves an operator's attention but not a failure. Named separately from `None` because the two differ: "no status we could read" vs "a status we read but do not know". |

## Bounded newtypes

`reason`, `deniedReason` and siblings are no longer `String`. Parsing them at the producer means an over-long value fails on the device that would otherwise sign a document the consumer must reject.

## The response gate caught a live violation

`passkey-vms/enroll-challenge` put the raw DID into WebAuthn's `userName` / `userDisplayName`, which 0.17 bounds at `maxLength: 64`. A `did:webvh` is ~85 characters, so the response was unconformant:

```
RESPONSE-CONFORMANCE VIOLATION  …/passkey-vms/enroll-challenge/0.1#response:
  "did:webvh:QmSRTjKQF54iQfv58QjbbcunzZ1GiDzvuFFPERVHwUF4kX:webvh-host.test:dids:persona"
  is longer than 64 characters
```

**The schema is self-contradictory here** — `userName`'s description says *"e.g. the DID"* while its constraint makes any `did:webvh` unrepresentable. I fixed it VTI-side rather than upstream because the constraint is the defensible half: WebAuthn L2 §5.4.3 lets an authenticator truncate at 64 bytes, so the raw DID was *already* producing a credential-picker entry cut mid-SCID — unreadable, and identical between two DIDs on the same host.

Nothing is lost. `userHandle` carries the DID-derived binding and is unbounded. `userName` now takes the operator's `label`, or the DID with its `did:<method>:<scid>:` prefix dropped — the host and path are the part a person recognises, the SCID is the part they cannot. Clamped on a `char` boundary, with five unit tests.

## Verification

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets`: exit 0
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` (CI's combination): exit 0
- `cargo fmt --all --check`: exit 0
- `vta-service --all-features`: **0 failed**, zero response-conformance violations
- `vta-sdk`, `vta-mobile-core`, `vti-common`, `vta-vault`, `vta-webvh`, `vtc-service`: **0 failed**
- `TRUST-TASK RESPONSE COVERAGE 88/109 (81%)` — unchanged

## Follow-up, not in this PR

`enforce_spec_policy` has **zero call sites** in VTI. It is 0.17's single source of truth for the flag-driven §7.2 checks — recipient-REQUIRED (item 5b), proof-REQUIRED (item 7 clause A), audience binding (item 8), and the new issuedAt-REQUIRED (§7.3 item 17).

The dispatch spine's own comment says *"`enforce_audience_binding` needs `P: Payload`, so each slice's typed handler runs it after `parse_payload`"* — that comment is the **only** occurrence of the name in the repo. No handler runs it. Adopting the 0.17 superset is the compliance half of this move and gets its own PR.

(VTI's *producers* are already clean on `issuedAt`: the SDK's single `build_task_document` always stamps it, and I scanned all 233 task-shaped `json!` blocks — every production one sets it.)

title: fix(sdk): point session_store's stubs at the binding the SDK actually calls
body:
Five tests in `vta-sdk/tests/session_store.rs` fail on `main`. They stub bespoke REST routes the SDK stopped calling:

| stub | what the SDK does now |
|---|---|
| `GET /config` | `get_config()` dispatches `config/show/0.1` over `POST /trust-tasks` |
| `GET /acl/{did}` + `POST /acl` + `DELETE /acl/{did}` | rotation is a single atomic `POST /acl/swap` |

Every one 404s on an unmatched stub.

## Why now

Nothing compiled the file. It is gated on `session` + `test-support`, neither default, and no CI step built that pair until #1140 added `cargo test -p vta-sdk --all-features` — for exactly this class of rot. That step could not *run* until #1142 got the same job's clippy green, so it surfaces today rather than two days ago.

## The rotation stubs collapse three mocks into one

That is the change, not tidying. Rotation used to read the temp entry, create one under the new DID, then delete the temp — a window in which **both DIDs were privileged**. `acl/swap-key` moves the entry's role and contexts across atomically, so the window does not exist. The new DID is minted inside `rotate_key` and unknown to the caller, which is why the swap carries a VP-JWT proving control of it rather than naming it.

## One test lost its premise

`ensure_authenticated_rotation_fails_when_acl_read_fails` asserted that window's safety property — that a failed read bailed *before* the delete. There is no delete to bail before any more.

It now asserts what is still true and still matters: a refused swap leaves the stored session on the temp DID, so an operator can fix the ACL and retry with the credential they still hold. Renamed to `ensure_authenticated_rotation_leaves_the_temp_did_authoritative_on_failure`, and it checks the error names both the operation that refused and the remedy.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vta-sdk --all-features --test session_store`: **24 passed, 0 failed** (was 19/5)
- `cargo test -p vta-sdk --all-features`: 0 failed
- `cargo clippy -p vta-sdk --all-features --all-targets`: exit 0
- `cargo fmt --all --check`: exit 0

title: W3C alignment: DataIntegrityProof, digestMultibase, and the CID 1.0 multibase headers
body:
_Moved from [trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf#37](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/issues/37) — this repo is where the spec text lives. Original issue closed in favour of this one._

Raised from the Trust Tasks Task Force side, while working through how Trust Ceremonies and DTG credentials compose. Three alignment items, in increasing order of effort. Happy to open PRs for any of them.

Context for why this is coming from us: the Trust Tasks framework recently converged its own digest and multibase conventions on the same W3C sources ([#195], [#207]), and the same choices in DTG would mean **one verifier implementation** across both layers rather than two.

---

## 1. `digest` → `digestMultibase` — the prose is already right, the example is not

`dtg.md` §7.3 (VWC), line 459, already specifies the correct thing:

> The hash is encoded as a multibase string (multihash + multibase).

But the example at line 479 contradicts it:

```jsonc
"digest": "sha256:e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855",
```

That value is hex with a `sha256:` prefix — not multibase, not multihash. (It is `sha256("")`, so evidently a placeholder.)

Three suggested changes:

- **Rename the property to `digestMultibase`**, which is the name [W3C VCDM 2.0](https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-model-2.0/) defines for exactly this, so VC tooling recognises it rather than treating it as a DTG-specific field.
- **Fix the example.** A faithful conversion of the same digest is `zQmdfTbBqBPQ7VNxZEYEj14VmRuZBkqFbiwReogJgS1zR1n` — `z` + base58btc over multihash `0x12 0x20` + the identical 32 bytes.
- **Name the canonicalization.** "the verifiable credentials canonical representation" is unstated; a digest whose canonicalization is unspecified is not reproducible by a second implementation. [RFC 8785 (JCS)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785) is the natural choice — see item 2 for why it compounds.

I have this as a two-line patch ready if useful.

> Worth noting *how* this drifted, because we hit the identical failure: prose is not machine-checked, so an example can contradict its own schema and validation stays green. We found published examples in our own registry doing exactly this.

---

## 2. Multibase headers — restrict to `z` and `u` (CID 1.0 §2.4)

[W3C Controlled Identifiers 1.0 §2.4](https://www.w3.org/TR/cid-1.0/#multibase-0) normatively requires exactly two multibase headers:

- `z` — base58btc
- `u` — base64url-no-pad

and says of the rest: *"Other Multibase encoding values MAY be used, but interoperability is not guaranteed between implementations using such values."*

Suggest DTG state the same restriction wherever a multibase value appears, and **enforce the alphabets** rather than assuming them. base58btc excludes `0`, `O`, `I` and `l` — when we tightened our own pattern it immediately caught three published examples carrying digests that were not valid base58 at all, each containing a `0`. A permissive pattern hides that class of bug indefinitely.

---

## 3. `Ed25519Signature2020` → `DataIntegrityProof` — the larger one

`Ed25519Signature2020` appears throughout (`@context` at lines 137, 163, 209, 250, 301, 355…; `proof.type` at 147, 173, 219), and `DataIntegrityProof` appears nowhere. The spec targets VCDM 2.0 (`validFrom`, the v2 context) but pairs it with the suite Data Integrity supersedes.

The underlying issue is the same one as item 1, one level up: **`sha256:` hard-codes an algorithm into a value; `Ed25519Signature2020` hard-codes one into a type name.** `DataIntegrityProof` makes the algorithm data (`cryptosuite`) rather than structure, which is what turns a post-quantum migration into a configuration change instead of a schema revision.

Four reasons it is worth the churn:

1. **`eddsa-jcs-2022` is offline-verifiable; `eddsa-rdfc-2022` is not.** RDFC requires JSON-LD expansion, which requires resolving `@context` — a network dependency *at verification time*. For local-first and offline use cases (including in-person ceremonies where credentials sync later) that is close to decisive.
2. **It makes canonicalization singular.** With `eddsa-jcs-2022` the proof and the digest (item 1) both canonicalize with JCS — one implementation, one set of corner cases, and no way for a digest and a proof over the same document to disagree about what that document *is*.
3. **Selective disclosure has a path.** §9 mentions ZKP and selective disclosure; `DataIntegrityProof` has `bbs-2023`, `Ed25519Signature2020` has nothing. Choosing now avoids a second migration.
4. **Shared verification with Trust Tasks.** [SPEC §4.7] already defines a Trust Tasks `proof` as a W3C Data Integrity Proof, so a consumer that verifies one would verify the other.

**This does not disturb the v1.1 compatibility story** in §3. `DataIntegrityProof` is defined by VC-DATA-INTEGRITY and works with both v1.1 and v2.0 given the right context — it is orthogonal to the `issuanceDate`/`validFrom` mapping, and applies uniformly to both. §3s existing implementation note (*"Issuers SHOULD use well-supported proof types"*) already anticipates this being a decision rather than a fixed property.

**Cost, stated honestly:** it touches every example in the document and changes the `@context` arrays, and existing `Ed25519Signature2020` verifiers will not read the new proofs. A real migration, not a relabelling — which is why I am raising it rather than opening a PR.

---

## Suggested target shape

| Concern | Choice | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Proof envelope | `DataIntegrityProof` | VC-DATA-INTEGRITY |
| Default suite | `eddsa-jcs-2022` | offline-verifiable |
| Selective disclosure | `bbs-2023` | same envelope |
| Digests | multibase-multihash over JCS, as `digestMultibase` | VCDM 2.0 |
| Multibase headers | `z` and `u` only, alphabets enforced | CID 1.0 §2.4 |

Items 1 and 2 are small and unambiguous. Item 3 is a genuine decision for the DTG editors.

[#195]: https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/195
[#207]: https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/207
[SPEC §4.7]: https://trusttasks.org/SPEC#47-proof
