title: fix(ceremony): reject recorder-minted terminal markers and duplicate step instances
body:
## Two receipts a malicious recorder could forge, and what stops them now

`trust-tasks-ceremony`'s `verify()` returned `Outcome::Complete` for two receipts
it should have rejected. Both are in the class the design note claims the receipt
layer defends against, and neither had a test.

### 1. The recorder minted the marker the spec says it cannot (HIGH)

`specs/trust-ceremony-receipt/0.1/spec.md` states:

> At least one enumerated step **MUST** have carried `ceremony.terminal` in its
> signed content. A recorder cannot mint that marker without the terminal step
> issuer's key.

Verifier rule 5 only required the verifier to "confirm at least one enumerated
step carries `terminal`", and `lib.rs` read `ReceiptStep.terminal` — a boolean on
the **receipt entry**, written by the recorder. `DefinitionStep.terminal` was
parsed and never consulted, and nothing ever looked at a held document's *signed*
`ceremony.terminal`.

**Before.** A recorder truncates the record just before the step that would have
changed the outcome, sets `terminal: true` on the last entry it kept, and the
receipt verifies `Complete`. Every remaining link still chains, because a chain
detects an omission through the *successor* and the dropped step has none. This
is precisely the truncation attack the marker exists for, and the recorder is the
party performing it.

**Now.**
- `terminal` on an entry whose step the definition does not declare `terminal: true`
  → `Invalid`. A recorder does not get to nominate a terminal step.
- The marker is confirmed from the **signed** `ceremony.terminal` of a held
  document. A `terminal` echo the held document contradicts → `Invalid`.
- Where **no** document is held for any definition-terminal step → `Unverifiable`
  naming the document that would have carried the marker. `Complete` now means
  the verifier actually saw it.
- Where every definition-terminal step **is** held and none carries the marker →
  `Incomplete`. That is a prefix, not an unanswerable question.

The spec explicitly permits verifying while holding no step documents
(`spec.md:132`), and that is exactly the case where nothing but the recorder's
word backs `terminal`. The honest outcome there is `Unverifiable`, not `Complete`.

### 2. Thresholds were inflatable by repetition (HIGH)

`*instances.entry(s.step.clone()).or_insert(0) += 1` counted every receipt entry,
with no de-duplication by document `id` or by `issuer`.

**Before.** A recorder lists one approver's single decision twice and satisfies
`threshold.ofStep` with `n = 2`. One party's approval becomes an M-of-N quorum.

**Now**, rejected before anything is counted:
- two entries sharing a document `id` (an `id` is globally unique per SPEC §4.3);
- two entries for one step at one `round` where multiplicity is `single`;
- two entries at one round from one `issuer` where multiplicity is `perRole`.

De-duplication alone does not close it — a recorder that cannot list one approver
twice can invent a second — so each step's `issuer` is now checked against the VIDs
the enactment bound to the role the definition names as that step's issuer.
`verify()` takes a new `Bindings` argument for this. It also fixes a latent bug:
`evidence.recorders` holds **role names**, so the old recorder check was comparing
a VID against a role name and could only pass if the caller passed a role name in.

## The gap between what the verifier claimed and what it checked

The design note's §7.9 lists eight verification steps. Each is now either
implemented or disclaimed in the spec — none is left silently unchecked.

| §7.9 | Check | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Group by `enactment`, reject `definitionDigest` disagreement | **Implemented** over held documents. `ceremony.enactment`, `ceremony.definitionDigest`, `ceremony.step`, `ceremony.round` and the document's `issuer`/`recipient` must agree with what the receipt enumerates. Spec rule 9. |
| 2 | Resolve each `step` in the definition | Was already implemented. |
| 3 | `round` within the repetition bound | Was already implemented. |
| 4 | Walk `prev`, check the salted digests | **Implemented** over held documents. A held document's signed `ceremony.prev` must name a predecessor the receipt enumerates, with the digest the receipt gives it, and that predecessor's step must be an ancestor of this one in the definition's `prev` graph — transitively, so an enactment that skips an optional step still verifies, and same-step for a bounded repetition. This is what carries the spec's claims at `:64` and `:74`; before this, "the recorder attests ordering" rested on nothing. A predecessor the receipt does **not** enumerate is `Invalid` — the omitted-intermediate-step attack. Recorder rule 5 (salt required where any step carries `prev`) is enforced too. Spec rule 10. |
| 5 | Bind `issuer`/`recipient` to the definition's roles | **Implemented**, with a new `bindings: &Bindings` argument as the task anticipated. `Definition` now parses `roles`; `DefinitionStep` parses `kind`, `issuer`, `recipient`, `multiplicity`, `prev` and `optional`, none of which existed before — so these could not have been checked however `verify()` was written. Spec rule 8. |
| 6 | Recurse into a nested ceremony step | **Narrowed.** The child's evidence is its own receipt against its own pinned definition; recursion needs input this verifier does not have. A receipt containing a `kind: ceremony` step now returns `Unverifiable` naming the nesting, rather than `Complete` on the strength of a step nobody verified. The spec now says a verifier is not required to recurse, and MUST NOT report the parent complete on an unverified child. (`scripts/validate-ceremonies.mjs:127` already warns that nested resolution is unimplemented at publication time; that is a sibling's file and is untouched.) |
| 7 | Evaluate the completion predicate | Was implemented; now evaluated over **de-duplicated** instances. |
| 8 | Confirm a terminal step | **Implemented from the signed marker** — see defect 1. |
| — | `maxDuration` | **Narrowed.** The receipt payload carries no step `issuedAt`, so the issuance window is not derivable from a receipt at all. The spec now says so explicitly and points a verifier holding the step documents at their timestamps instead. |

The spec also gained a **"What a verifier is not required to check"** section, and
its attack table now says which of its defences require the verifier to hold
documents — two of the four do. A verifier holding none learns that *a recorder
the definition names enumerated a set of steps satisfying the completion rule*,
which is a real claim and strictly weaker than "this enactment completed".

No required member was removed and no rule was weakened. Where the spec was right
and the code was behind, the code moved; the spec changes are additional MUSTs
plus honest disclaimers of things it never actually required.

## Tests and fixtures

43 tests pass (was 22). Fixtures are **built** rather than pasted — each step's
digest is computed from the document under the enactment salt, so a test cannot
assert against a digest no document produces. New:

*The two attacks, directly:*
- `terminal_on_a_step_the_definition_does_not_declare_terminal_is_invalid` — truncated receipt, recorder-minted marker
- `a_terminal_marker_no_held_document_backs_is_unverifiable_not_complete` — **the receipt that used to verify Complete**
- `a_terminal_echo_the_signed_document_contradicts_is_invalid`
- `a_signed_terminal_marker_on_a_non_terminal_step_is_invalid`
- `every_terminal_candidate_held_and_unmarked_is_a_prefix`
- `one_approvers_step_listed_twice_does_not_satisfy_a_two_of_n_threshold` — **the duplicate-entry threshold inflation**
- `a_threshold_over_instances_is_satisfied_by_distinct_bound_parties` — the control, so the rejection above proves something
- `an_unbound_issuer_cannot_stand_in_for_a_second_approver`
- `the_same_document_enumerated_twice_is_invalid`
- `a_single_multiplicity_step_enumerated_twice_at_one_round_is_invalid`
- `a_repeatable_step_at_distinct_rounds_is_not_a_duplicate` — de-duplication must not break bounded repetition

*The newly implemented checks:*
- `a_predecessor_the_receipt_does_not_enumerate_is_invalid`, `a_prev_digest_the_receipt_contradicts_is_invalid`, `a_prev_naming_a_step_that_is_not_an_ancestor_is_invalid`, `a_chain_that_skips_an_optional_step_still_verifies`, `a_receipt_carrying_prev_without_the_salt_is_invalid`
- `a_step_issuer_the_enactment_did_not_bind_is_invalid`, `a_document_addressed_outside_the_recipient_role_is_invalid`, `unsupplied_role_bindings_are_reported_not_assumed`
- `a_held_document_from_another_enactment_is_invalid`, `a_held_document_pinning_another_definition_is_invalid`, `a_document_signed_by_someone_other_than_the_enumerated_issuer_is_invalid`
- `a_nested_ceremony_step_is_reported_unverifiable`
- `the_published_definition_deserializes_with_every_member_verification_needs` — parses the registry's real `ceremonies/vtc/member-onboarding/0.1/ceremony.json`, since the members added here went unparsed before

`holding_no_step_documents_is_not_a_failure` asserted `Complete` and is the test
that encoded the hole; it is now `holding_no_step_documents_is_unverifiable_not_a_failure`
and asserts the reason names the marker that could not be checked.

Receipt-level attack fixtures live in the crate rather than in
`ceremonies/ceremony.invalid-examples.json`: that file is a **definition**-level
harness driven by `scripts/validate-ceremonies.mjs --test`, which has no
receipt-verification code path (and is owned by a sibling on this branch set).
A fixture file nothing executes is the "checker never shown to fail" antipattern
the repo warns about, so these go where they run. `ceremonies/` is untouched.

## Breaking change

`trust-tasks-ceremony` 0.1.1 → **0.2.0**, and this is breaking in two ways worth
stating plainly:

1. **Receipts that used to verify `Complete` now return `Unverifiable`** unless
   the caller holds the terminal step's document *and* supplies the enactment's
   role bindings. That is the fix, not a side effect — both were being credited
   as checked when neither was.
2. `verify()` gains a `bindings: &Bindings` argument between `recorder` and
   `held`. Pass `Bindings::unbound()` if you do not have them; the role rules are
   then reported as unchecked rather than assumed to pass.

New public types: `Bindings`, `StepKind`, `Multiplicity`, `DefinitionRole`, plus
new fields on `Definition` and `DefinitionStep`. CHANGELOG updated. No in-repo
callers.

## Checks

```
cargo build   -p trust-tasks-ceremony    Finished
cargo test    -p trust-tasks-ceremony    43 passed; 0 failed
cargo clippy  -p trust-tasks-ceremony --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings   Finished (no warnings)
cargo fmt --all -- --check               clean
cargo doc     -p trust-tasks-ceremony --no-deps --all-features   Finished
npm run validate                         Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas
npm run validate-ceremonies              Validated 2 ceremony definition(s), 0 warning(s)
npm run test-ceremonies                  20/20 invalid definitions correctly rejected
```

(The `npm run validate` warnings are pre-existing and in `vta/*` schemas, outside
anything this PR touches.)

## Bindings regeneration

**Not required.** `specs/trust-ceremony-receipt/0.1/payload.schema.json` is
deliberately **unchanged** — every spec edit is prose and conformance rules, which
do not reach the generators. `spec.md` was amended in place rather than versioned:
its front matter is `status: draft`, and SPEC §5.2 permits changing a draft's
schema and prose without minting a version. The Rust and TS binding trees are
untouched, per the instruction not to collide with the codegen owner.

## Files outside the owned paths

One line of `Cargo.lock` (`trust-tasks-ceremony 0.1.1 → 0.2.0`), the mechanical
consequence of the version bump. Nothing else outside `trust-tasks-ceremony/`,
`ceremonies/` (untouched) and `specs/trust-ceremony-receipt/`.

title: fix(ceremony): reject recorder-minted terminal markers and duplicate step instances (#270)
body:
fix(ceremony): reject recorder-minted terminal markers and duplicate step instances (#270)

* fix(ceremony): reject recorder-minted terminal markers and duplicate step instances

Two receipts a malicious recorder could produce verified as Complete.

`verify()` read `ReceiptStep.terminal` — a boolean the recorder writes on the
receipt — while `DefinitionStep.terminal` was parsed and never consulted and
nothing looked at a held document's signed `ceremony.terminal`. The receipt
specification's claim that "a recorder cannot mint that marker without the
terminal step issuer's key" was therefore not implemented, and a truncated
prefix carrying `terminal: true` produced Complete: exactly the truncation
attack the marker exists for.

Instance counting was `*instances.entry(s.step).or_insert(0) += 1` over every
receipt entry, with no de-duplication by document `id` or by `issuer`. Listing
one approver's single decision twice satisfied `threshold.ofStep` with n = 2.

`terminal` is now accepted only on a step the definition declares terminal, and
is confirmed against the signed marker in a held document; where no terminal
step document is held the outcome is Unverifiable naming what could not be
checked, so Complete means the verifier saw the marker. Duplicate `id`s, two
entries for one step at one round, and two entries at one round from one issuer
of a perRole step are all rejected before counting.

De-duplication alone does not close the threshold — a recorder that cannot list
one approver twice can invent a second — so `verify()` also takes the
enactment's role bindings and checks each step's issuer against the role the
definition names. `evidence.recorders` holds role names, so the recorder check
was previously comparing a VID against a role name; it now resolves properly.

Also implements the `prev` chain walk and envelope agreement over held
documents, and parses the `roles`, `issuer`, `recipient`, `multiplicity`,
`prev` and `kind` members that were absent from the definition types. A nested
ceremony step is reported Unverifiable rather than passed as Complete.

Breaking: receipts that verified Complete under 0.1.x return Unverifiable
unless the caller holds the terminal step document and supplies role bindings.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(ceremony-receipt): require the signed terminal marker and disclaim what a verifier does not check

Verifier rule 5 said "confirm at least one enumerated step carries `terminal`",
which the recorder-supplied `steps[].terminal` satisfies — contradicting the
same document's claim that a recorder "cannot mint that marker without the
terminal step issuer's key". The rule now requires the marker in the step
document's signed content, and requires a verifier holding no terminal step
document to report that it could not verify completion.

Adds the de-duplication rule that makes an instance threshold a threshold, the
role-binding rule that makes a distinct issuer a distinct authorised party, the
envelope-agreement and chain-walk rules that carry the ordering claim, and a
section naming what a conforming verifier is NOT required to establish: nested
ceremonies, `maxDuration`, and the omission of a step with neither a held
successor nor a terminal marker. The attack table now says which of its
defences need the verifier to hold documents, since two of them do.

Amended in place rather than versioned: `status: draft`, which SPEC §5.2
permits. Prose and conformance rules only — `payload.schema.json` is unchanged,
so no binding regeneration is required.

title: spec(keys): a key that derives from nothing needs a word for itself
body:
A maintainer may hold keys generated from a CSPRNG rather than derived from a
seed — reproducible from nothing, recoverable by no means once the maintainer's
storage is gone. **The value of such a key is precisely that it cannot be
exported.**

Neither the request nor the response vocabulary could express it:

- `keys/create/0.1` is `additionalProperties: false`, so a consumer asking for
  one is rejected outright.
- `KeyOrigin` offered only `derived` and `imported`, so a maintainer that
  minted one could not describe it.

## What is added

| where | member |
|---|---|
| `keys/create/0.1` request | `internal: boolean` |
| `keys/_shared/0.1` `KeyOrigin` | the value `internal` |

## The response side matters more than it looks

A consumer asks for an unexportable key **because it needs that property**. A
maintainer that ignored an unrecognised member and returned a derived key would
hand back something that looks identical and is not — same shape, same `keyId`,
same `publicKey`, and none of the guarantee.

`origin` is `internal` iff the request was honoured, so the difference is
detectable rather than a matter of trust. The specification now states that a
maintainer which cannot mint such a key MUST reject the request rather than
silently downgrade it, and that consumers MUST confirm via `origin`.

This was found from the other end. In an implementation, a CLI printed a full
non-recoverable-key warning, required the operator to type a confirmation
phrase, and then dropped the flag before it reached the wire — so the operator
was told they had created a key that could never be exported, and had not. The
CLI *did* check `origin` on the way back, which is the right instinct and the
reason this member belongs in the specification rather than in an extension.

## `derivationPath` and `internal` are contradictory

An internal key derives from no seed and records no path, so a request carrying
both is incoherent. Documented on `derivationPath`, which a maintainer SHOULD
reject when combined with `internal: true`.

## Why `internal` declares no `default`

`"default": false` reads naturally and the first version had it. A declared
default is **materialised by the generated bindings**, so an absent `internal`
reappears as an explicit `false` on re-serialisation — `keys/create`'s own
request example failed its round-trip immediately. Same trap as
`VaultEntry.status` in #268; the semantics are stated in prose instead, where a
binding cannot act on them.

## Compatibility

Additive. Both members are optional, and `KeyOrigin` gains a value rather than
changing one, so no previously-valid document becomes invalid.

## Gates

- `npm run validate` — 349 specs
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` + `cargo fmt --all`
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` + `npm run check-bindings` — all agree
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — green

Releases `trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.17 / `trust-tasks-ts` 0.12.17.

title: docs(spec): release framework version 0.5.0
body:
docs(spec): release framework version 0.5.0

Bumps the framework to 0.5.0 and records the revision in Appendix B:
identifier correlation, one document lifecycle, freshness bounds, the
retention, ingest and identifier-scope declarations, bounded free-text
members, the empty-response acknowledgement and the trust-task-ok
deprecation, discovery hardening, the error-model rules, and the two
named digests.

Additive with one deprecation: the wire format gains no member, the
three new front-matter declarations are SHOULD with fail-safe readings
of an absent value, and every document conforming to 0.4.0 still
conforms. The entry flags the two items needing a companion change in
the registry repository.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78

title: docs(spec): name the two digests the framework computes
body:
docs(spec): name the two digests the framework computes

taskDigest excludes the top-level proof and asks what the document
says; stepDigest includes it and asks which serialization arrived. Both
are called digestMultibase in the places they appear, so an
implementation with one function of that name has picked one answer and
applies it to both questions — and whichever it picked is wrong for
one of them. Adds a table stating the difference beside the citation
rule that depends on it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78

title: docs(spec): bound error message disclosure, details size and cancelled effects
body:
docs(spec): bound error message disclosure, details size and cancelled effects

The message-sanitization rule was normative for identityMismatch alone
and SHOULD guidance in an informative section for everything else, yet
every rejection is emitted on the same path, to the same
possibly-unauthenticated party, before any authorization decision. It
is now normative for every code: a message MUST NOT reveal
consumer-internal state, the contested value of a mismatched party, or
resolver, verifier or key-status internals, because otherwise each
error response is an identity- and reachability-probing oracle the
consumer operates on the sender's behalf.

details was the one error-payload member with no size bound, travelling
in the direction no producer-side bound reaches. A specification
defining a details shape MUST declare a bound; absent one, 4096 bytes
of JCS or 16 immediate members. An oversized details is ignored, never
grounds to discard the code.

The cancelled code gains a framework-defined details shape: the same
array-of-effects trust-task-control already defines for a
producer-requested stop, so what had already landed is machine-readable
whichever party decided.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78
significance_reasons: Normative requirement language changed

title: docs(spec): harden discovery against unauthenticated responses
body:
docs(spec): harden discovery against unauthenticated responses

The discovery specification justifies an OPTIONAL proof requirement by
saying the parties "have already authenticated through the transport".
That is false over the HTTPS binding, whose own security profile states
it provides no producer-to-consumer end-to-end guarantee — so a
discovery exchange there is between parties that have authenticated
nothing, and Permitting proof to Be Omitted already refuses to read a
guarantee off a transport's name.

Raises the applicable proof requirement to RECOMMENDED, and adds the
discoverer-side rule the next-step specification already carries: MUST
NOT act on a response whose origin it can authenticate neither in-band
nor from the transport. A responder's advertised requirements — a
requiredExt namespace, say — are untrusted and MUST NOT cause a
producer to attach data it would not otherwise send. A request's
pattern list SHOULD be bounded, since the matching work is paid by the
party that did not choose it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78

Security, privacy, threat, or vulnerability relevance

title: docs(spec): acknowledge a fire-and-forget task with an empty response
body:
docs(spec): acknowledge a fire-and-forget task with an empty response

Forbidding a fire-and-forget specification from emitting #response is
the sole reason trust-task-ok exists, and that slug is defined so it
cannot carry meaning: a consumer MUST NOT require any member and a
producer MUST NOT rely on receiving one. A registry entry, a schema and
a generated type per language to say "something arrived", on a type
bearing no relation to the one the producer sent.

A fire-and-forget consumer MAY now return <type>#response with payload
{}, and a producer still MUST NOT rely on it. trust-task-ok is
deprecated in favour of it — producers MUST keep accepting it, the slug
stays reserved permanently, and retirement of the registry entry is a
separate matter for the registry.

Adds a table of the three response dispositions beside the fragment
rule. "Is this a response?" was answerable in three separate places, so
implementations hard-code a slug list the next reserved slug
invalidates.

title: docs(spec): bound free-text payload members
body:
docs(spec): bound free-text payload members

A free-text member is the one place in a Trust Task document where the
schema constrains the shape and nothing constrains the content, so it
is where personal data arrives in a task declaring it ingests none,
where a pasted secret arrives, and where instructions to a downstream
reader arrive in a field the specification took for a comment. An
unbounded string is also an unbounded document, and Parser Hardening
puts the limit at the transport layer, where one figure covers every
task a consumer implements.

Specification Requirements gains item 19: any free-text member MUST
declare a maxLength, SHOULD be optional, and the specification MUST
state who reads it, whether it is retained, and whether it is trusted.
Prefer a closed enum plus one bounded note. task-consent/request/0.1's
500-character attributed, explicitly-untrusted note is the model.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78
significance_reasons: Normative requirement language changed
Interoperability, canonicalisation, conformance, or protocol behaviour

title: docs(spec): declare retention, ingested data and identifier scope
body:
docs(spec): declare retention, ingested data and identifier scope

Three additive front-matter declarations, each descriptive on the same
terms as the existing sideEffects and exposure items — they describe a
task, never authorize it, and each carries a fail-safe reading of an
absent or unresolvable value.

retention (class of transient, exchange or durable, plus rationale)
gives the framework a retention vocabulary it has never had: every
existing rule that says "retain" mandates more retention and none
bounds it, so the safe reading of every task has been to keep
everything.

exposure.ingests closes the response-only blind spot in the exposure
class: a task that ingests a full verifiable presentation or free-text
personal data declares discloses: none today and is correct. Absent or
unresolvable is read as no less sensitive than personal.

parties[].identifierScope makes the pairwise-identifier rule
machine-readable; absent is read as no less correlatable than public.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78

title: docs(spec): require a bounded freshness window for accepted documents
body:
docs(spec): require a bounded freshness window for accepted documents

The duplicate-execution record of Consumer Requirements item 11 is
implementable only inside a bounded window, and nothing obliged a
document to carry a timestamp that could place it in one. A document
with no expiresAt and no usable issuedAt never leaves the set a
consumer must recognize, so its record has to be kept forever.

Consumer Requirements gains item 13: reject a document whose issuedAt
is in the consumer's future beyond its skew tolerance, and one whose
expiresAt is at or before its issuedAt. Both are malformedRequest
rather than expired, because expired names a document that was once
acceptable. Specification Requirements gains item 17: a specification
defining a consequential Trust Task MUST require issuedAt.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78
significance_reasons: Normative requirement language changed

title: docs(spec): state one document lifecycle and what silence means
body:
docs(spec): state one document lifecycle and what silence means

The lifecycle a consumer follows was implied in five places — the
acceptance bound of item 4, the duplicate record of item 11, the
re-evaluation of item 12, task control, and the error section — and no
section named the whole set, so implementations inferred five
overlapping lifecycles from one document.

Adds a normative state table (received, validated, accepted, executing,
suspended, responded, errored, cancelled, expired) naming the reserved
reply that carries each transition and what silence means in each
state. Silence had acquired four distinct meanings across the document;
it now signifies no state at all. A transport binding MUST map the
table onto its own protocol, so a 202 is not read as acceptance and a
dropped connection is not read as cancellation.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78
significance_reasons: Normative requirement language changed
Interoperability, canonicalisation, conformance, or protocol behaviour

title: docs(spec): bound identifier correlation and linkability
body:
docs(spec): bound identifier correlation and linkability

The framework has never said anything about what its own identifiers
disclose about the parties. The median document on the wire names both
parties in clear, is signed, and is worth retaining, so party
identifiers and correlation handles are joinable by anyone who holds
two of them.

Party identifiers SHOULD be relationship-scoped unless a specification
states why a public identifier is intrinsic to what the task asserts.
The three correlators — id, threadId, ceremony.enactment — MUST be
freshly minted and unguessable, and MUST NOT be derived from subject
data. issuedAt MAY be coarsened where sub-minute freshness is not
needed. A ceremony enactment links every counterparty in a flow by
default; enactmentPrivacy: blinded is the mitigation.

title: test(vta): gate response conformance, and measure the coverage that qualifies it
body:
Closes the last two violations #1113 found, turns the layer into a gate, and —
the part that matters most — makes the number that qualifies the gate
measurable.

## An empty inventory is not the same as a clean surface

`KNOWN_VIOLATIONS` is now empty and the layer fails the build. That reads like
the end of the job. It is not, and shipping the zero without the second number
would be the misleading move:

```
TRUST-TASK RESPONSE COVERAGE  29/109 (27%) — 80 never exercised
```

A full suite run exercises **29 of the 109 tasks whose response schema is
published**. The other eighty emit no success response anywhere under `tests/`,
so the gate has never looked at them. And they are not the quiet corners:

| uncovered | what it is |
|---|---|
| `keys/sign`, `keys/derive-and-sign`, `keys/derive-and-sign-document`, `keys/import` | the signing oracle |
| `vault/release`, `vault/proxy-login`, `vault/sign-trust-task` | the credential release path |
| `device/wipe`, `device/disable` | remote device control |
| every `consent/*` | the DTTE ceremony |
| `vta/contexts/*`, `vta/did-templates/*`, `vta/app-state/*` | whole families |

That is the highest-stakes surface in the workspace, and the conformance layer
has no opinion about any of it.

## So the coverage figure is now produced, not estimated

`scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` runs the suite and prints the figure plus the
uncovered list. Two design points:

- **Coverage is a property of a run, not a process.** Every binary under
  `tests/` is its own process (twenty-eight here, thirty-five on the VTC), so an
  in-memory set answers "what did *this* binary touch", which is not the
  question. The layer appends each newly-seen task to a file named by
  `TRUST_TASK_OBSERVED_FILE`; the reporter aggregates. Appends are `O_APPEND`,
  one line at a time, below `PIPE_BUF` — concurrent binaries interleave lines
  rather than corrupt them.
- **The denominator is derived, never hand-listed** — `dispatched_uris()`
  filtered to those whose `#response` schema resolves. A hand-kept denominator
  drifts, and a coverage figure over a drifted denominator is worse than none.

The reporter is `#[ignore]`d: without a preceding suite run it would report zero
coverage and say nothing true.

### A correction to #1113's description

That PR said "29 of the 79 bound tasks". **79 was wrong** — it came from
`grep -c 'checked!'` on the witness table, which counts occurrences of a macro
name, not a census. Measured properly: 132 URIs dispatched, 109 with published
schemas (the bare and `#response` sets coincide exactly), 29 observed. The
coverage fraction is worse than reported, not better.

## The vault pair, closed upstream

`vault/{get,list}/0.1` leaked `status` / `graceUntil` / `deletedAt` — #540's
archival lifecycle, added to the storage row and never to the wire contract.

The fix was upstream, because the specification was inconsistent with itself:
`vault/list/0.1` defines a `status` filter whose `all` value "lists every entry
regardless of lifecycle state", while `VaultEntry` is
`additionalProperties: false` and carried no lifecycle member — so that view
returned a mixed list no consumer could partition.
[dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#268](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/268)
adds the members; this bumps to the `trust-tasks-rs 0.11.16` that carries them.
No service change was needed: the daemon was already right.

## The gate

A violation now replaces the response with an error document, so the test that
provoked it fails on its own assertion. Not a panic: the spine unwinds through
whichever transport is driving, and for DIDComm and TSP that is a background
inbound loop, where a panic reads as "the peer went away" and names nothing.

`KNOWN_VIOLATIONS` stays as the place to record a violation genuinely blocked on
something external, with the blocker named. Nothing consults it at runtime, so
re-adding an entry does not make a violation tolerable — it only records it.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings`
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites green, **0 violations** with the gate live, coverage 29/109
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

Refs #1059

title: fix(vta)!: three of the four responses the conformance layer found
body:
Closes three of the four violations #1113's layer reported. The inventory goes
**4 → 2**, and the two that remain are blocked on a dependency rather than on a
decision here.

## `vta/webvh/dids/get/1.0` — a flatten that no conforming client could read

The record has been under `#[serde(flatten)]` since #849, which folded
`dids/get-log` into `dids/get`. The stated reason was good: flattening made the
merged response a strict superset of both shapes it replaced — the bare
`WebvhDidRecord` this task used to return, and the `{did, log}` of the retired
task — so callers of either kept working.

That superset was a superset of the two *old client types*, and of nothing
else. The published response is `additionalProperties: false`, so a flattened
record fails on **all eleven members at once** and omits `record`, which is
required. The `ext` slot was unreachable too.

The spec (#240, 19 Aug) postdates the flatten (#849, 29 Jul), so which side
should move is a real question and not an assumption — this repository has
guessed it the wrong way three times. **Its own sibling settles it.**
`dids/list` carries the same `WebvhDidRecord` component nested under `dids` and
has always conformed. Flattening made `get` the one outlier in its family, and
a top-level `log` beside a flattened record is a name collision waiting for the
record to grow one.

### The compiler could not see this, and the test could

Both SDK client methods decoded the flat response *directly* into their return
types — `get_did_webvh` into `WebvhDidRecord`, `get_did_webvh_log` into
`GetDidLogResponse`. Unflattening breaks both at runtime, and
`cargo build --workspace --all-targets` stays green throughout, because the
break is in serde, not in types.

`webvh_get_did_round_trips_after_the_get_log_fold` was written for precisely
this. Its doc comment reads:

> "superset" only helps because neither client type sets
> `deny_unknown_fields`. If either did, **or if the flatten were dropped for a
> nested `record` object, both calls would fail at runtime while every mocked
> test stayed green.**

It was right, and it caught it — for a reason it did not anticipate. The
comment expected the flatten to be dropped by choice; it was dropped because
the shape could not conform. Both client methods now project the envelope, and
the test still asserts what it always did: that values *survive*, not merely
parse, which is the property that made it catch this.

The REST route shares the response type, so `GET /webvh/dids/{did}` moved with
the Trust Task. The registry note claiming the REST response "is a superset of
the old `{did, log}`" is updated rather than left to rot.

## `provision/integration/0.2` — two nulls out of five

`adminTemplateName` and `webvhServerId` were the only two of five
`Option<String>` members without `skip_serializing_if`, so they serialised as
`null` against members the schema types `string`. Their three siblings already
skipped, which is what makes this a slip rather than a decision.

This is the sixth member in the programme to ship `null`-for-absent.

## Not here: the vault pair, and why it became a spec change

`vault/{get,list}/0.1` leak `status` / `graceUntil` / `deletedAt` — #540's
archival lifecycle, added to the storage row and never to the wire contract.

The fix is upstream, in
[dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#268](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/268),
because the specification is inconsistent with itself: `vault/list/0.1` already
defines a `status` request filter whose `all` value "lists every entry
regardless of lifecycle state", while `VaultEntry` is
`additionalProperties: false` and carries no lifecycle member. A consumer that
asks for every state gets a mixed list it cannot partition. Same shape as the
`extensions` gap in #267, found the same way.

Two notes from doing it, both of which would have been easy to get wrong:

- It adds **four** members, not the three observed. `archivedAt` is
  `skip_serializing_if` and simply had no test that archives then reads.
  Fixing only what the probe saw would have repeated the coverage gap the layer
  exists to expose.
- `status` deliberately declares **no JSON Schema `default`**. Writing
  `"default": "active"` is the natural thing and the first version did; codegen
  materialises a declared default into a non-`Option` field, so an absent
  `status` came back as an explicit `"active"` and broke round-trip idempotence
  for `vault/list`'s own response example.

The two entries stay in `KNOWN_VIOLATIONS` with the blocker named, and
`the_inventory_is_still_accurate` moves from 4 to 2 with them.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p vta-service --no-fail-fast` — 27 suites, only the two blocked vault violations reported
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

BREAKING CHANGE: `vta/webvh/dids/get/1.0` and `GET /webvh/dids/{did}` return the
record under `record` instead of flattened at the top level.
`provision/integration/0.2` omits `adminTemplateName` and `webvhServerId`
instead of sending them as `null`.

Refs #1059

title: spec(vault): VaultEntry carries the archival-lifecycle state its own list filter selects on
body:
`vault/list/0.1` specifies a `status` request filter whose `all` value lists
"every entry regardless of lifecycle state". **That view is not usable.**
`VaultEntry` is `additionalProperties: false` and carries no lifecycle member,
so a consumer that asks for every state receives a mixed list it has no way to
partition.

A specification that offers a filter and then withholds the member the filter
selects on is inconsistent with itself — the same shape as
`CredentialCreationOptions` without `extensions` in #267, and found the same
way: by validating what an implementation actually emits rather than what a
fixture says it emits.

## What is added

Four optional members on the shared `VaultEntry` component:

| member | meaning |
|---|---|
| `status` | `active` / `archived` / `deleted`. Absent means `active`. |
| `archivedAt` | when archived; present iff `status` is `archived` |
| `deletedAt` | when soft-deleted; present iff `status` is `deleted` |
| `graceUntil` | deadline after which a `deleted` entry is irreversibly purged |

`graceUntil` is the one that matters most in practice. A `deleted` entry is a
tombstone, not an absence, and without a deadline a consumer cannot distinguish
"still restorable" from "gone" — which is the difference between a holder
recovering their credential and losing it.

## Why `status` declares no `default`

It reads naturally to write `"default": "active"`, and the first version of
this change did. A declared default is **materialised by the generated
bindings**: `status` became a non-`Option` field with `#[serde(default = …)]`,
so an absent `status` reappeared as an explicit `"active"` on
re-serialisation. That broke round-trip idempotence for `vault/list`'s own
response example — a document that had never carried the member came back
carrying it.

The semantics are unchanged (absent still means `active`); they are stated in
prose, where a binding cannot act on them.

## Compatibility

Additive. Every member is optional, so no previously-valid document becomes
invalid, and a maintainer that models no archival lifecycle omits all four.

Five specifications reference the shared component and pick the members up:
`vault/{get,list,sync,upsert}` and `sync/event`.

## Gates

- `npm run validate` — 349 specs, 533 example documents
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` + `cargo fmt --all`
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` + `npm run check-bindings` — 349 specs against 349 TS and 344 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — 452 passed

Releases `trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.16 / `trust-tasks-ts` 0.12.16.

title: spec(vault): VaultEntry carries the archival-lifecycle state its own list filter selects on (#268)
body:
spec(vault): VaultEntry carries the archival-lifecycle state its own list filter selects on (#268)

`vault/list/0.1` specifies a `status` request filter whose `all` value lists
"every entry regardless of lifecycle state". That view was not usable:
`VaultEntry` is `additionalProperties: false` and carried no lifecycle member,
so a consumer that asked for every state received a mixed list it had no way to
partition. A specification that offers a filter and then withholds the member
the filter selects on is inconsistent with itself, the same way
`CredentialCreationOptions` without `extensions` was in 0.11.15.

Adds `status`, `archivedAt`, `deletedAt` and `graceUntil`, all optional. An
absent `status` means `active`, so a maintainer that models no archival
lifecycle omits them and every existing document stays valid.

`graceUntil` is the member that matters most in practice: a `deleted` entry is
a tombstone, not an absence, and without a deadline a consumer cannot tell
"still restorable" from "gone".

`status` declares no JSON Schema `default`. A declared default is materialised
by the generated bindings, so an absent `status` would reappear as an explicit
`"active"` on re-serialisation — which broke round-trip idempotence for
`vault/list`'s own response example on the first attempt.

Five specifications referencing the shared component pick the members up:
`vault/{get,list,sync,upsert}` and `sync/event`.

title: fix(vta)!: three of the four responses the conformance layer found (#1114)
body:
fix(vta)!: three of the four responses the conformance layer found (#1114)

Closes three of the four violations #1113 reported. The fourth is the vault
pair, blocked on trust-tasks-rs 0.11.16 (dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#268).

`vta/webvh/dids/get/1.0` carried its record under `#[serde(flatten)]` since
#849, to make the folded task a strict superset of the two shapes it replaced.
That superset was readable by no conforming client: the response is
`additionalProperties: false`, so a flattened record fails on all eleven
members and the `ext` slot is unreachable. Its sibling settles which side
moves — `dids/list` carries the same component nested under `dids` and has
always conformed, so flattening made `get` the outlier in its own family.

Both SDK client methods decoded the flat shape straight into
`WebvhDidRecord`, so the workspace compiled clean while the wire broke. They
now project the envelope. `webvh_get_did_round_trips_after_the_get_log_fold`
predicted exactly this in its doc comment and caught it.

`provision/integration/0.2` sent `null` for `adminTemplateName` and
`webvhServerId`, the only two of five `Option<String>` members without
`skip_serializing_if`.

BREAKING CHANGE: `vta/webvh/dids/get/1.0` and `GET /webvh/dids/{did}` return
the record under `record` instead of flattened at the top level.
`provision/integration/0.2` omits `adminTemplateName` and `webvhServerId`
instead of sending them as `null`.

title: test(vtc)!: make response conformance fail the build
body:
The response-conformance layer now **fails the build**. Until this, a green
suite was not evidence of conformance — #1107's own memory note said to grep
the run rather than trust the exit code, which is a signal nobody has to obey.

Also retargets `relationships/{list,graph}` to the `0.2`s published in
trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#266, closing the last VTC-family violations.

**The VTC family is now clean. Every remaining violation is `auth/*`.**

## The gate

A violation outside the allowlist returns `500` with the schema error, so the
test that provoked it fails on its own status assertion and prints the reason.

Chosen over panicking in middleware deliberately: a panic there surfaces at the
call site as a transport error — "the request failed" — which says nothing
about which task, or why.

## The allowlist, and why it can only shrink

Eight `auth/*` tasks, each listed with `ALLOWED_COUNT` asserted beside them.
Same discipline as `KNOWN_DRIFT_COUNT`, for the same reason: **the cheapest way
to make a failing check pass is to add a line to a list nobody is watching.**
Closing an entry means deleting it *and* lowering the count; adding one needs a
reason in review.

An allowlisted violation is still *reported*, just not fatal — pinned by a
test, because a list that suppressed the evidence would mean rediscovering each
entry before it could be closed.

## Two guards caught me, both correctly

**The allowlist named `login/{start,finish}/0.1`; the service binds `0.2`.**
Those two entries protected nothing, and the gate failed six step-up tests on
the first run. I had built the list from the violation *output* — which prints
whatever the request header said — rather than from the route mounts. Now taken
from `routes/mod.rs`.

**`every_bound_canonical_task_exists_in_the_registry` flagged a fake URI in my
own unit test.** I had used `trusttasks.org/spec/not/a/task/9.9` to exercise
the unknown-task path; that guard scans the crate for bound canonical URIs and
was exactly right that *"binding a `trusttasks.org/spec/` URI asserts the
registry serves it"*. Now `example.invalid`, with a comment saying why — a
guard that scans source for a URL pattern will find your fixtures too, and the
fix is to make the fixture obviously-not-real rather than to weaken the guard.

## A seeder that could never have caught a digest bug

`relationships/list` still failed after the `0.2` retarget, and it was not the
service: `seed_relationship` wrote `seed-{uuid}` into `vrcDigestMultibase`.
Unique per row, which is all the storage layer needed — and it meant **no test
ever exercised a digest that looked like a digest**, so the whole suite was
structurally blind to the format. It now computes a real multibase multihash
over the seeded credential.

## What remains

Eight `auth/*` tasks, all in the shared families both daemons serve. The models
genuinely differ (`passkeys` against `credentials`; `whoami`'s session needs an
`issuedAt` this service does not currently record).

The direction is settled: **follow the spec**, and where the spec cannot serve
one of the daemons, amend the spec — carefully — rather than bend an
implementation to fit. Each of the eight gets that question asked individually;
`whoami` is not a case of the spec being wrong but of this service not
recording something it should.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast` — 54 suites, no failures
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.14.

Refs #1059

title: test(vta): observe real Trust Task responses against their published schemas
body:
Brings the VTC's response-conformance technique (#1107–#1112) to this service.
**Reporting only — no behaviour change, and it is compiled out of production
builds.** Fixing what it finds is a follow-up, the same two steps the VTC took
across #1107 and #1111.

## Why, when the witness reads zero drift

`trust_tasks::conformance` reports **79 tasks at zero drift**, and that number
is true — *of the fixtures*. It says nothing about what a handler emits, because
a fixture is written separately from the thing it describes.

The VTC ran this exact experiment. Its witness also read zero drift; the
equivalent layer then found **134 violations across 23 tasks**, five of them in
a family the table called fully conformant. The failure mode that matters is the
flattering one: a fixture that *omits* a member reports a non-conformant route
as conforming, and no amount of re-reading a table produces the sentence
`invalid type: string, expected struct IssuedCredential`.

## The spine, not middleware

The VTC's version is axum middleware reading a `Trust-Task` request header.
That works there because the VTC serves Trust Tasks over REST only.

This service serves them over **REST, DIDComm and TSP**, and all three converge
on `dispatch_trust_task_core`, which returns a `TrustTaskOutcome` whose body
*is* the serialised result document. That document names its own `#response`
type in its `type` member — so one check at the spine covers every transport and
needs no header at all. Middleware would have covered one transport of three,
and would have been blind to precisely the two that carry no HTTP request to
read a header from.

## What it found

Four tasks, and every one is a class the VTC hit too — which is the argument for
the layer. These are not exotic; they are what happens to any wire type nothing
observes.

| task | violation |
|---|---|
| `vta/webvh/dids/get/1.0` | returns its eleven members flat where the schema requires them under `record` — a required property the response omits entirely |
| `vault/get/0.1` | leaks `status` / `graceUntil` / `deletedAt` |
| `vault/list/0.1` | the same three |
| `provision/integration/0.2` | `null` for two members the schema types as `string` |

The vault pair is the instructive one. The archival lifecycle (#540, `VaultStatus
{Active,Archived,Deleted}`) was added to the storage row and never to the wire
contract, so three storage members have been leaking onto a closed response ever
since. That is the storage-vs-wire split the VTC hit twice, most recently in
#1112.

`provision/integration/0.2` is the `null`-for-absent class, which wants
`skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"` — the fifth member in the programme to
ship `null` where a typed member is required.

## The number that matters more is the coverage

**A full suite run observes 29 of the 79 bound tasks.** The other fifty produce
no success response anywhere under `tests/`, so "four" is a floor taken over a
third of the surface, not a total.

This is worth more attention than the four defects. The witness census covers
all 79 — as fixtures, which is exactly the assurance this module exists to
qualify. Closing the coverage gap is what makes the remaining fifty knowable at
all, and is the natural sequel to this PR.

Four more tasks (`vault/{archive,unarchive,restore,purge}/0.1`) dispatch and
resolve no schema. Those are locally-defined openvtc extensions, consistent with
the CLAUDE.md note, and are correctly not reported.

## Two false readings on the way here

Both produced a confident "zero violations" that meant "never measured", and
both are worth recording because either one alone is enough to make this whole
technique lie:

- **`#[cfg(test)]` does not reach `tests/*.rs`.** Those binaries link the lib
  built *without* it, so a probe gated that way runs for the lib's own unit
  tests and nothing else — three dispatches, against the suite's 112. Hence the
  `any(test, feature = "test-support")` gate, matching how `test_support` itself
  is already gated.
- **The test harness captures stderr from passing tests.** A reporting layer
  that prints is invisible without `--nocapture`. This also means the VTC's
  green suite is evidence *because it gated* (a violation became a 500 and
  failed a test), not because a grep of the log came back empty.

## Discipline

`KNOWN_VIOLATIONS` is an **inventory, not an allowlist** — nothing consults it
at runtime. It exists so the work is written down where it will be read again,
and `the_inventory_is_still_accurate` asserts both the count and that every
entry still resolves a published response schema, so fixing one forces the note
to move with it and a stale entry cannot sit there quietly.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p vta-service --no-fail-fast`
- `cargo build -p vta-service` — the layer compiles out; `test-support` is not a default feature
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

Refs #1059

title: fix(vtc)!: follow the spec on every auth response, and close the conformance gate
body:
Closes the last eight response-conformance violations — all of them in
`auth/passkey/*` and `auth/whoami` — and **empties the allowlist**, so
`test_support/response_conformance.rs` stops being a report with exceptions
and becomes an unconditional gate.

**Violations across the whole 35-binary suite: 0.**

## Where the divergences actually were

The witness table called these "shared-family tasks served by both daemons",
and deferred them as a "which service's shape is canonical" decision. That
framing was wrong, and it is worth saying why: **not one of the eight needed a
canonical-shape ruling.** Seven were this service under-reporting or renaming
members the schema already defines, and the eighth was a genuine gap in the
spec. Nothing had to be decided between two implementations, because the
published component was already the answer in every case.

| task | what diverged |
|---|---|
| `enroll/start/0.2` | sent webauthn-rs's `{publicKey: …}` wrapper; the schema describes the *inner* options |
| `enroll/start/0.2` | schema had no `extensions` — **the one real spec gap**, amended upstream (#267) |
| `enroll/finish/0.2` | missing `subject`, `registeredAt` |
| `list/0.1` | `passkeys` → `credentials`; `label` → `deviceLabel`; `lastUsedAt: null` |
| `login/start/0.2` | the same wrapper problem |
| `login/finish/0.2` | missing the required `purpose` |
| `revoke/start/0.1` | the same wrapper problem |
| `revoke/finish/0.1` | missing `revokedAt`, `remaining` |
| `whoami/0.1` | flat `{did, role, …}`; the schema publishes a `Session` envelope |

## The wrapper, and why unwrapping is the fix

Four tasks sent `{publicKey: {challenge, rp, user, …}}`. That is
`webauthn-rs`'s `CreationChallengeResponse` / `RequestChallengeResponse` — the
shape a *browser API call* takes, not the shape the `CredentialCreationOptions`
component describes. The service was publishing its Rust dependency's
convenience type as its wire contract.

The proof that the wrapper was never load-bearing is in the SPA it serves: it
declared `registerOptions: { publicKey: JsonPublicKeyOptions }`, then did
`decodePublicKeyOptions(start.registerOptions.publicKey)` and re-wrapped the
result one line later for `navigator.credentials.create({ publicKey })`. The
wrapper was unwrapped and re-wrapped in the same function. It is gone from both
ends now.

## `extensions`, and the one careful spec change

`enroll/start` failed on `Additional properties are not allowed
('extensions' was unexpected)` — and here the service was right and the
specification was not. `extensions` is a standard member of
`PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptions`; a schema that closes over it cannot
describe a conforming WebAuthn ceremony at all. Amended upstream in
[#267](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/267), as an
8-insertion / 0-deletion edit to the shared `webauthn.schema.json` rather than a
reserialisation, and this PR moves onto the `trust-tasks-rs 0.11.15` that
carries it.

That is the whole of the "if the spec can't work, update the spec" branch:
**one** member, in a shared component, where the spec described something no
implementation could satisfy. Every other divergence went the other way.

## Storage rows are not wire shapes

`list/0.1` is the interesting one. `RegisteredPasskey` is `Deserialize`d out of
the `admin:<did>` fjall record, so its member names *are* the on-disk format —
renaming `label` to `deviceLabel` on that struct would orphan every passkey
already enrolled. So it keeps its names, and a `RegisteredCredential` wire view
sits in front of it. Same split as `GenerationRow` / `EndorsementRow` /
`CredentialReference` elsewhere in this service.

Two differences survive that boundary, and both are the schema being more
careful than the storage row:

- **`deviceLabel` is absent, not `""`.** The schema is explicit that a consumer
  must not synthesize a label, "because an invented one is indistinguishable
  from a chosen one to somebody deciding which credential to revoke" — and an
  empty string is an invented one. The SPA renders unlabelled credentials as
  unlabelled rather than as `""`.
- **`lastUsedAt` is omitted, not `null`.** `null` is a type error against a
  `date-time` member. This is the fourth member in this family to have shipped
  `null`-for-absent (`policyDecision` in #1099, `extensions` twice in #1108),
  and the schema notes it deliberately does not distinguish "never used" from
  "not tracked" — no generated binding could carry the difference.

## `whoami` and `AuthClaims.issued_at`

`whoami/0.1` publishes the shared `Session` component, whose `issuedAt` this
service could not produce: `AuthClaims` carried `access_expires_at` but not the
JWT's `iat`, even though the claim had been parsed and thrown away. Added, and
threaded through all 47 construction sites across five crates.

Two of those sites are not tests and took a real decision:

- `messaging::auth::auth_from_did` uses **`session.created_at`, not "now"**.
  These sessions are persistent and DID-keyed, so every message from a peer
  resolves the same row — stamping arrival time would make each message look
  like a fresh login.
- `ceremony_claims` uses `0`, following the existing `access_expires_at: 0`
  sentinel, for the stronger reason that no session row exists at all: there is
  nothing that was issued.

## `login/finish` needed its own response type

The login branch was reusing `AuthenticateResponse`, which serves
`auth/authenticate/0.1` — a closed schema with no `purpose`. One struct cannot
satisfy both tasks, and the reuse is exactly what left `login/finish/0.2` short
of a required member. The step-up branch already had its own
`PasskeyStepUpResponse` and was already conformant; the login branch now has
`PasskeyLoginResponse` beside it.

## The allowlist is empty

`ALLOWED_COUNT` is 0. The machinery stays, because the discipline is the point:
a task that starts failing must be *fixed*, and if one genuinely cannot be,
adding it back is a visible decision in a diff rather than a silent one.
`an_allowlisted_violation_is_recorded_but_not_fatal` had no allowlisted task
left to exercise, so it is now `a_violation_is_recorded_as_well_as_raised` —
guarding the property that survives an empty list: recording and raising are
separate, and recording is what let the original inventory of 134 be taken in
one run.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast` — 35 binaries, 0 violations
- `cargo fmt --all --check`
- `npx tsc --noEmit` in `admin-ui`

BREAKING CHANGE: `auth/passkey/{enroll,login,revoke}/start` send the inner
WebAuthn options instead of the `{publicKey: …}` wrapper. `auth/passkey/list`
returns `credentials` (was `passkeys`), whose members are `deviceLabel` (was
`label`, now absent when unset) and `lastUsedAt` (now absent rather than null).
`auth/passkey/enroll/start` returns `enrollmentId` (was `registrationId`).
`auth/passkey/{enroll,revoke}/finish` gain `subject`/`registeredAt` and
`revokedAt`/`remaining`. `auth/passkey/login/finish` gains `purpose`.
`auth/whoami` returns `{session, roles, scopes}` instead of a flat object.
`vti_common::auth::AuthClaims` gains `issued_at`.

Refs #1059

title: Migrate the Trust Tasks framework specification into Spec-Up-T
body:
Populates this repository — intended as the **canonical source** for the Trust Tasks framework — from `SPEC.md` in [`trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf), restructured onto the ToIP specification template.

The source is a single 1,476-line numbered markdown file. This splits it across the five Spec-Up-T sources declared in `specs.json`, drops the scaffolding the tooling now generates, and adds the sections the ToIP template requires.

**Individual Trust Task specifications are not part of this move.** `kyc-handoff`, `acl/grant`, `trust-task-error` and the rest stay in the registry repository, along with the transport bindings, the website, and the generated Rust and TypeScript client libraries. Only the framework document moves here.

## What went where

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `spec/header.md` | ToIP header block — version, document status, editors, abstract, IPR terms. Replaces the source's metadata table and its "Status of This Document" section. |
| `spec/intro.md` | Introduction, the status prose, Design Goals, Requirements Language. |
| `spec/terms-definitions/*.md` | The nineteen terms of the source's Terminology section, one file each, as `[[def: ...]]` entries with aliases. |
| `spec/body.md` | The normative body (Trust Task Documents … Task Control), then the template's considerations, conformance, and references sections. |
| `spec/appendix.md` | Appendix A (worked example), Appendix B (changelog), Appendix C (acknowledgements). |

## Mechanical changes

- **Section numbers removed from every heading.** Spec-Up-T generates the table of contents and the `§` anchors, so manual numbering would double up. All **380 in-page cross-references** were rewritten from `[§4.7](#47-proof)` to `[Proof](#proof)`. Every one resolves against a heading in the assembled document, and no two headings produce the same anchor — checked mechanically, not by eye.
- **Bibliography markers became links.** `[[RFC8259]]` is Spec-Up-T's term-reference syntax and would have been swallowed by the renderer; the eighteen occurrences now point at the RFC or W3C document directly.
- **Glossary references.** The first italicised occurrence of each defined term in every top-level section is now `[[ref: ...]]` — one route to the glossary from wherever a reader lands, without turning every paragraph into a link farm. `npm run render` reports no dangling definitions.
- A few headings were renamed to keep their anchors unambiguous: Discovery's `Request` / `Response` / `Privacy considerations` became `Discovery Request` / `Discovery Response` / `Privacy of Discovery Responses` (the last would otherwise have collided with the top-level Privacy Considerations section), and the ceremony subsections gained a `Ceremony` qualifier.

## Content changes

All of these are required by the template rather than chosen:

- **"Security and Privacy Considerations" splits in two.** The source's combined section becomes the template's separate Security Considerations (cross-recipient replay, parser hardening, schema-validation DoS, error-response identity leakage) and Privacy Considerations (data visibility, retention, plus pointers to the two subsections that carry privacy weight elsewhere).
- **Governance, Internationalization, and Accessibility Considerations are new.** Governance points at the registry policy, the stability commitment, and the framework's deliberate silence on authorization — all of which the source already stated, in scattered places. The other two record what the framework does and does not constrain today (UTF-8, ASCII lowerCamelCase identifiers; a data format rather than a user interface) and defer the rest until the document advances beyond Working Draft.
- **Conformance moves to the end**, as Conformance Targets (the three conformance classes from the source's §3) and Conformance Tests (none published yet; the registry repository's schemas and generated libraries are named as the expected basis).
- **References** are restated as Normative and Informative markdown lists, matching `dtgwg-cred-spec`.

**Every normative sentence is carried over unchanged.** The restructuring moves prose between files and rewrites references; it does not reword requirements. The one normative addition in this PR is the versioning change below, made deliberately rather than as a side effect of the move.

## This document now uses SemVer

The framework document's own version becomes three-part: **0.4.0**, and the framework is **published in the registry at that full version**. Its *Type URI* becomes `https://trusttasks.org/spec/trust-task/0.4.0`, and the `targetFrameworkVersion` a specification declares is that same three-part value.

**Why publish at the full version rather than keep `PATCH` off the wire.** Stability forbids altering the normative content served at a published *Type URI*. That left errata to a published framework version with nowhere to go: correcting `0.4` in place is precisely what that rule forbids for every other artifact in the registry, and minting `0.5` for a repaired example overstates what changed. A `PATCH` release now mints a new URI, exactly as every other registry artifact does.

A new **Versioning of This Framework Specification** subsection states the rule, adds a `framework-version` ABNF production alongside the existing one, and defines what each component means for this document: `MAJOR` for a change breaking for consumers or for the specification-authoring contract, `MINOR` for a backwards-compatible addition, `PATCH` for an errata-only correction that changes neither the wire format nor what a conforming specification must declare.

**The three-part form is confined to the exact reserved slug `trust-task`.** Individual Trust Task specifications keep the two-part `MAJOR.MINOR` of Version Scheme — and so do the framework-defined ones under the `trust-task-` and `trust-ceremony-` prefixes. `trust-task-error/0.4` is a Trust Task specification and versions like one. `https://trusttasks.org/spec/kyc-handoff/1.0` is untouched, as is the `specs/<slug>/<MAJOR.MINOR>/` registry layout and everything generated from it.

**Nothing already published stops resolving.** `0.1` through `0.4` denote `0.1.0` through `0.4.0` — `0.4` and `0.4.0` are the same release, and the changelog entries stand as published. A two-part `targetFrameworkVersion` resolves as `M.N.0`, and the registry **MUST** continue to serve the two-part framework URIs `.../trust-task/0.1` through `/0.4` as aliases of the corresponding `.0` release. Specifications published or re-issued from this version onward declare the three-part form. **The document wire format is unchanged.**

Carried through Type URI (version-segment exception, reserved-slug note, bare-URL redirect), Schema Scope, Stability, Consumer Requirements item 1, Specification Requirements item 3, the Appendix A worked example, and the changelog. Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 joins the normative references.

**Registry-side follow-up:** `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` needs `specs/_framework/0.4/` moved to `specs/_framework/0.4.0/`, with the two-part framework URIs kept resolving as aliases. Not in this PR.

## The version number itself

The source's header table said **version 0.3**, but its changelog documents a **0.4** release and the registry repository ships `specs/_framework/0.4/`. This PR records **0.4.0**, on the basis that the changelog and the published framework schema agree with each other and the header table does not. Say the word if that reads the wrong way.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

Syncing the framework back into `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` so the registry website keeps rendering it. Once this lands, that repository's `SPEC.md` should stop being the source and start being a copy — either a build step that pulls the rendered output, or a submodule. Worth agreeing the mechanism before wiring it up.

## Verification

```sh
npm install
npm run render     # clean: 19 terms indexed, no dangling definitions
```

The rendered `docs/index.html` has 217 anchors and no broken in-page links.

title: spec(auth): WebAuthn options may carry extensions, as the dictionary says
body:
`CredentialCreationOptions` and `CredentialRequestOptions` each say they mirror
a W3C dictionary, and each omits a member that dictionary defines. Both are
`additionalProperties: false`, so **a server emitting standard WebAuthn options
cannot conform.**

## The contradiction

> Server-issued options for `navigator.credentials.create({ publicKey: ... })`.
> **Mirrors the WebAuthn Level 2 `PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptions`
> dictionary**; binary fields are base64url-encoded strings…

That dictionary defines `extensions`. These components did not. Closed objects
plus an incomplete mirror is a contradiction the schema cannot resolve in the
implementer's favour: the widely-used server libraries populate `extensions` by
default, so conforming meant **stripping a standard WebAuthn field on the way
out** — deleting a capability to satisfy a schema that only meant to describe
one.

Found by a reference implementation validating its real handler responses
against these schemas. It had been sending webauthn-rs's `{publicKey: …}`
wrapper, which failed for a different reason; unwrapping it to the shape this
component asks for exposed `extensions` underneath.

## Why the value is unconstrained

`{"type": "object"}`, nothing more. The set of extensions is open and
registered outside this framework, so enumerating them here would date the
schema against a registry it does not own — and a closed list would reproduce
the original defect one revision later, for whichever extension is registered
next.

## Scope

One shared file. Additive, so a patch bump, and `0.1` of the component is
edited in place rather than versioned — an added optional member leaves every
document that was valid before still valid.

Reaches `auth/passkey/enroll/start/{0.1,0.2}`, `auth/passkey/login/start/0.2`
and `auth/passkey/revoke/start/0.1`, which all `$ref` these components.

## Checks

- `npm run validate` — 349 specs, 65 shared schemas, 533 example documents
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` — no drift
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — no drift
- `npm run check-bindings` — 349 specs against 349 TS and 344 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test --workspace` — 33 suites, no failures

The diff is **8 insertions, 0 deletions**. My first attempt reserialised the
file with a JSON library and produced 220 changed lines of pure reformatting;
this one is a surgical text insertion, because a hand-formatted schema should
not be rewritten to add two properties.

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.15 and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.12.15.

title: fix(vtc): hex digests, and five ways round the extension slot
body:
Stacked on #1109. Closes `audit/*` and `policy/activate` — **68 → ~22
violations**, all remaining ones needing a decision rather than a fix.

## Hex digests where the schema requires multibase

`audit/list` sent `prevHash` / `entryHash` as bare hex; the canonical digest
pattern is `^(z[1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]+|u[A-Za-z0-9_-]+)$` — multibase-wrapped
multihash. `audit/verify`'s `head` moved with them, so the two still agree,
which is the property that actually matters and is now what the test asserts.

The old comment justified hex as *"matching the encoding `audit/verify` uses
for `head` — a caller comparing the two must not have to reconcile hex against
the base64 the stored envelope uses."* Every word true, and it reconciled the
**two internal** encodings while overlooking the third: the one the published
schema requires. A bare digest is also self-describing in neither its hash
function nor its encoding, which is what multihash and multibase each exist to
fix.

**The chain is untouched.** Stored envelopes still hold `[u8; 32]` and hash
over bytes; this is the wire view only.

## Three more ways to bypass the extension slot

With #1109's invalid key and #1107's flattened key, that makes **five distinct
ways** `ext` was worked around in this service, each locally reasonable and
none checked against SPEC §4.5.1:

| where | what was wrong |
|---|---|
| `policy/*` (#1109) | `org.openvtc.authorDid` — capital letter, invalid key |
| `audit/list` | `"vtc"` — one segment, where reverse-DNS needs two |
| `policy/activate` | `sha256` at the top level of a closed response |
| `audit/verify` | `checkpoints` at the top level of a closed response |

The last two are the interesting pair. `sha256`'s own doc called it *"VTC
extension"* — the word was right there and the member was not in `ext`. Both
now sit under `org.openvtc`.

`checkpoints` is not a nicety: it is the signed-checkpoint evidence "a
store-level adversary cannot satisfy", so it is carried rather than dropped —
and it is worth proposing upstream so it need not live in an extension at all.

`"vtc"` as a namespace deserves a note: a single-segment key claims a name
nobody owns, which is the collision reverse-DNS exists to prevent.

## A test that pinned an encoding nobody chose

`entry_hashes_are_hex_matching_audit_verify_head` asserted `h.len() == 64`.
The body's real invariant is that `verify`'s `head` and `list`'s newest
`entryHash` are the same string — true before and after. The name and the
length check pinned hex, which nothing had decided deliberately.

Renamed `entry_hash_and_audit_verify_head_agree`, and the format assertion in
`audit_verify` now checks the `z` prefix rather than a character count —
`len() == 64` would also accept a base64 digest of the wrong thing.

## What remains, and why it is not here

**`auth/passkey/*` — six tasks**, and not a wrapper problem: the models
genuinely differ (`passkeys` vs `credentials`; missing `subject`,
`enrollmentId`, `registeredAt`). These are shared-family tasks served by both
daemons, which is exactly the "which service's response shape is canonical"
decision the witness header names. Picking a side here would be guessing.

**`vtc/relationships/{list,graph}`** — the *spec* looks stale, not the
service: `list` sends `vrcDigestMultibase` where the schema still says
`vrcSha256` (this workspace moved to multibase deliberately), and `graph`
returns a materially richer shape. Both want an upstream `0.2`, with the graph
shape confirmed by whoever designed it.

**`auth/whoami`** — one violation, unexamined.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast`
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

BREAKING CHANGE: `GET /v1/audit` returns `prevHash` / `entryHash` and `GET
/v1/audit/verify` returns `head` as multibase-wrapped multihash instead of
hex. `audit/list` carries its VTC members under `ext["org.openvtc"]` instead
of `ext["vtc"]`. `policy/activate`'s `sha256` and `audit/verify`'s
`checkpoints` move into `ext["org.openvtc"]`.

Refs #1059

title: fix(vtc): an invalid ext key, and three acl responses missing their envelope (#1109)
body:
fix(vtc): an invalid ext key, and three acl responses missing their envelope (#1109)

Two classes from #1107's inventory, both in the shared task families the
conformance table's census deliberately excludes. 134 → 68 violations.

`policy/*` emitted an `ext` key of `org.openvtc.authorDid`. SPEC §4.5.1
constrains every immediate `ext` key to `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*(\.[a-z0-9-]+)+$`, so
the capital D made the key invalid — a framework violation rather than a style
preference, and the only one of five `org.openvtc.*` keys in the workspace that
failed. Renamed `author-did`, matching `match-code` and `step-up`.

`acl/grant`, `acl/show` and `acl/change-role` returned a bare row where all
three schemas require `{entry: …}`. The rows always conformed; only the wrapper
was missing.

These survived longer for a structural reason: the shared
`spec/{acl,audit,auth,config,policy}/*` families are outside the witness
census — a stated limit, since both daemons serve them — so no fixture ever
described these responses and nothing could have caught it. The
response-conformance layer needed neither a census nor a canonical-shape
decision to observe the divergence. Acting on the remaining shared-family
violations still needs that decision; a missing required envelope did not,
being wrong under any reading.

BREAKING CHANGE: `POST /v1/acl`, `GET /v1/acl/{did}` and `PATCH /v1/acl/{did}`
return `{entry: …}` instead of the bare row; `policy/*` spells the extension
key `org.openvtc.author-did`.
