title: spec(vtc): tell a member when a community removes them (#256)
body:
spec(vtc): tell a member when a community removes them (#256)

Removal is the most consequential thing a community does to a member and, so
far, the one it delivers with the least information — none. The only signal a
removed member can observe is a side effect: the revocation bit on their
membership credential flips. They infer their own removal from a status list
and learn nothing about why.

`vtc/members/removal-notice/0.1` says who removed them, when the decision took
effect, and the reason given.

Deliberately not a receipt. `vtc/members/self-remove-receipt` answers a request
the member made and is correlated to it; this answers nothing, because the
member did not ask, is not waiting, and may well be offline. That asymmetry is
what drives the rest of the design — `decidedBy` and `reason` are carried here
and not there, because a departing member already knows why they left.

`proof` is REQUIRED, not RECOMMENDED. This is the one member-facing message
whose value depends on being shown to somebody else: an appeal, a dispute,
another community assessing a rejected applicant. Authenticated transport
establishes the sender to the recipient and stops there, so an unsigned notice
evidences nothing the moment it is forwarded.

`decidedBy` names the deciding administrator rather than the community. That is
more disclosure than a community strictly has to make, and the alternative is
worse: "the community removed you" is unanswerable and unappealable.

The spec states a delivery *property* rather than a transport, because this task
has a problem no other member-facing task has — the act it reports is the act
that ends the member's ability to ask about it. A producer therefore cannot rely
on the member being reachable at that moment, and cannot offer a poll as the
fallback: the endpoint that would answer is the one that now refuses them. Hence
durable retrying delivery over a window measured in weeks, on a channel that
survives the removal.

Structured with `## Request` and no `## Response` — the fire-and-forget shape
from CONTRIBUTING-SPECS. That is also what earns the two examples their
generated round-trip tests; under `## Examples` the codegen would not have
harvested them, which is why the adjacent receipt spec has none.

trust-tasks-rs 0.11.3 -> 0.11.4, @openvtc/trust-tasks 0.12.3 -> 0.12.4.

Refs: OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1053

title: build: validate example documents against every framework version on disk
body:
Fixes #254.

`checkExampleDocuments()` compiled envelope validators from a hard-coded
`['0.1', '0.2', '0.3']`. A spec declaring `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.4"`
resolved to no validator, and its example documents were skipped by a silent
`continue` — indistinguishable in the build output from a clean pass.

## What changed

Both of the hardenings the issue proposed, because they close different things:

1. **Derive the version list from disk** (`specs/_framework/*/trust-task.schema.json`)
   rather than hand-listing it. A new framework version is covered the moment its
   envelope schema lands. This is what stops the recurrence at 0.5.
2. **`warn()` when a document's target resolves to no validator**, counted per
   target. Deriving the list closes this instance; the warning is what would have
   *caught* it, and it still catches the next way a target can name a version with
   no schema — a typo in front matter, or a schema not yet written.

## Verification

On `100471d` (the commit the issue reports against):

```
before:   validated 476 example documents against the framework envelope schema
after:    validated 531 example documents against the framework envelope schema
```

The build **passes** with the check enabled — no `fails the framework 0.4
envelope schema` errors, no unvalidated-target warnings, and the only remaining
warnings are the pre-existing `$defs.Response` ones. Every document that was
being skipped happens to be valid, which is exactly what makes turning this on
cheap now and expensive once 0.5 has a backlog behind it.

The warning path was exercised directly by pointing `trust-task-control/0.1` at a
nonexistent `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.9"`:

```
  warn: 3 example document(s) target framework 0.9, for which no envelope schema
  compiled — add specs/_framework/0.9/trust-task.schema.json, or correct the
  targetFrameworkVersion that names it. These documents were NOT validated
  validated 498 example documents against the framework envelope schema
```

531 → 498 with the 3 documents named rather than silently dropped. Working tree
restored afterwards; that edit is not in this branch.

## One correction to the issue's numbers

The issue says 22 specs / 55 documents. On `main` today it is **16 specs** — the
55-document delta includes the six unmerged `vta/app-state` specs from #252/#253.
The 476 → 531 figure reproduces exactly either way, since those specs are what the
issue author had in tree when measuring.

## Scope

Build script only — no spec, schema, or generated-library changes, so no binding
regeneration or version bumps are implicated. Nothing else hard-codes the framework
version list (`build-ts-bindings.mjs` references `_framework` only in comments and
path conventions).

title: checkExampleDocuments() silently skips every framework-0.4 example (55 documents unvalidated)
body:
`checkExampleDocuments()` in `scripts/build-registry.mjs` compiles envelope validators for framework `0.1`–`0.3` only. A spec declaring `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.4"` therefore resolves to **no validator**, and its example documents are skipped without a warning.

## Where

`scripts/build-registry.mjs:558`

```js
for (const version of ['0.1', '0.2', '0.3']) {
```

The skip itself is a silent `continue` further down:

```js
const target = targetByTypePrefix.get(bare) ?? '0.2';
const validate = validators.get(target);
if (!validate) continue;          // <- 0.4 lands here, no warning
```

`specs/_framework/0.4/trust-task.schema.json` exists, so there is a schema to compile — the version is simply absent from the list.

## Scale

**22 specs** currently declare `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.4"`, contributing **55 example documents** that are never checked.

## Reproduction

On `100471d` (current `main`):

```
$ npm run build
  validated 476 example documents against the framework envelope schema
```

Add `'0.4'` to the list on line 558 and re-run:

```
$ npm run build
  validated 531 example documents against the framework envelope schema
```

476 → 531. The 55-document delta is the gap.

## The fix appears safe to land as-is

With `'0.4'` added the build still **passes** — no `fails the framework 0.4 envelope schema` errors, and no new warnings beyond the pre-existing `$defs.Response` ones. So every currently-unvalidated document happens to be valid, and enabling the check does not require fixing a backlog first.

That is worth stating because it is the thing that makes this cheap now and expensive later: the longer 0.4 stays unchecked, the more likely it is that turning it on surfaces a real failure in someone else's spec, and then the fix and the cleanup arrive together.

## Why it matters beyond the count

The function's own docstring makes the case:

> an example document is the thing implementers copy: a wrong one is a bug that propagates, and nothing checked them before.

That reasoning applies to 0.4 examples exactly as much as to 0.1–0.3 — and 0.4 is where new specs are being written, so the unvalidated set is the *growing* one.

## Suggested hardening

Beyond adding `'0.4'`, the failure mode is worth closing permanently: the list is hand-maintained and will drift again at 0.5. Two options —

1. Derive the versions from `specs/_framework/*/trust-task.schema.json` on disk rather than hard-coding them, so a new framework version is covered the moment its envelope schema lands.
2. Failing that, `warn()` when a document's target resolves to no validator, so the skip is at least visible. Today it is indistinguishable from "validated fine".

Option 1 is what stops this recurring; option 2 is what would have caught it.

## Context

Found while adding `vta/app-state/*` (#252, #253), which targets 0.4 — I validated those six specs' documents out of band against `_framework/0.4/trust-task.schema.json` (56 documents, 30 payloads, 0 failures) precisely because the build would not. Filing rather than fixing inline, since turning the check on newly validates 16 other specs and that is not mine to land inside an unrelated spec PR.

title: fix(service)!: make AppStateParts non-exhaustive so adding a field stops being a break (#1057)
body:
fix(service)!: make AppStateParts non-exhaustive so adding a field stops being a break (#1057)

`AppState` was marked `#[non_exhaustive]` in #1024 for a defect this struct
has too, and the two are constructed side by side. `AppStateParts` is all
public fields with no private field and no constructor guard, so any crate
could write an `AppStateParts { .. }` literal — including the
functional-update form — which made *adding a field* a source break under
`constructible_struct_adds_field`.

Not hypothetical, and recent: #1049 added `audit_sink`, and #1051 nearly added
`app_state_locks` before the break was spotted and routed around by taking the
value off the built `AppState` instead. That workaround was the right call for
a feature PR, but it treated the symptom.

Construction inside this crate is unaffected. Outside it, `Default` plus field
assignment replaces the literal:

    let mut parts = AppStateParts::default();
    parts.audit_sink = Some(sink);

`tests/audit_sink.rs` now does exactly that. It is worth noting *why* that file
had to change: an integration test is a separate crate, so it was the first
thing the attribute broke — which makes it a fair proxy for what a consumer
has to do, and a standing check that the supported shape keeps working.

BREAKING CHANGE: `AppStateParts` can no longer be built with a struct literal
from outside `vta-service`. Use `AppStateParts::default()` and assign the
fields you need. This is a one-line change per call site, and it is the last
one this struct will require — that is the point of the attribute.

Marked `!` deliberately. `cargo-semver-checks` does report this class
(`constructible_struct_adds_field` is how the earlier additions surfaced), but
the marker is what makes release-plz move the compatibility field rather than
ship it as a patch.

title: chore(deny): scan every feature, and drop three ignores that are now dead
body:
Started as "is the `RUSTSEC-2026-0258` ignore stale?" — it is not, and finding out why turned up a coverage gap worth more than the cleanup.

## The scan was missing the AWS path entirely

`cargo deny` was reporting **seven** of its own ignores as `advisory-not-detected`. That reads as "stale, delete them". For four of them that is exactly the wrong conclusion.

cargo-deny resolves the graph with **default features**, and the AWS SDK — carrying `hyper` 0.14, `h2` 0.3 and `rustls` 0.21, which is where most of the ignores point — reaches the graph only through the **`tee` feature**. Those crates were never in frame. So the job was not enforcing the ignores, and more importantly **could not have caught a new advisory anywhere in that path**. The advisories most worth catching were the ones not being checked.

`[graph] all-features = true` fixes it. All four checks (advisories / bans / licenses / sources) pass under the wider graph.

The secondary benefit is that `advisory-not-detected` now means what it says — a genuinely stale entry stands out instead of hiding among false ones. That is what made this hard to spot: the signal was there, but drowning.

## Three ignores are genuinely dead

Verified absent from `Cargo.lock` outright, at any feature combination:

| Advisory | Crate | Why it's gone |
|---|---|---|
| `RUSTSEC-2024-0370` | proc-macro-error | dropped with the uniffi / syn 3 refresh |
| `RUSTSEC-2025-0134` | rustls-pemfile | dropped out in #1055 |
| `RUSTSEC-2026-0215` | smallstr | no longer reached via the ssi-json-ld stack |

## Four stay — and are now actually enforced

`RUSTSEC-2026-0258` (h2 0.3) and the `rustls-webpki` 0.101 trio (`-0098`, `-0099`, `-0104`). All still live under `tee`. Previously they were declared but unenforced; now they are both.

## Verification

- `cargo deny check advisories bans sources licenses` — all four ok
- `cargo deny check advisories` — **0** `advisory-not-detected` warnings (was 7)

No source or dependency changes; `deny.toml` only.

title: chore(deps)!: bring every dependency to latest, collapsing two duplicates (#1055)
body:
chore(deps)!: bring every dependency to latest, collapsing two duplicates (#1055)

`cargo outdated` reported 13 direct dependencies behind and `cargo update`
had 36 compatible updates waiting. Both are now clear: `cargo outdated`
reports "All dependencies are up to date".

Two of these were not cosmetic.

**p256 was duplicated in the build.** Our crates declared `0.13` while
`affinidi-crypto` — reached through `affinidi-data-integrity` and the TDK —
already pulled `0.14`, so the graph carried two copies of a curve
implementation. The lock now holds a single `p256 0.14.0`. The bump brings
`elliptic-curve` 0.14 and `ecdsa` 0.17, which rename the SEC1 family:
`EncodedPoint` -> `Sec1Point`, `From/ToEncodedPoint` -> `From/ToSec1Point`.
Renamed across `vta-keys`, `vta-service` and `vti-webauthn`.

**tokio-tungstenite was load-bearing, not incidental.** `vta-mobile-core`
depends on it solely as a feature enabler: iOS has no native trust store, so
`rustls-tls-webpki-roots` has to be on graph-wide or the mediator WebSocket
fails with "no native root CA certificates found". Features unify per major
version, so the declaration only works while it matches the version
`affinidi-messaging-sdk` pulls — and the SDK moved to 0.30 in this refresh.
Updating everything *except* this one would have stranded the enabler and
broken iOS `wss://` silently.

The rest:

- `rcgen` 0.13 -> 0.14 (dev). `signed_by` takes an `Issuer` rather than a
  `(certificate, key)` pair, and `self_signed` borrows instead of consuming.
  The mdoc IACA test helper builds its issuer with `Issuer::from_params`,
  which is also a more direct statement of what it wanted.
- `syn` 2 -> 3 (dev). No source change; syn 3 was already in the graph via
  `trust-tasks-rs`.
- `rmcp` 1.7 -> 3.1.4. Two majors, one rename: `Content` -> `ContentBlock`.
  The `#[tool_router]` / `#[tool_handler]` macro surface the crate is built
  on is unchanged.
- 36 lockfile updates, including `trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.3 (the corrected
  `vta/app-state` error taxonomy from dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#253) and the AWS
  SDK set. `rustls-pemfile`, one of the unmaintained crates `cargo audit`
  flags, drops out of the graph entirely.

Two deliberate choices where the shortest path was worse:

`vti-webauthn` keeps parse-then-validate rather than collapsing to the
one-shot `PublicKey::from_sec1_bytes`. That call merges "malformed SEC1
encoding" and "valid encoding, point not on the curve" into one error, and
those say different things to whoever reads the log — a broken client versus
a point somebody chose.

BIP-32 P-256 derivation replaces the now-deprecated `FieldBytes::from_slice`
with `TryFrom` and a real error arm. The input is a fixed 32-byte window of a
SHA-512 HMAC so it cannot fail, but the length check is now explicit rather
than resting on a panic inside a deprecated helper.

Unchanged and still suppressed: the four `cargo audit` advisories ignored in
`deny.toml`, all transitive through the AWS SDK's hyper 0.14 / rustls 0.21
path. `cargo deny check advisories` passes.

BREAKING CHANGE: `vta_keys::derivation::P256Secret` has a public
`secret_key: p256::SecretKey` field, re-exported as
`vta_service::keys::derivation::P256Secret`. Moving p256 0.13 -> 0.14 changes
that field's type, so a consumer holding its own p256 0.13 and passing values
across that boundary stops compiling.

`cargo-semver-checks` does NOT report this. It compares rustdoc JSON, and both
versions render the field as the same path string, so the change is invisible
to it — the job's output on this branch is identical to the pre-refresh
baseline and names only the unrelated `audit_ks` -> `audit` renames already on
main. The marker is therefore hand-applied rather than tool-derived.

Marked because this workspace's rule is that a break is allowed but must be
KNOWN, so the release moves the compatibility field instead of shipping it as
a patch. Left unmarked, `chore(deps)` would have released this as one.

title: Default relationship communication to pairwise R-DIDs and govern P-DID fallback
body:
Surfaced by an external RAHP/DRARM assessment of the Cypress release
(sankarshanmukhopadhyay/rahp-toolkit#18, finding `OVTC-RAHP-04`). Confirmed as
reported.

## Problem

Pairwise relationship identity is opt-in, and the fallback is the persona DID.

- TUI request form: `generate_r_did` defaults to `false`
  (`openvtc/src/state_handler/relationship_actions.rs:1056`); the user has to
  find and toggle the checkbox on field 3 to get privacy.
- TUI inbox accept: `a` accepts **without** an R-DID, `A` accepts **with** one
  (`openvtc/src/ui/pages/main/mod.rs:914-930`). The convenient key is the
  linkable one.
- CLI: requires `--generate-did` (`docs/relationships-vrcs.md:60-66`), which
  states plainly that without an R-DID, subsequent communication uses the P-DID.

So the safe path is the one the operator has to know to ask for, on a decision
whose consequences are invisible at the moment they make it.

## Why this is worse here than the generic pattern

The assessment scores this as stable-identifier correlation. In our case the
stable identifier is a **published, resolvable `did:webvh`** that frequently
carries a verified agent name. Two counterparties do not need traffic analysis
to correlate the same persona across contexts — they compare a string, and can
then resolve it to a named identity. The linkage is not merely possible, it is
a lookup.

That argues for flipping the default rather than warning on the fallback.

## Proposed change

1. **Default `generate_r_did` to `true`** on the request form and make the
   R-DID-generating accept the primary key binding in the inbox. Keep the
   P-DID path available, deliberately chosen, and labelled with what it costs.
2. **CLI:** make R-DID generation the default and introduce an explicit opt-out
   flag rather than an opt-in one. `--generate-did` becomes a no-op that warns,
   for one release, so existing scripts do not silently change meaning in the
   other direction.
3. **No silent revert.** Once a relationship has an R-DID, subsequent messages
   must not fall back to the P-DID — define the bootstrap-to-pairwise migration
   point and assert it. A fallback that can re-expose the P-DID mid-relationship
   defeats the default.
4. **Test:** given two relationships established from the same persona, assert
   that protocol-visible identifiers do not permit the two counterparties to
   correlate them.
5. **Docs:** update `docs/relationships-vrcs.md` — the current text presents the
   R-DID as an optional privacy extra rather than the norm.

## Upstream question

Whether VTC should *require* pairwise identifiers for relationship
communication rather than leaving it to client defaults is a protocol question
for `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. If it does, this issue reduces to
conformance. Raising it there separately; this change stands either way.

## Acceptance

- A new relationship request and a new relationship acceptance both mint an
  R-DID with no extra keystroke.
- Choosing the P-DID path is possible and states the linkability cost at the
  point of choice.
- A relationship with an R-DID never emits the P-DID on a subsequent message.

title: feat(relationships): default to a pairwise R-DID, and say what the choice costs
body:
Client-side half of #241 (RAHP finding `OVTC-RAHP-04`). Makes pairwise the
default and puts the trade-off in front of the operator at the moment they
choose.

## What changed

**Request form** — `generate_r_did` now defaults to `true`. The toggle reads
`Contact you as: Pairwise R-DID (recommended) / Your persona DID` and renders
the consequence of whichever is selected, rather than a bare Yes/No.

**Inbox accept** — the convenient key is now the private one:

| Key | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a` | accept with persona DID | accept with pairwise R-DID |
| `A` | accept with R-DID | accept with R-DID (unchanged) |
| `p` | — | accept with persona DID |

`A` deliberately keeps its old meaning, so anyone with existing muscle memory
gets the private outcome they always got. No keystroke that used to produce an
R-DID now produces a persona DID.

**Docs** — `docs/relationships-vrcs.md` gains a *Choosing your identifier*
comparison table and drops the `--generate-did` example. That flag, and the
whole `openvtc relationships` subcommand, have not existed since the v0.2.0 TUI
rewrite (`1f31455`); the file also contradicted itself, with a diagram showing
pairwise as the normal flow and prose calling it optional. Added a note that
the remaining command examples are stale — rewriting the guide for the TUI is a
separate job.

**Regression guard** — `established_pairwise_relationship_never_pings_from_the_persona_did`
pins criterion 3: an established relationship's ping takes its `from`, its
recipient and its listener from the relationship record. The property held
already; nothing tested it. Verified the test fails when `prepare_ping` is made
to read `persona_did_arc()` instead.

## What this does *not* do

It does not satisfy acceptance criterion 4. Two counterparties can still
correlate you, for two reasons that are not client-side:

- The three handshake messages (request/accept/finalise) are routed
  persona-to-persona by design — the mediator has to route them before a
  pairwise channel exists.
- The VRC `issuer` must be the persona DID, because the VTC's
  `relationships.rego` requires issuer *and* subject to be current ACL-listed
  members. A VRC issued under a pairwise R-DID is rejected today.

Raised upstream as OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1054. The commit
message and the docs both say so, so a flipped boolean does not later read as
"correlation solved".

Also corrected on the issue: proposal 2 (CLI opt-out flag) has nothing to
change, since the CLI it refers to is gone.

## Checks

`cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`,
`cargo test --workspace` (all green), and
`RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps`.

Refs #241

title: feat(relationships): default to a pairwise R-DID, and say what the choice costs (#254)
body:
feat(relationships): default to a pairwise R-DID, and say what the choice costs (#254)

The persona DID is a published, resolvable `did:webvh` that often carries a
verified agent name. Reusing it across contacts makes correlation a lookup
rather than an inference — two counterparties compare a string and resolve it
to a named identity. Yet pairwise was opt-in, on a decision whose consequences
were invisible at the moment it was made: the request form defaulted to `No`,
and in the inbox the convenient unshifted `a` was the linkable accept while the
private one hid behind Shift+A.

Flip both. A new request mints an R-DID unless the operator turns it off, and
`a` now accepts pairwise. `A` stays wired to the pairwise accept too, so anyone
with the old muscle memory keeps getting the private outcome they always got;
the persona-DID accept moves to `p`, where it names itself.

Neither surface makes the choice silently. The request form's toggle reads
"Contact you as: Pairwise R-DID / Your persona DID" and spells out the
consequence of whichever is selected; the inbox detail states both outcomes
above the footer. The docs gain a comparison table, and lose the `--generate-did`
invocation for a CLI subcommand that has not existed since the v0.2.0 TUI
rewrite.

Also guards the property the default depends on: an established relationship
must never revert to the persona DID. That holds today and nothing tested it —
`established_pairwise_relationship_never_pings_from_the_persona_did` pins the
message `from`, the recipient and the listener to the relationship record.

Scope, deliberately: this does not make two counterparties unable to correlate
you. The three handshake messages are routed persona-to-persona because the
mediator must route them before a pairwise channel exists, and the VRC issuer
must be the persona DID because the VTC's `relationships.rego` requires issuer
and subject to be current ACL-listed members. Full pairwise operation is a
protocol change, tracked in OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1054.

Refs #241

title: feat(app-state): a third store for versioned, namespaced application state
body:
Closes #1029. Implements `vta/app-state/{get,put,list,delete,get-many,put-many}/1.0` — a third store beside the secrets vault and the credential vault, for versioned, namespaced, per-context JSON an application owns and the VTA does not interpret.

The specs were published upstream first, as §7 of `docs/05-design-notes/appstate-store.md` requires: **trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#252** (merged) and **#253** (merged, correcting the error taxonomy). This depends on the released `trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.2 — there is **no `[patch.crates-io]`** in this diff.

## Why a third store

Records are addressed `(contextId, namespace, key)`. The namespace scopes one application so several tools share a context without colliding, and is the seam a per-namespace grant would later use — which is why it is part of the address rather than a prefix convention on the key.

In 1.0 a namespace is **collision avoidance, not a trust boundary**. An application with write access to a context reaches every namespace in it; the `put` and `delete` specs say so normatively in their `## Authorization` sections, and say what to do instead — separate contexts. `delete` is where that coarseness has teeth, and its spec says that too.

Not built on `vta/memory/*`: `MemoryItem` has nothing to hang a precondition on and its `list` returns the whole context — but the settling argument is that *"forget everything"* must stay a safe thing to ask an agent, which it cannot be if account state lives there.

## Three properties, and what building it changed

**One counter per `(contextId, namespace)`, not per record.** This is the one place the design note was wrong, and it is corrected in the note. `sinceVersion` compares a watermark against record versions, and per-record counters are not comparable to each other, so no single number means "everything after this point" — a per-record counter would have forced a second sequence kept consistent by hand. One counter serves as both the CAS token and the watermark. The cost is that a record's version jumps by whatever its neighbours consumed, which the wire contract states.

**A failed precondition returns the current version *and value*.** A bare rejection obliges a re-read and the re-read races the next write; the pattern has no fixed point under contention. Normative, not a courtesy.

**Tombstones, and they are actually reaped.** Retention is `app_state.tombstone_retention_days` (default 30, following the vault's `grace_days` — a destructive window is an operator's choice). `list` advertises the *configured* value, since consumers schedule against it; advertising 30 while reaping at 7 would strand exactly the clients that trusted the number.

The sweeper reaps a **prefix, not a set**: each namespace walks tombstones in version order and stops at the first still inside the window. Reaping a later tombstone while leaving an earlier one makes the reap watermark unstateable — no single number would describe what survives, which is precisely what `watermarkTooOld` has to be able to say. `0` days disables reaping, enforced at the **call site** rather than as a zero cutoff, which would mean the opposite.

## Defects found while building, all fixed

- **`Option<Value>` silently ate stored JSON nulls.** serde deserializes a present `null` to `None`, so a legitimately-stored null read back as "absent" — the exact three-way conflation the spec warns against. Fixed with `deserialize_with` on every value-bearing member; regression-tested.
- **The version counter was never fsynced.** `vti_common::store::counter` makes this argument for BIP-32 counters and it transfers exactly: a counter surviving only in the journal buffer can be re-derived after a crash and reissue a used value. Here a reused version means two records collide on one `appv:` index key, so one disappears from the change feed and every incremental consumer misses that change permanently, silently. `reserve_versions` now fsyncs and re-seals the TEE integrity manifest, reserving a **block** so a batch pays one fsync rather than 64.
- **`deny_unknown_fields` rejected the `ext` slot the schemas declare**, which would have broken interop with a conforming producer. Explicit `ext` fields added; typo-rejection kept.
- **A crash-safety bug in the write ordering**, with a comment asserting the opposite of what the code did. Superseded by the reservation above, which makes reuse impossible rather than merely unlikely.

Reserving before validating means a rejected write burns a version, leaving a gap. Gaps are safe and there is a test pinning that the change feed tolerates them; the test that had encoded the old behaviour was changed rather than preserved.

## Concurrency: a lock, not a compare-and-swap

Considered and rejected, recorded in the note's §9. fjall takes an exclusive lock on the database directory, so two processes cannot open one store. The vsock protocol has six opcodes, none atomic — its `insert_if_absent`/`swap` are already non-atomic get+insert fallbacks that log a warning. A real CAS needs a seventh opcode in `deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy`, a separate non-workspace crate on the parent EC2 instance, plus version negotiation between two independently-deployed artifacts.

Added today it would be atomic exactly where the lock already suffices and warn-and-fallback exactly where it would need to be real — reading as multi-writer safety while providing none. If that topology becomes reachable, the fix is a store-layer CAS landing *with* the vsock opcode.

## Retry safety

Reads `ReadOnly`; `delete` `RetrySafe` (a second delete finds a tombstone and deliberately takes **no** new version, so a watcher sees nothing); `put`/`put-many` `Keyed` — a `put` without `expectedVersion` does not converge, and the class is per URI, not per payload. The reasoning sits beside the entries, because "optimising" `put` to `RetrySafe` on the strength of the precondition looks like a cleanup and is not.

## Scope notes

- Blobs deliberately out of scope in 1.0; a `blobRef` is additive later.
- Conformance witnesses cover all six URIs — nothing enters `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`.
- `trust-tasks-rs` pinned to a minimum patch so an older resolve fails as a stale dependency rather than as "you are serving unspecced URIs".
- The sweeper lives in `vta-service`, not `vta-sweepers`, for the reason the backup-bundle sweeper does: it is coupled to this module's key layout.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace` — 149 suites, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- 49 app-state tests + 2 config tests (an existing TOML with no `[app_state]` section still loads; an explicit `0` is not rewritten to the default)

title: Application-state store: versioned, namespaced, per-context metadata for VTA consumers
body:
## Summary

Applications built on a VTA have nowhere to keep versioned metadata. OpenVTC needs one to make an account recoverable from its Trust Context; this proposes a store rather than a field on an existing one.

**Blocking** the remaining half of OpenVTC recovery: labels, relationships, contacts, join history.

## Why not agent memory

The obvious candidate is `vta/memory/{put,list,delete}/0.1`. It does not fit, for three reasons — the first on its own settles it:

1. **"Forget everything" would delete your account.** Clearing an agent's memory is a reasonable, expected user action. It must not take your community memberships with it.
2. **`list` returns the entire context.** No prefix, no pagination — an agent with a large memory makes every application read expensive, and the two grow independently.
3. **No versioning, and nothing to add it to.** `MemoryItem` is `{key, value}` — no version, no timestamp, no ETag. Two writers overwrite each other and neither can detect it afterwards.

## Why not the existing vaults

- **Secrets vault** (`vault/upsert`) is shaped as a password manager: `secret_kind` of `password`/`passkey`/`oauth-tokens`, required site-oriented `targets`. Application records are not site credentials, and storing them there would pollute a user-facing vault UI.
- **Credential vault** is correct for VCs and OpenVTC already uses it — but application metadata is *about* credentials, not a credential.

Three stores, three jobs: secrets, verifiable credentials, application state.

## Proposed: `spec/vta/appstate/{get,put,list,delete}/1.0`

Addressed by `(contextId, namespace, key)`. The **namespace** scopes an application — `openvtc`, `cnm`, a future agent runtime — so several tools share a context without colliding, and it gives a natural seam for per-namespace ACLs later.

| Property | Behaviour | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | Server-assigned, monotonic per record; returned by `get`, `list`, `put` | The thing that does not exist today |
| `expectedVersion` on `put` | Optional precondition. On mismatch, a typed conflict **carrying the current version and value** | Returning the loser's view with the rejection saves a round trip and removes the re-read race |
| `expectedVersion: 0` | "Create only — fail if it exists" | Makes lease acquisition safe; without it two instances can both believe they won |
| `prefix` + pagination on `list` | Scoped enumeration | Read one record family without dragging every record |
| `sinceVersion` on `list` | Only records changed since a watermark | Makes write-behind reconcile incremental instead of a full pull per connect |
| **Tombstones on delete** | Versioned tombstone, reaped after a retention window | Without it incremental sync **cannot converge** — a peer pulling `sinceVersion` never learns a record was deleted |
| Documented size limit | A stated per-record cap, and an explicit error on exceeding it | OpenVTC has already lost a join to a size limit that dropped a write silently |
| Not for secrets | Stated in the protocol docs | The boundary has to be written down or it erodes |

### Latency, from experience

- **Batch `get_many` / `put_many`**, each write carrying its own `expectedVersion`, with **per-record results**. A rebuild or a write-behind flush becomes one round trip instead of N.
- `put_many` takes an explicit **mode**. `independent` (default) applies each write on its own merits, so one conflicted record does not block the other nine — what a flush of unrelated edits wants. `atomic` is available for records carrying a joint invariant. An atomic default would let one stale record silently wedge an entire flush.
- **`includeValues` on `list`**, so a prefix scan is one call rather than a scan plus N gets.
- **Out-of-band blobs**: a record may carry an attached blob, versioned with it but **never returned by `list`** — only a `blobRef` with size and digest. The `backup_export_via_descriptor` → `download_blob` pattern already in this repo fits exactly, and keeps large payloads outside the trust-task envelope. *Caveat: that path is documented REST-only, and OpenVTC speaks DIDComm.*
- **JSON merge-patch on put** (RFC 7386). Cuts payload, and more usefully cuts *conflicts*: two instances editing different fields of one record stop colliding.

The store should stay **schema-agnostic** — it manipulates generic JSON structure on request but never validates, migrates, or interprets what a record means. A dumb store needs no migration when a consumer's model changes.

## Additive

`vta/memory` is untouched. Agent memory keeps its semantics, including being safe to clear.

## Context

Full design rationale, including what OpenVTC would store and why, is in `docs/design/vta-authoritative-state.md` (E2) in OpenVTC/openvtc. Happy to write this up as a spec in this repo if that is the better home.

title: fix(deps): take the patched h2, and document the line that has no patch
body:
## The advisory

**RUSTSEC-2026-0258** — h2 accepts and queues empty DATA frames without limit.
A peer that never drains can drive unbounded memory growth, or a panic if the
length overflows. Upstream rates it **Low** and patched it in **0.4.16**.

The graph carried two h2 lines. They end differently, and the difference is the
whole PR.

## 0.4.14 → 0.4.16 — fixed

A straight bump to the patched release.

The lockfile moves **exactly one package**. I checked this rather than eyeball
the diff, because the raw diff also shows `windows-sys`, `syn` and `socket2`
lines that look like downgrades — they are dependency-list ordering inside
packages that already had both versions in the graph:

```
REMOVED: ['h2@0.4.14']
ADDED:   ['h2@0.4.16']
```

## 0.3.27 — cannot be fixed here, now an explicit exception

There is no version to move to: **0.3.27 is the newest 0.3**, and upstream
patched only the 0.4 line.

It arrives as `hyper 0.14 → hyper-tls 0.5 → reqwest 0.11 → ssi-dids-core 0.1.3
→ affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk`, reaching **`trust-tasks-tsp`** (via
`affinidi-tsp`) and **`trust-tasks-proof`**. That is the *normal* graph, not a
dev-dependency — crates we publish link it.

Nothing in this repo can shorten that chain:

- our requirements are already open — `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk = "0.8"`,
  `affinidi-tsp = "0.1"`
- every 0.8.x of the resolver SDK **up to and including the newest, 0.8.22**,
  requires `ssi-dids-core ^0.1`
- `ssi-dids-core 0.1` is what pins reqwest 0.11, hence hyper 0.14, hence h2 0.3

I tried bumping the Affinidi crates (0.8.7 → 0.8.13, affinidi-tsp 0.1.6 →
0.1.14). It does not clear the advisory and churns the lockfile substantially,
so it is deliberately **not** in this PR.

### Exposure, stated rather than waved away

`reqwest` is an HTTP **client** here, used to resolve DIDs. Reaching the flaw
needs a hostile or compromised resolution endpoint, and the cost is
availability only — memory growth or a panic, with no confidentiality or
integrity component. That is the entire argument for accepting it, and it is an
argument for accepting it *temporarily*.

### Why this exception is different from the others

Every entry already in `deny.toml`'s ignore list is a **maintenance-status**
notice that says "no active CVE". This is the first that is a real
vulnerability. The comment marks it as such so nobody reads the list as
uniformly harmless, and states the clearing condition: it goes when
`affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` moves to `ssi-dids-core 0.3+`, which is on
reqwest 0.12 / hyper 1.x and so on the patched h2 line. Worth re-checking
whenever the Affinidi crates are bumped.

## Why this is a separate PR

It surfaced on #240, but that PR only adds JSON Schemas and touches neither
`Cargo.lock` nor `Cargo.toml`. The advisory was published after main's last
green run, so **main fails it too** — this is not a regression from #240 and
should not be buried in a spec change.

## Test

- `cargo deny check` — clean across advisories, bans, licenses, sources
- `cargo test --workspace` — **493 passing, 0 failures**

title: spec(vta): an application-state store, versioned and namespaced
body:
Adds `vta/app-state/{get,put,list,delete,get-many,put-many}/1.0` — a third store on the VTA, beside the secrets vault and the credential vault, for versioned, namespaced, per-context JSON that an application owns and the VTA does not interpret.

Input for this is the design note [`docs/05-design-notes/appstate-store.md`](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/blob/main/docs/05-design-notes/appstate-store.md) in `OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`, which is §7 step 1 of the sequence tracked by [#1029](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/issues/1029).

## Why a third store

Records are addressed by `(contextId, namespace, key)`. The namespace scopes one application so several tools can share a context without colliding, and is the seam a per-namespace grant would later use — which is why it is part of the address rather than a prefix convention on the key.

Agent memory (`vta/memory/*`) is the closest existing fit and is the wrong home for three reasons, the first of which settles it on its own:

- **"Forget everything" must stay safe to ask an agent.** It must not take an account's community memberships with it.
- `MemoryItem` is `{key, value}` — no version, nothing to hang a precondition on.
- `list` returns every entry in the context. Application state and agent memory grow independently, so every application read would pay for the agent's memory.

The secrets vault is shaped as a password manager (`secret_kind`, site-oriented `targets`); the credential vault is right for VCs, and application metadata is *about* credentials rather than being one.

## Three properties that make this a store rather than a field

**`version` is a per-`(contextId, namespace)` counter, not per record.** This is the one refinement over the design note, and it is load-bearing. A record's `version` is the counter value its most recent write took, so one number is simultaneously the optimistic-concurrency token `expectedVersion` compares against and the watermark `sinceVersion` compares against. A per-record counter serves the first but cannot serve the second: two records' per-record counters are not comparable to each other, so no single number could mean "everything changed after this point". The cost is that a record's version jumps between writes, which the shared schema states normatively.

**A failed precondition returns the current version *and value*.** A bare rejection obliges the caller to re-read, and between the rejection and the re-read the record can change again — the pattern has no fixed point under contention. Returning the winner's view with the rejection removes the race rather than narrowing it. This is normative, not a courtesy.

**`delete` leaves a versioned tombstone.** Without one, a consumer pulling from a watermark learns of every create and update and never of a deletion, so deleted records resurrect on its next rebuild and it disagrees with peers that saw the delete live. Retrofitting this later silently invalidates every watermark already in the field. Recommended retention is 30 days, and `list` refuses a `sinceVersion` older than the oldest retained tombstone with `watermarkTooOld` rather than serving an incomplete feed.

## Decisions worth review

- **`list` has two modes and the split is explicit.** Without `sinceVersion` it is a key-ordered snapshot; with it, a version-ordered change feed that always includes tombstones. `includeDeleted: false` together with `sinceVersion` is refused as a contradiction rather than honoured — a change feed that omits deletions cannot converge.
- **`highWatermark` on the response** is what a consumer stores, *not* `max(version)` over the returned records, which is wrong whenever a `prefix` filtered a later change out and undefined when the page is empty.
- **`put-many` defaults to `independent`.** An atomic default would let one stale record silently wedge an entire flush, and the caller could not distinguish a wedged flush from a slow one. `atomic` is available and reports per-record outcomes (`skipped` for writes not attempted) through `atomicBatchRejected`.
- **`get-many` accounts for every requested key** in exactly one of `records` / `missing` / `deferred`. `deferred` exists because the per-record cap times the key ceiling exceeds any sane response limit, and the alternative — refusing the whole batch — makes a caller bisect for a workable size.
- **Recommended per-record cap of 65536 bytes**, refused loudly with both `limitBytes` and `actualBytes`. A limit that drops a write silently has already cost a real deployment a lost join.
- **Blobs are deliberately out of scope in 1.0.** Adding a `blobRef` later is additive, and nothing in the first consumer's requirements needs one.
- **Namespaces are collision avoidance, not a trust boundary, in 1.0.** Both `put` and `delete` say so in `## Authorization`: mutually distrusting applications go in separate contexts. The address supports a future per-namespace grant, which is why namespace names should be chosen as though one existed.

## A codegen property this surfaced

A JSON-Schema `default:` is materialised by the codegen into a non-`Option` field with no `skip_serializing_if`, so an example omitting that member can never round-trip — the generated conformance test fails. `vault/list` avoids this only by accident: its request examples sit under `## Examples` rather than the `## Request` heading the codegen harvests from, so only its responses are round-trip tested.

Resolved deliberately here: `put-many.mode` keeps its schema `default` (which mode is the default is the spec's central claim, and a client transmitting it explicitly is correct) and its example states it; the convenience booleans carry their defaults in prose instead, matching what `list.includeDeleted` already did.

Worth a separate look, not fixed here: `checkExampleDocuments()` in `scripts/build-registry.mjs` compiles envelope validators only for `['0.1','0.2','0.3']`, so a `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.4"` document resolves to no validator and is silently skipped. That is currently every 0.4-targeting spec — 16 before this PR. The examples added here were validated against `_framework/0.4/trust-task.schema.json` out of band (56 documents, 0 failures), along with their payloads against their own payload schemas (30 payloads, 0 failures).

## Verification

- `npm run build` — 343 specs validated, 64 shared schemas indexed, no new warnings
- `npm run check-bindings` — 343 specs against 343 TS and 338 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — 450 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo test --workspace` — green

Bindings regenerated; `trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.1 → 0.11.2 and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.12.1 → 0.12.2 (additive, patch per this crate's versioning policy).

title: release: publish the six siblings that now require trust-tasks-rs 0.11
body:
## The bug

#245 and #246 moved the sibling crates' `trust-tasks-rs` requirement to 0.11
**without moving their own versions**. `cargo publish` skips a version already
on crates.io, so none of them republished:

| crate | local | published | requires |
|---|---|---|---|
| trust-tasks-didcomm | 0.9.0 | 0.9.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |
| trust-tasks-https | 0.9.0 | 0.9.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |
| trust-tasks-proof | 0.9.0 | 0.9.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |
| trust-tasks-tsp | 0.9.0 | 0.9.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |
| trust-tasks-capability-client | 0.8.0 | 0.8.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |
| trust-tasks-didcomm-v1 | 0.8.0 | 0.8.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |

main requires 0.11; the registry still serves tarballs built against 0.9.

**That's not cosmetic.** A consumer taking trust-tasks-rs 0.11 together with any
of these gets two semver-incompatible copies of the same types. This is how it
was found — from `vtc-service`, trying to move VTI onto 0.11:

```
error[E0308]: expected `TrustTask<Value>`, found a different `TrustTask<Value>`
```

Minor bumps, because these crates carry `trust_tasks_rs` types in their public
APIs, so a semver-incompatible move of that dependency is breaking for their
consumers.

## The guard I added in #245 should have caught this

It didn't, and the reason matters: it watched `trust-tasks-rs/src/specs` only.
A change that alters **what a crate publishes without touching its source** —
which is exactly what a dependency-requirement bump is — was invisible to it.

It now checks **every publishable workspace member** against any change under
its directory. That's the shape the TDK's equivalent guard has had all along,
and what I should have written the first time. Twice now this guard has been
too narrow; the general form is the correct one.

## Verification

Replayed on the committed tree:


title: spec(vta): withdraw an extended code the framework already names
body:
Follow-up to #252, fixing a defect in the error taxonomy it published. Found while implementing the slice in `OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure` ([#1029](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/issues/1029)) — the implementation could not emit two of the codes the specs declared, which is the useful kind of feedback an implementation gives a spec.

## `vta/app-state:permissionDenied` is withdrawn

It was declared as an **extended** code for a failure [SPEC §8.3](https://trusttasks.org/SPEC.md#83-standard-error-codes) already names as a **standard** one. Two consequences, both worse than the duplication:

- A consumer switching on the standard `permissionDenied` would not match it — exactly the consumer it was meant to serve.
- `TrustTaskCode::Extended` maps to `taskFailed` for status purposes, so emitting the extended form downgrades a 403-shaped refusal into a generic task failure.

A conforming VTA answers an unauthorized caller with the standard code, so the extended one was unreachable in practice as well as wrong in principle.

Note this pattern exists elsewhere in the registry (`vault/list:permissionDenied` and siblings). Not touched here — one slug per PR, per CONTRIBUTING — but worth a sweep if others agree it is the same defect.

## `vta/app-state:contextNotFound` is restated as OPTIONAL

Kept rather than removed: it is a real diagnostic where a maintainer's authorization model can distinguish "no such context" from "not permitted to reach it".

But where the ACL *enumerates* the contexts a caller may act in — the shape the reference VTA uses — a caller can only ever ask about contexts its grant names, so both conditions produce the same answer and the code is never emitted. The previous wording made it a `MUST` such a maintainer cannot satisfy, which is the kind of requirement that gets quietly ignored rather than met. It now reads as a `MAY`, with the standard `permissionDenied` named as the conforming answer to both.

## Scope

No payload, response, or generated-type changes — the declared `errorCodes` and the Conformance prose move, nothing on the wire does. `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` produces no diff under `trust-tasks-rs/src/`, which is the check that this is prose-only.

## Verification

- `npm run build` — 343 specs validated, no new warnings
- `npm run check-bindings` — 343 specs against 343 TS and 338 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — 450 passed, 0 failed

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.2 → 0.11.3 and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.12.2 → 0.12.3.

title: test(approvals): prove a reprovision can be gated on a human, and say what that does not buy
body:
#1030 argues that self-service recovery is already just DTTE: register the
provisioning task URI as consent-requiring and the existing ceremony does the
rest. The argument is sound and had never been run, which is the condition every
bug `delegated_consent_e2e.rs` exists for was found in. So this runs it.
Closes #1030.

## What the test establishes

`provision/integration/0.2` is dispatched and classified `[Mutating Secret
false]`, so the PDP gate sees it and it is not ceremony-exempt. That makes
consent-gating *plausible*; it does not make it work. The new case drives the
whole ceremony over the real router: the reprovision is refused with
`auth:consent_required` and a challenge-salted digest, a VTA-signed
`task-consent/request` is minted for the nominated approver, the approver signs
a decision, and the same payload in a fresh envelope then executes.

The approver deliberately holds **no ACL entry** — approver-set membership alone
authorizes the decision (#907), which is the property that lets a recovery
approver be a device rather than an administrator. Without that, the phone
approving your laptop's recovery would need admin rights over the context, and
the whole arrangement would be worse than the operator it replaces.

## The framing correction

The issue reads as though this delivers recovery for a new install. It does not,
and the gap is worth stating where operators will read it rather than leaving it
to be discovered during one.

Consent is the *policy* gate. It sits behind the bearer/authcrypt gate that
authenticates the caller, so a brand-new install holding no credential cannot
dispatch the task at all — approval rule or not. What the rule buys is recovery
**without an operator**, not recovery **from nothing**: an already-enrolled
device relays the request for the new one, which is exactly the
relayer-is-not-the-holder split provisioning was built around. The docs now say
so, and add the practical consequence — nominate the approver set while you
still have two devices, because a set established at recovery time is not a
recovery mechanism.

## The wire shape, found rather than assumed

The first draft sent `contextId`, the spelling most neighbouring tasks use. The
published `provision/integration/0.2` schema is `additionalProperties: false`
and names it `context`, so the spine refused the document as malformed.

That is the whole reason the refusal assertion checks
`details.reason == "auth:consent_required"` rather than just "the call failed".
A malformed-request rejection satisfies "it was refused" perfectly well, and the
remaining four steps would then have been exercising a ceremony that never
started — a green test proving nothing, which is the failure mode this file's
header is about.

## Also

`sealed-bootstrap.md` said `Status: **Design — not yet implemented**`. It is
implemented, and the stale line cost a reader a wrong assumption in a downstream
design doc, which is what #1030 reported. Corrected against the tree rather than
from memory: `sealed_transfer` plus the `vta`/`pnm bootstrap` surfaces, the
unified `POST /bootstrap/request` with its single-use carve-out and the retired
`GET /attestation/admin-credential`, `keys/wrapping.rs` built on
`sealed_transfer`, and no plaintext bundle encode paths left in `vta-sdk`. The
phase plan is retained as the design record with a note not to read it as
outstanding work.

No production code changes.

title: Allow reprovision to run as a DTTE-consentable task, for self-service recovery
body:
## Summary

Recovering a lost client today needs an operator with `pnm`:

```
new install   pnm bootstrap request --out req.json
operator      pnm context reprovision --id <ctx> --recipient req.json
new install   pnm bootstrap open --bundle <f> --expect-digest <hex>
```

That works, and the out-of-band step is a genuine security boundary — anything that lets an unauthenticated caller re-issue an admin credential means anyone who knows your context id can become you.

But where the user can already prove a **second registered factor**, the human in the loop is not adding security, only friction.

## This is just DTTE

Approvals are already *"one rule list keyed on **Trust Task type URI**"* in the reserved `approvals` policy row; `requires: consent` routes through the PDP to the ceremony — `task-consent/request/0.1`, `task-consent/decision/0.1` (DI-signed by the approver), `task-consent/granted/0.1`. And provisioning is already dispatched: `TASK_PROVISION_INTEGRATION_0_2`.

So the ask collapses to: **register the provisioning task URI as consent-requiring, with a recovery approver set.** Everything else is existing behaviour.

Three properties make it the right fit rather than merely a convenient one:

- **Approver-set membership alone authorizes a decision — an ACL entry is not required** (#907). The phone approving your laptop's recovery need not itself hold admin rights over the context.
- **Consent binds to the payload digest, not a session.** The approver approves *this* reprovision — this context, this recipient key — rather than elevating anything. Delegated step-up was deliberately deleted in favour of exactly this, and for recovery it is the difference between "approve one act" and "grant a capability".
- The approver only ever sees the challenge-salted `wire_digest`.

## Side benefit

`task-consent/decision/0.1` is signed by the approver, so an approved recovery produces a **second independently verifiable artifact** alongside the sealed bundle's `ProducerAssertion` — proof that a human approved, and which one. Better evidence than an audit row, and it needs no change to the audit log.

## Caveats

- Approvals are inert unless `policy.enforcement = true`, which defaults false — so this is opt-in per deployment.
- The `pnm approvals` surface is Trust-Task transport only; the SDK's REST arm is unimplemented and a REST client gets a 404. Fine for DIDComm clients, but a REST-only VTA cannot configure this today.

## Not urgent

Convenience, not capability — the operator path already delivers the recovery story. Worth doing when a second enrolled device is normal, which today it usually is not.

## Also, while here

`sealed-bootstrap.md` still says **"Status: Design — not yet implemented"**. `pnm-cli` implements the whole Mode A flow. That header cost me a wrong assumption in a design doc; worth a one-line fix.

## Context

`docs/design/vta-authoritative-state.md` (E1, D23) in OpenVTC/openvtc. D23 there is the product half: an approver set established *at recovery time* is not a recovery mechanism, so OpenVTC would prompt to nominate one during setup.

title: spec(vta): an application-state store, versioned and namespaced (#252)
body:
spec(vta): an application-state store, versioned and namespaced (#252)

Applications built on a VTA have had nowhere to keep versioned metadata.
Adds `vta/app-state/{get,put,list,delete,get-many,put-many}/1.0` — a third
store beside the secrets vault and the credential vault, for JSON an
application owns and the VTA does not interpret.

Records are addressed by `(contextId, namespace, key)`. The namespace scopes
one application so several tools can share a context without colliding, and
is the seam a per-namespace grant would later use — which is why it is part
of the address rather than a prefix convention on the key.

Three properties are the reason this is a store rather than a field on an
existing one:

- `version` is a monotonic counter maintained per `(contextId, namespace)`,
  not per record. One number is therefore both the optimistic-concurrency
  token `expectedVersion` compares against and the watermark `sinceVersion`
  compares against; a per-record counter serves the first but cannot serve
  the second, because two records' counters are not comparable to each other.
- A failed precondition returns the maintainer's current version *and value*
  with the rejection. A bare rejection obliges a re-read, and the re-read
  races the next write — the pattern has no fixed point under contention.
- `delete` leaves a versioned tombstone. Without one a consumer pulling from
  a watermark learns of every create and update and never of a deletion, so
  deleted records resurrect on its next rebuild. Retrofitting tombstones
  later silently invalidates every watermark already in the field.

Agent memory is untouched and remains safe to clear, which is the settling
argument for not building this on it: "forget everything" is a reasonable
thing to ask an agent and must not take an account's memberships with it.

Blobs are deliberately out of scope in 1.0; adding a `blobRef` is additive.

`put-many` keeps a schema `default` on `mode` because which mode is the
default is the spec's central claim, and the generated clients transmit it
explicitly. The convenience booleans state their defaults in prose instead,
so that an example omitting them round-trips exactly.

Regenerates both bindings and bumps trust-tasks-rs 0.11.1 -> 0.11.2 and
@openvtc/trust-tasks 0.12.1 -> 0.12.2.

title: chore(deps): affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19.10, so a refused socket says why
body:
Floor `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.19.9 → 0.19.10 (affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#718). Manifest note and lockfile only; no code changes.

## Why

Two instances of this app on the same persona reconnect-loop against each other and it presents as a **network fault** rather than as "you have this open twice". The cause is not the mediator's one-socket-per-DID rule — it is that nothing on either side ever said what happened.

- **Server half.** `WebSocketCommands::Close` carried no reason, so the handler answered all three of its senders identically — the `duplicate-channel` problem report and `"replaced by a newer connection"`. That includes a newcomer **refused** by the duel damper, whose own connection was never displaced: the exact inverse of true.
- **Client half.** The sdk's websocket transport matched the close frame as `Message::Close(_)` and discarded it, logging `WebSocket connection closed by server` at debug. So even a correct reason on the wire changed nothing here.

#718 gives `Close` a `CloseReason`, maps each to its own problem-report code and close text, and surfaces the close code and reason at WARN in the sdk.

## Compatibility

`duplicate-channel` is preserved verbatim for the genuinely-replaced case. This repo matches on it only in doc comments and `openvtc-core/tests/didcomm_transport_e2e.rs`, and those are unaffected — hence a floor bump with no code change.

The eviction **policy** is deliberately untouched upstream. Displacement is what triggers the mediator's `spawn_inbox_redelivery`, and this repo is not representative in pulling stored mail explicitly via `message_pickup` — refusing outright would silently drop the stored-mail re-cover for clients that don't.

## Known gap

The mediator half of #718 is `affinidi-messaging-mediator` 0.18.21, and the newest `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` (0.2.52) still embeds 0.18.20. The `#[ignore]`d transport e2e therefore still exercises the old close behaviour until a fixture carrying 0.18.21 publishes; the new reasons reach a live client only against a deployed mediator ≥ 0.18.21.

## Verification

`cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and `cargo test --workspace` all pass locally.

Closes the client-side half of OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1028.

title: feat(audit)!: make the audit destination a deployment choice, not a protocol one
body:
`AuditLogEntry` is `{id, timestamp, action, actor, resource, outcome, channel,
contextId, detail}` — no signature, no hash chain. The log corroborates what
happened; it cannot prove it, and a compromised VTA can rewrite its own history.
The canonical `AuditEnvelope` already names the members that would change that
(`prevHash`, `entryHash`, `schemaVersion`) and records why this maintainer omits
them: its log is flat and unchained.

This does not add tamper-evidence, deliberately. It adds the seam, so an
operator who needs a stronger guarantee implements one — an append-only file, a
transparency log, a blockchain anchor, a hash chain filling in those three
members — without the VTA committing to any scheme. Closes #1031.

## The shape

`vta_audit::AuditSink` takes the whole entry, one method. `KeyspaceAuditSink` is
today's behaviour and **owns the `log:{ts:020}:{uuid}` key format**, because that
format is a property of that backend rather than of the caller — a remote or
anchored sink has no use for a key. `FanOutAuditSink` composes several.

Modelled on `vti_common::telemetry::TelemetrySink`, whose own docs already name
"append-only log, blockchain anchor" as the backends it exists to admit: shared
`Arc` on `AppState`, defaulted through `AppStateParts`, `None` → unchanged
behaviour. The two stay separate for the reason recorded there — telemetry is
high-volume and query-oriented, audit is security-relevant and durable.

## Writes go through the sink; reads and retention do not

`cleanup_expired_logs` and the audit-list query still take a `KeyspaceHandle`,
and `AppState` carries both `audit_ks` and `audit_sink`. This is the design, not
an omission. A sink is free to be write-only and remote, and "delete rows older
than N days" is not an operation an append-only or anchored backend can offer —
the immutability is the point. Retention therefore stays a property of the local
keyspace, which is what the retention API is documented to govern.

The consequence is that swapping the sink outright would take `GET /audit/logs`
and the retention sweep with it. `FanOutAuditSink` is the answer: keep the
keyspace sink, add the new backend beside it. Every sink is attempted and the
first error returned only after all of them have run — short-circuiting would let
a failing sink hide an entry from the ones behind it, which for an audit log is
the failure mode that matters.

## The sweepers get the same sink object

Built once in `run()` and handed to both `AppStateParts` and the storage thread,
rather than reconstructed there. A sweeper's `acl.expire` is an unattended
removal — nobody was watching when the entry vanished — which makes it precisely
the row an operator installs a tamper-evident backend to capture. Rebuilding a
sink on the storage thread would have routed it back to the keyspace whatever
they configured, and the gap would surface only when someone went looking for a
deletion that was never recorded. `VtaState` clones the same `Arc` for the same
reason it shares the config `RwLock` (P1.1): two transports resolving audit
differently is a gap you find during an incident.

## Tests

Three unit tests on the sink module, five integration tests in
`vta-service/tests/audit_sink.rs`. The load-bearing one asserts **both** halves —
the installed sink receives the row *and the keyspace does not*. Without the
second assertion it would pass on a sink that merely observes alongside an
unchanged keyspace write, which delivers none of the property this exists for.
The others pin the default (no sink installed → the keyspace, exactly as
before), the sweeper path, the shared `Arc` across transports, and the fan-out
composition keeping the query API alive.

`storage_key` is pinned separately: the retention sweep stops at the first key
past its cutoff and the list query is a prefix scan, so both are correct only
while the key sorts by time *as a string* — which is what the zero-padding buys.

## Breaking

`vta_audit::{record, record_with_detail, record_consent}` take a
`&SharedAuditSink` where they took a `&KeyspaceHandle`. The alternative — keeping
the old signature and adding a parallel sink-taking one — would leave a second
way to write an audit row that bypasses the sink entirely, and a
tamper-evidence backend with a bypass is not one.

Mechanically this moved ~57 call sites across 24 files and a dozen `Deps`
structs, because the audit keyspace was threaded by hand everywhere rather than
carried once. `vta_keyspaces::Keyspaces.audit` is deliberately untouched: that
bundle's audit handle is a keyspace because backup export dumps it.

title: Mediator should protect the established connection, not evict it for a newcomer
body:
## Summary

The mediator's ceiling is **one websocket per DID**, and it enforces that by **evicting the established connection** in favour of the newcomer. That is backwards.

The incumbent is authenticated, live, and possibly mid-exchange. The newcomer has proved only that it can *also* authenticate. Preferring the newcomer means any second process silently takes over a live session — and when both retry, they take turns doing it, forever.

## This is a live bug, not a hypothetical

Two OpenVTC instances presenting the same persona reconnect-loop indefinitely, and it presents as a **network fault** rather than as "you have this open twice". It is the listener-flapping class already debugged in OpenVTC/openvtc#231 and the upstream affinidi-tdk-rs `force_refresh` fix.

Anyone who opens the app twice hits it today.

## Requested

An established, authenticated connection for a DID is **kept**. A second attempt is **refused**, with a reason the client can render — "this DID already has a live connection" — so the newcomer can say so instead of looping.

## The carve-out is probably unnecessary

Displacing a socket is currently how stored-mail redelivery gets triggered (OpenVTC/openvtc#218), so the obvious worry is that refusing would regress it.

Checked, and it does not for OpenVTC: it already collects stored mail explicitly through the standard message-pickup protocol (`affinidi_messaging_sdk::protocols::message_pickup`, via `Messaging::pickup_stored`). Redelivery does not need eviction, because there is a pull for it.

**Worth confirming across other clients before removing it** — the check is "does anything actually depend on connect-time displacement", not "assume nothing does". If OpenVTC is representative, the rule can simply be that the incumbent wins, with no opt-in displacement flag needed at all.

## Context

Raised from OpenVTC's side while building multi-instance detection (OpenVTC/openvtc#246). OpenVTC now registers as a device and heartbeats, so it can *tell* the user another instance is live — but detection is a workaround for the eviction behaviour, not a fix. Design notes in `docs/design/vta-authoritative-state.md` (E3) in that repo.

title: Pluggable audit sink, so tamper-evidence can be a deployment choice
body:
## Summary

`AuditLogEntry` is `{id, timestamp, action, actor, resource, outcome, channel, contextId, detail}` — **no signature, no hash chain**. The log corroborates what happened; it cannot prove it. A compromised VTA can rewrite its own history.

This issue deliberately **does not ask for tamper-evidence in the protocol**. The more useful move is an extension point.

## Requested

An audit sink trait the VTA writes through, with today's database sink as one implementation. An operator who needs stronger guarantees can then add one — an append-only log, a transparency log, a blockchain anchor — without the VTA committing to any particular scheme.

That keeps the crypto decision out of the protocol and turns "make the audit tamper-evident" from a design argument into a deployment choice.

## Why it is not urgent

For the case that matters most — proving a *recovery* was authorised — the evidence already exists elsewhere and is signed: the sealed bundle opened during bootstrap carries a `ProducerAssertion` (`AssertionProof::DidSigned`, or an attestation quote for a TEE VTA), which is independently verifiable. OpenVTC intends to retain that as a recovery receipt.

So the property is obtainable today where it counts. This is about making the log itself evidence rather than testimony, for everything else it records.

## Context

`docs/design/vta-authoritative-state.md` (E4, D20) in OpenVTC/openvtc.

feat(audit)!: make the audit destination a deployment choice, not a protocol one (#1049)

`AuditLogEntry` is `{id, timestamp, action, actor, resource, outcome, channel,
contextId, detail}` — no signature, no hash chain. The log corroborates what
happened; it cannot prove it, and a compromised VTA can rewrite its own history.
The canonical `AuditEnvelope` already names the members that would change that
(`prevHash`, `entryHash`, `schemaVersion`) and records why this maintainer omits
them: its log is flat and unchained.

This does not add tamper-evidence, deliberately. It adds the seam, so an
operator who needs a stronger guarantee implements one — an append-only file, a
transparency log, a blockchain anchor, a hash chain filling in those three
members — without the VTA committing to any scheme. Closes #1031.

## The shape

`vta_audit::AuditSink` takes the whole entry, one method. `KeyspaceAuditSink` is
today's behaviour and **owns the `log:{ts:020}:{uuid}` key format**, because that
format is a property of that backend rather than of the caller — a remote or
anchored sink has no use for a key. `FanOutAuditSink` composes several.

Modelled on `vti_common::telemetry::TelemetrySink`, whose own docs already name
"append-only log, blockchain anchor" as the backends it exists to admit: shared
`Arc` on `AppState`, defaulted through `AppStateParts`, `None` → unchanged
behaviour. The two stay separate for the reason recorded there — telemetry is
high-volume and query-oriented, audit is security-relevant and durable.

## Writes go through the sink; reads and retention do not

`cleanup_expired_logs` and the audit-list query still take a `KeyspaceHandle`,
and `AppState` carries both `audit_ks` and `audit_sink`. This is the design, not
an omission. A sink is free to be write-only and remote, and "delete rows older
than N days" is not an operation an append-only or anchored backend can offer —
the immutability is the point. Retention therefore stays a property of the local
keyspace, which is what the retention API is documented to govern.

The consequence is that swapping the sink outright would take `GET /audit/logs`
and the retention sweep with it. `FanOutAuditSink` is the answer: keep the
keyspace sink, add the new backend beside it. Every sink is attempted and the
first error returned only after all of them have run — short-circuiting would let
a failing sink hide an entry from the ones behind it, which for an audit log is
the failure mode that matters.

## The sweepers get the same sink object

Built once in `run()` and handed to both `AppStateParts` and the storage thread,
rather than reconstructed there. A sweeper's `acl.expire` is an unattended
removal — nobody was watching when the entry vanished — which makes it precisely
the row an operator installs a tamper-evident backend to capture. Rebuilding a
sink on the storage thread would have routed it back to the keyspace whatever
they configured, and the gap would surface only when someone went looking for a
deletion that was never recorded. `VtaState` clones the same `Arc` for the same
reason it shares the config `RwLock` (P1.1): two transports resolving audit
differently is a gap you find during an incident.

## Tests

Three unit tests on the sink module, five integration tests in
`vta-service/tests/audit_sink.rs`. The load-bearing one asserts **both** halves —
the installed sink receives the row *and the keyspace does not*. Without the
second assertion it would pass on a sink that merely observes alongside an
unchanged keyspace write, which delivers none of the property this exists for.
The others pin the default (no sink installed → the keyspace, exactly as
before), the sweeper path, the shared `Arc` across transports, and the fan-out
composition keeping the query API alive.

`storage_key` is pinned separately: the retention sweep stops at the first key
past its cutoff and the list query is a prefix scan, so both are correct only
while the key sorts by time *as a string* — which is what the zero-padding buys.

## Breaking

`vta_audit::{record, record_with_detail, record_consent}` take a
`&SharedAuditSink` where they took a `&KeyspaceHandle`. The alternative — keeping
the old signature and adding a parallel sink-taking one — would leave a second
way to write an audit row that bypasses the sink entirely, and a
tamper-evidence backend with a bypass is not one.

Mechanically this moved ~57 call sites across 24 files and a dozen `Deps`
structs, because the audit keyspace was threaded by hand everywhere rather than
carried once. `vta_keyspaces::Keyspaces.audit` is deliberately untouched: that
bundle's audit handle is a keyspace because backup export dumps it.

title: chore(deps): affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19.10, so a refused socket says why (#253)
body:
chore(deps): affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19.10, so a refused socket says why (#253)

The transport matched the server's close frame as `Message::Close(_)` and threw
it away — `debug!("WebSocket connection closed by server")` — so every close
looked identical from here: the socket vanished and the reconnect loop went
again. Two instances of this app on one persona therefore duelled, and the user
was shown a transport error rather than "you have this open twice".

The mediator half was also lying. `WebSocketCommands::Close` carried no reason,
so all three of its senders got the same `duplicate-channel` problem report and
the same "replaced by a newer connection" close text — including a newcomer
*refused* by the duel damper, whose own connection was never displaced. That is
the inverse of what happened to it.

affinidi-tdk-rs #718 gives `Close` a reason, maps each to its own problem-report
code, and surfaces the close code and reason at WARN in the sdk.
`duplicate-channel` is preserved verbatim for the genuinely-replaced case, so
the places this repo matches on it are unaffected and no code change is needed
here — the floor and the manifest note are the change.

The eviction policy is deliberately untouched upstream: displacement is what
triggers the mediator's stored-mail redelivery, and this repo is not
representative in pulling explicitly via `message_pickup`. Raised from this side
as OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1028.

Not yet observable in the e2e fixture: the mediator half is 0.18.21, and the
newest `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` (0.2.52) still embeds 0.18.20. The
`#[ignore]`d transport e2e keeps asserting the old behaviour until a fixture
carrying 0.18.21 publishes.

fmt, clippy -D warnings, and `cargo test --workspace` pass.
